articles.title: Ukraine drone attack kills two in Crimea as Kyiv targets bridge to Russia
articles.excerpt: A Ukrainian drone attack has killed at least two people in Russian-annexed Crimea as Kyiv has targeted the only bridge connecting southern Russia to the Black Sea peninsula for the second consecutive ...
articles.body_text:
A Ukrainian drone attack has killed at least two people in Russian-annexed Crimea as Kyiv has targeted the only bridge connecting southern Russia to the Black Sea peninsula for the second consecutive day, according to the Moscow-installed governor.

In a Telegram post, Sergei Aksyonov said traffic has been suspended after Tuesday’s attack on the Kerch Bridge.

Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelenskyy confirmed the “unprecedented” attack, publishing footage on social media on Tuesday that showed the main arch of the bridge for cars and part of its roadway collapsed.

He said the targeting came in response to Russian strikes on Ukraine’s infrastructure.

The bridge in the Kerch Strait, which connects the Black Sea and the Sea of Azov, stretches for 19km (11.8 miles) and is also used by trains.

Reporting from Moscow, Al Jazeera’s Yulia Shapovalova said Russia came under one of the largest Ukrainian drone attacks on Monday night.

“According to official data from the Ministry of Defence, Russian air defence systems destroyed more than 1,400 drones over 23 regions, including border regions and regions in central Russia. Meanwhile, the mayor of Moscow said that more than 800 drones flew towards the capital,” Shapovalova reported.

Also on Tuesday, Moscow attacked two bridges in Kyiv, Russia’s Ministry of Defence said.

Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said in a Telegram post that ⁠the Northern and ⁠Southern bridges had been hit and the subway ⁠system ⁠had also been damaged. He added that water and power supplies had been ‌partially cut.

The Russian Defence Ministry said it also targeted Ukraine’s military infrastructure in attacks on Monday night, including facilities used to produce cruise missiles and long‑ and medium‑range drones. The ministry said transport and energy facilities were also targeted as well as port infrastructure and ships used by the Ukrainian military.

Al Jazeera’s Audrey MacAlpine said the first of a “series of very loud explosions” rang out in Kyiv just before midnight.

“Another round of explosions was heard just after 5am [03:00 GMT] this morning,” she said.

“Some bridges were damaged. We understand that they are still standing, but there is no traffic on either of them. These are bridges that are used every day by civilians to commute around the city. These attacks also cut heating to hundreds of apartment buildings on Kyiv’s Left Bank.”

The exchange of attacks comes just days before a meeting of Presidents Vladimir Putin of Russia, Xi Jinping of China and Donald Trump of the United States in China’s Shenzhen region.

The Chinese Ministry of Foreign Affairs said Thursday’s talks will focus on topics of “groundbreaking significance”, including “safeguarding world peace”.

Trump has made securing an end to the war between Russia and Ukraine a key part of his presidency. Despite another round of talks held in the United Arab Emirates last week, US mediators have failed to make a breakthrough.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy had warned that Kyiv would carry out attacks on Russia in the days before the meeting.

articles.title: Japan sends up jets after alleged Russian incursion of its airspace
articles.excerpt:
Japan's Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said the flight paths of the Russian aircraft were "completely unacceptable"

Japan says it launched fighter jets and "strongly" protested after two suspe...
articles.body_text:
Japan's Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said the flight paths of the Russian aircraft were "completely unacceptable"

Japan says it launched fighter jets and "strongly" protested after two suspected Russian aircraft violated its airspace early on Tuesday.

South Korea also says it deployed fighter jets, while Taiwan says it "responded" to Russian military aircraft detected in their respective air defence identification zones.

These are unofficial buffer areas beyond territorial airspace where governments identify approaching aircraft for security purposes. Moscow has yet to comment.

The alleged incursions are a reminder of Russia's military power ahead of the Apec economic summit in China this week, which Vladimir Putin will attend alongside US President Donald Trump.

Japan's Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara said the flight paths of the Russian aircraft, off the south-western Okinoshima island, were a "serious infringement of Japan's sovereignty" and "completely unacceptable".

The last such incursion was in 2024, when a Russian military patrol plane entered Japanese airspace off Rebun island, Hokkaido.

Taiwan says its military "responded accordingly" after two Russian military aircraft entered its air defence identification zone, also on Tuesday.

South Korea says it sent up jets after an unspecified number of Russian military aircraft entered its air defence identification zone over the Sea of Japan. The aircraft departed without violating South Korean airspace, authorities said.

It is unclear if the three neighbours were responding to the same or different aircraft.

The East China Sea contains self-declared, overlapping air defence identification zones between China, Taiwan, Japan and South Korea.

Foreign military aircraft are expected, but not legally required, to notify governments before entering such air defence identification zones.

Tensions are flaring between Japan and Russia, which are locked in a decades-old territorial dispute over a cluster of islands in the Pacific Ocean.

For months, Moscow has been ratcheting up the pressure on Tokyo.

In August, Putin paid his first visit to one of these islands, prompting sharp rebuke from Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi. In October, Russia detained a Japanese journalist on spying allegations.

articles.title: Bahrain thwarts drone attack; Iran claims targeting US radar
articles.excerpt: Bahraini air defence has thwarted a drone attack, according to the Gulf country’s state television, after Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) launched a barrage of unmanned aerial vehicles...
articles.body_text:
Bahraini air defence has thwarted a drone attack, according to the Gulf country’s state television, after Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) launched a barrage of unmanned aerial vehicles (UAVs).

The IRGC said on Tuesday that it carried out a drone attack on a US radar system at the Isa airbase in Bahrain.

The reported attacks in Bahrain – home to the US Navy’s Fifth Fleet – come amid stalled diplomatic efforts to end the US-Israel war ⁠on Iran, which began ⁠on February 28 and has affected the entire Gulf region and beyond.

It is the latest of several Iran-claimed attacks on US radar systems in Bahrain in recent days.

The IRGC said the attack was “part of efforts to counter the hostile activities of US forces in the region”, according to a statement carried by Iran’s state broadcaster IRIB.

Blasts echoed over the Bahraini capital, Manama, after residents received a mobile phone alert warning of a “potential threat”. Explosions were heard after the Ministry of Interior’s alert urged residents to “proceed to the nearest safe location”. It later issued an “all clear” message.

In a statement, the ministry said “precautionary measures remain in place” and urged the public to exercise caution.

On Sunday, the IRGC launched six drones at a US air defence radar system at Bahrain’s Riffa airbase, which hosts US forces, in response to what it described as hostile US actions.

On Friday, the IRGC also claimed to have targeted a US early-warning radar system in Bahrain, but the US military denied that the facility had been hit, saying it intercepted two Iranian drones without damage or casualties.

“Since Friday, it seems that the rules of engagement have changed,” said Al Jazeera’s Resul Serdar, reporting from Tehran, stating that a pattern has emerged, with Iran now trying to restore deterrence.

“First, Iran warned that if the US escorts ships carrying oil that do not coordinate with Iran [through the Strait of Hormuz], then Tehran would attack US military installations. Now, Iran is saying its attack on a US radar system in Bahrain is because of the US’s continued violations of Iranian airspace.

It is not a response to a specific US attack, but rather the continued violation of its airspace.”

Bahrain has faced renewed security concerns amid escalating tensions between Washington and Tehran.

articles.title: Ukraine accuses Russia of targeting rescue operation after 'double-tap' strike kills 72
articles.excerpt:
Ukrainian officials have accused Russia of targeting rescue and recovery operations two weeks after a deadly "double-tap" strike at a village close to the front line killed at least 72 people.

Ukrain...
articles.body_text:
Ukrainian officials have accused Russia of targeting rescue and recovery operations two weeks after a deadly "double-tap" strike at a village close to the front line killed at least 72 people.

Ukraine says Russia carried out two attacks in succession on a humanitarian aid centre in the village of Komyshuvakha on 2 November - including the use of what it said was a 3,000kg (6,600lb) aerial bomb on a shelter where residents had fled for safety.

Verified images posted in the days after the attack show damage to emergency vehicles and excavation equipment at the site.

The State Emergency Service of Ukraine (DSNS) told BBC Verify there were multiple Russian strikes during the rescue.

The DSNS said three police officers, four workers and two rescue dogs were injured while five vehicles were damaged during the operation, which has now concluded.

With the DSNS saying the death toll had risen to at least 72 people, the attack on Komyshuvakha has become the second deadliest single incident of the Ukraine war.

Emergency service vehicles have also been targeted

Oleksiy, an intelligence officer investigating the incident for Ukraine's SBU security service, who asked to be identified only by his first name, said rescue vehicles were "clearly marked" and accused Russia of "deliberately destroying humanitarian equipment".

He added the village's infrastructure and the people still living in Komyshuvakha are also being systematically targeted by drones and bombs. Oleksiy accused Russian forces of "outright terror against civilians, against peaceful residents" to make life on the front line impossible.

BBC Verify has confirmed videos being shared by Ukrainian police that show rescue workers at the scene shouting "drone, drone" and running for cover on the day after the 2 November attack. A group can also be seen treating a victim.

Oleksiy said rescue crews operated under a constant threat of attack. "The enemy knows perfectly well that what is being carried out there is essentially a humanitarian operation to search for the dead," he said.

BBC Verify has asked the Russian Ministry of Defence for comment specifically about the Komyshuvakha attacks but has not received a response.

A general statement released on 2 November by the Russian MoD said it had targeted energy and transport infrastructure used by the Ukrainian military across the country.

While there are no military or industrial facilities in Komyshuvakha it is close to a key route used for Ukrainian troop movements, supplies and evacuations. The village was previously reported to have been struck by the Russians on 28 October.

Local people headed to the shelter area on 2 November after being told by a local Telegram group that aid would be distributed between 10:00 and 12:00 local time (08:00-10:00 GMT). Ukrainian authorities said an initial strike, at 09:45 local time, hit buildings above ground killing one woman.

Video shows moments between deadly Russian attacks on village in Ukraine

Bodycam footage, released by Ukrainian police in edited segments and analysed by BBC Verify, shows people trying to free a casualty from the rubble before declaring she had died.

Throughout the footage, warnings of an impending second strike can be heard on police radios with increasing urgency until people are instructed to run to the underground shelter.

The same footage, which was taken around an hour after the first attack, goes on to show people in a shelter. As they wait in silence a large explosion can be heard and the video goes dark.

Aftermath video filmed later shows bodies being recovered from a large crater immediately above the shelter. Twisted iron and rubble from the structure below can be seen beneath the surface.

Funerals have been held almost daily for the victims of the attack, including locals working to administer aid distribution, those seeking to collect it and soldiers who officials say arrived to assist with rescue efforts.

Trevor Ball, bomb disposal expert at intelligence firm at Armament Research Services, said a crater seen in the footage was consistent with the damage and depth left by a FAB-3000, a 3,000kg Russian bomb which can destroy underground structures.

His comments were echoed by Chris Proops, an ex-UK National Crime Agency investigator, who said the scale of the damage at the scene matched the size of the FAB-3000.

The remnants of the wing from a glide bomb guidance kit

Ball and Proops both confirmed verified photos of munition fragments obtained by BBC Verify from Ukrainian authorities show part of a guidance kit that is compatible with the FAB-3000, which increases the weapon's accuracy and allows it to be fired from a greater distance from the target.

International law experts told BBC Verify that Russia had committed a war crime if it knowingly attacked rescue workers.

Ben Saul, professor of international law at the University of Sydney, said this "appears to be either a deliberate attack on civilians or civilian objects - a war crime - or an indiscriminate attack - also a war crime".

Prof Samuel Moyn of Yale University said "directly targeting rescuers or their equipment is a gross violation of international humanitarian law". Precautions have to be taken to ensure that strikes target combatants rather than others, he added.

Additional reporting by Margaryta Maliukova, BBC Monitoring

What do you want BBC Verify to investigate?

articles.title: Stories of survival and pain: Children amid Israel’s war on south Lebanon
articles.excerpt: Kfar Reman, Lebanon – It was the morning of September 7 when we arrived at the site of an Israeli attack in the village of Kfar Reman in southern Lebanon. Bulldozers were digging through the rubble of...
articles.body_text:
Kfar Reman, Lebanon – It was the morning of September 7 when we arrived at the site of an Israeli attack in the village of Kfar Reman in southern Lebanon. Bulldozers were digging through the rubble of a home destroyed in an overnight air strike, searching for the bodies of two children.

Ten members of the same family, spanning three generations, had already been found in the building’s collapsed rooms, among them two survivors.

Two months later, I met 10-year-old Zainab and her eight-year-old brother Mustafa. After losing their parents and elder sister, Fatima, and their one-month-old brother, Ahmed, they now live with their grandmother. Both were thrown out of the house due to the intensity of the blast, but their physical wounds were no longer visible.

Zainab had a constant smile, but she was hiding sadness which she did not know how to express in words.

Mustafa was different. There was no smile. He is angry at Israel. When I asked him to share his story or a message to the world instead of speaking to me, he looked straight at the camera.

“What they did is they took my home and my parents from me,” Mustafa said. He paused for a few seconds and continued, “Because of them I no longer live in peace.”

More than a thousand children were injured in Israeli attacks between March and August this year, according to the United Nations.

Some lost a parent or both their parents while more than 260 were killed. That figure represents an average of seven children killed or injured every day over those six months – nearly double the number at the start of the latest on-again, off-again conflict between Hezbollah and Israel in late 2023.

We have repeatedly filmed children’s clothes, toys and school books among the rubble of homes destroyed in Israeli strikes, and repeatedly attended funerals of children killed alongside their parents. It is just as difficult emotionally to talk to survivors who show signs of trauma and tell us they live in fear.

In the village of Tibnine, close to the northern edge of the area occupied by the Israeli army, 11-year-old Bannine took us to the second floor of an orphanage, to show us what a nearby Israeli air strike did to their rooms.

“We were not here when this happened,” Bannine told us in a room full of debris and broken glass. Stuffed animals and clothes were still scattered on the floor.

Hundreds of thousands of people returned to their villages in southern Lebanon because of a reduction in violence in recent months. But there is little sense of security, with Israeli strikes and home demolitions continuing in front line areas.

“We wake up and sleep to the sound of bombing and warplanes and irritating drones,” Anaya Sultan told us. Her father was killed when the Israeli military escalated the conflict earlier this year. “He was my soul … he was everything to me,” she added.

Some of the girls here are not orphans, but their parents are too poor to care for them. According to Lebanese officials, the region’s economy is in a state of collapse.

Recurring conflicts, ruined infrastructure, blocked access to agricultural land, and mass displacement are making it hard for families in southern Lebanon to sustain themselves.

The UN identified southern Lebanon – alongside impoverished northern and eastern regions such as Akkar and Baalbek – as areas of greatest concern where families are struggling to survive.

According to a joint report released by the UN Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO), the World Food Programme (WFP), and Lebanon’s Ministry of Agriculture, more than 1 million people in Lebanon – about 21 percent of the recorded population – are facing crisis levels of acute food insecurity.

“Unfortunately, so many people are displaced … many of them used to support and help us. They are not present and they themselves are struggling,” Bassima Fawaz, who helps manage the orphanage, told us as we walked through the cold hallways and rooms of the building.

“We had to cover the windows with plastic sheeting because there’s no money to replace the glass shattered by Israeli bombardment. One of our girls is in hospital with pneumonia.”

articles.title: Bangladesh police clash with garment workers amid protests over wages
articles.excerpt:
Bangladeshi police have fired tear gas and stun grenades at thousands of garment workers protesting after a key wage board meeting was postponed.

Protesters on Tuesday hurled bricks, torched vehicles...
articles.body_text:
Bangladeshi police have fired tear gas and stun grenades at thousands of garment workers protesting after a key wage board meeting was postponed.

Protesters on Tuesday hurled bricks, torched vehicles and blocked the main highway between the capital, Dhaka, and the key financial district of Mymensingh.

Bangladesh is the world’s second-biggest garment exporter behind China, producing clothes for big international brands, including Fruit of the Loom and Levi Strauss.

But growing worker unrest over wages, which began last month, has disrupted the industry that generates $38bn annually and employs more than four million people.

Workers are demanding a minimum monthly wage of 30,000 taka ($240) – a 140-percent increase on the current 12,500 taka, as they struggle to cope with rising food, housing, transport and healthcare costs.

About 500 of the country’s 4,500 garment factories are shut, sources told the AFP news agency, further stoking unrest among workers.

A “no work, no pay” provision in the country’s labour laws allows factory owners to suspend operations and withhold wages when production is disrupted.

“The owners seem unwilling to meet our salary demands. They are already dragging their feet,” one worker, Khanom, 24, told AFP.

Tensions were also running high in the garment hubs of Savar and Ashulia on Dhaka’s outskirts.

The wage board, comprising representatives of employers and workers, was set up by the government earlier this month to negotiate a pay rise.

The new minimum wage would be announced in December and take effect in January next year.

“We want to return to our machines,” garment worker Rakib, 28, told AFP.

“We are not sure if the wage board members are aware of our demands,” he said, adding that workers feared their concerns might not be reflected in the revised wage proposal.

Most factories had opened on Tuesday morning, but were shut down as protests spread to the highway, Rakib said.

In a joint statement, the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) and the Bangladesh Knitwear Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BKMEA) called for a resumption of wage negotiations as soon as possible.

A wage board meeting scheduled for Monday was postponed after a member representing the garment workers said he was unwell, a BGMEA source told AFP.

The next meeting would be held on November 23, the board said.

In the wake of Tuesday’s protest, Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) stepped up patrols across the industrial zone, deploying hundreds of personnel.

“BGB headquarters has been closely observing the situation from a monitoring cell,” it said in a statement.

The force said it was also using drones, body-worn cameras and other devices to keep a close watch on demonstrations.

articles.title: State Department presses Egypt to respect religious freedom as Christian convert faces possible execution
articles.excerpt:
Grace Drexel says her father, Pastor Ezra Jin, remains imprisoned for leading one of China’s largest independent churches.

The State Department has intensified its efforts to compel the majority Musl...
articles.body_text:
Grace Drexel says her father, Pastor Ezra Jin, remains imprisoned for leading one of China’s largest independent churches.

The State Department has intensified its efforts to compel the majority Muslim state of Egypt to honor the religious liberty protections for an Egyptian who converted to Christianity and is facing either the death penalty or a lengthy prison term.

The prosecution of Said Mansour Rezk Abdelrazek has catapulted his case and has attracted publicity within the U.S., Britain and across the global Christian community. Egypt receives $1.3 billion in annual funding from the U.S.

In July, Fox News Digital reported on Abdelrazek’s trial for his embrace of Christianity in 2016.

TRUMP DOJ EXPANDS RELIGIOUS LIBERTY PROTECTIONS AFTER MAJOR SUPREME COURT RULINGS

Said Mansour Rezk Abdelrazek could face a death sentence or some twenty years in jail. (Fox News)

A State Department spokesperson told Fox News Digital that, "We are monitoring his trial closely. Religious freedom is a fundamental human value and we encourage the Egyptian government to protect the religious freedom rights of all its citizens."

The situation for Abdelrazek has become dire, according to his attorney and human rights advocates for Coptic Christians in Egypt. He faces execution or a 25-year prison sentence for his conversion to Christianity, according to the office of his lawyer, Said Fayez.

Fayez’s office said that in early November the "Public Prosecution presented its closing arguments and requested that the maximum penalty prescribed by law be imposed upon him."

PAKISTAN’S TOP COURT UPHOLDS CHRISTIAN MAN’S DEATH SENTENCE FOR BLASPHEMY

File picture showing Egyptian Coptic Christians attending the Resurrection Mass at the Monastery of Saint Simon Al-Kharaz during Holy Saturday services on April 19, 2025 in Cairo, Egypt.  (Ahmad Hasaballah/Getty Images)

Fox News Digital reached out multiple times to Egypt’s Embassy in Washington D.C. and its Foreign Ministry for a comment. According to Amnesty International, in "July 2025, security officers arrested Egyptian national and Christian convert Said Abdelrazek from his home in Cairo. After nine months of arbitrary pretrial detention, Said Abdelrazek was referred to trial before the Terrorism Circuit of the First Criminal Court in Badr on charges stemming from his conversion and religious beliefs."

Coptic Solidarity reported he faces charges that include contempt for Islam, and inciting unrest and spreading false information.

Abdelrazek’s fiancée Sophia, an Australian-Egyptian citizen, has been energetically campaigning to secure his freedom. She told Fox News Digital that she is "pleading for them to release him." She declined to use her last name because of "some extreme threats" against her.

Lindsay Rodriguez, a spokeswoman for Coptic Solidarity, told Fox News Digital that "Coptic Solidarity is deeply concerned that Egyptian prosecutors are seeking the maximum penalty against Said Abdelrazek, a Christian convert whose case has become an important test of religious freedom and judicial impartiality in Egypt."

She continued that he "has been detained since July 2025 and is being prosecuted before a terrorism court, primarily on an allegation of joining a banned terrorist organization, as well as charges of contempt for Islam, inciting unrest and spreading false information. These remain prosecution allegations, not findings of guilt. His defense will present its closing arguments on Dec. 8. Reported religious remarks attributed to the judge during the Nov. 3 hearing further heighten concerns about whether a Christian convert can receive a genuinely impartial hearing."

His supporters say the prosecution has yet to name the terrorist organization in question while noting there is no known terrorist group associated with Christians listed in Egypt.

This picture taken on Nov. 1, 2022 shows a view of the United Kingdom embassy headquarters (L) and the United States embassy (R background) headquarters in the Garden City district of Egypt's capital Cairo. (Amir Makar / AFP via Getty Images.)

Rodriguez added that "Peaceful religious conversion and expression must not be treated as terrorism or national-security offenses. The United States, European Union and Australia should use the Dec. 8 hearing as a clear test of Egypt's willingness to uphold basic religious-freedom and fair-trial standards."

Rodriguez said, "The U.S. Embassy in Cairo, EU Delegation, and Member State embassies should seek access to monitor the hearing and raise Said's case directly with Egyptian authorities. Members of Congress and the European Parliament should publicly demonstrate that they are following the case. Australia also has a particular responsibility: Said's fiancée is an Australian citizen, and DFAT [ Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade] should press his case while Home Affairs ensures a viable humanitarian pathway for reunification upon his release."

The Egyptian Christian community makes up an estimated 10% of the nation’s 120 million people.

Benjamin Weinthal reports on Israel, Iran, Syria, Turkey and Europe. You can follow Benjamin on Twitter @BenWeinthal, and email him at benjamin.weinthal@fox.com

articles.title: Hundreds arrested in anti-Trump protests in Philippines amid anger over Iran war and AI pact
articles.excerpt:
Organisers say up to 10,000 people could join next round of demonstrations as US president arrives for Asean summit

Hundreds of people have been arrested in heated demonstrations against Donald Trump...
articles.body_text:
Organisers say up to 10,000 people could join next round of demonstrations as US president arrives for Asean summit

Hundreds of people have been arrested in heated demonstrations against Donald Trump in Manila, as the US president arrived in the city for a leaders’ summit.

Organisers claimed as many as 10,000 people would be joining protests against Trump in the capital of the Philippines on Tuesday, where he is attending the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) summit. The crowds were expected to try to march to the summit site.

Authorities have arrested nearly 300 people in widespread protests in held in the days leading up to the summit, with large parts of the capital closed off and tight security in place.

Some burned effigies of Trump and faced off with police officers armed with batons and shields. Slogans on placards called the American leader the world’s “No 1 terrorist” in protests held on Monday.

Demonstrators angry at the cost of living and energy shock caused by the Iran war, and the new US-led Pax Silica initiative on AI and critical minerals, tried to reach the summit at the Philippine International Convention Center on Monday, but were blocked by police.

Pax Silica has sparked tensions in the Philippines over plans to build a tech hub outside Manila that critics say will affect water and energy supplies, and displace members of the Ayta Indigenous community.

Large sections of central Manila were closed to the public as part of the security cordon and public holidays put in place for the Asean summit.

After departing from Fairbanks in Alaska, Trump emerged from Air Force One at Ninoy Aquino International airport at 5.54pm local time (0954 GMT), live video showed.

Trump will meet with the leaders of Australia, Japan and India on Tuesday night before heading to Shenzhen in China on Wednesday. There he will attend the Asia Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit and hold trilateral talks with China’s president, Xi Jinping, and Vladimir Putin of Russia.

The backlash against Trump follows the ousting of the boss of Nvidia, Jensen Huang, and allegations members of the US administration, including the commerce secretary, Howard Lutnick, knew about his affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

Trump’s delegation was expected to include Elon Musk.

Protest leader Renato Reyes blamed the arrests in Manila on the heavy handed response of the government on the president, Ferdinand Marcos Jr, calling Monday the largest single day of police arrests since Marcos came to office in 2022.

“It is really crazy that the Philippine government is rolling out the red carpet for someone who has been so flatly rejected by the American people,” Reyes said. “Trump started a war that devastated the global economy and pushed oil prices in the Philippines to historic highs. It has caused untold suffering on the Filipino people.

“So, yes, Trump will have to pay for his crimes and he will have to be answerable, not just to the American people, but to the people of the world.”

The Philippine national police said some officers were injured during confrontations with demonstrators opposed to the summit, including when objects were allegedly thrown at officers.

Pax Silica will include a technology hub planned at New Clark City in Tarlac, about 100km from Manila.

Intended to bolster western stocks of AI technology and reduce “excessive dependencies” on single source supply chains, including from China, Pax Silica will provide chips and critical minerals to 26 participating signatory governments.

Amnesty International said demonstrations should not be forcibly or violently dispersed.

“Reports of arrests during the protests demand immediate scrutiny,” Amnesty’s director for the Philippines, Ritz Lee Santos III, said. “Authorities must explain the specific grounds for each arrest and any continued detention. Anyone detained solely for peacefully exercising their rights must be released immediately.”

articles.title: What do Democrats’ sweeping midterm wins mean for Trump’s ICE crackdown?
articles.excerpt:
Despite House and Senate majorities, Democrats face a battle to enact legislation – but they have the power to conduct tough new oversight

The Democrats’ midterm “blue wave” wins gave them strong maj...
articles.body_text:
Despite House and Senate majorities, Democrats face a battle to enact legislation – but they have the power to conduct tough new oversight

The Democrats’ midterm “blue wave” wins gave them strong majorities in both chambers of Congress, new governors’ mansions and power in some unexpected places. Voters dealt a stunning rebuke to Donald Trump – and his ruthless deportation campaign and violent ICE raids across the country were among the key issues that cost Republicans support. But what will Democrats do about the immigration crackdown?

The US Congress theoretically has the ability to force many changes on ICE through legislation, such as taking away funds, restricting detention centers and mandating a focus on migrants with violent records – after Trump’s pledges to target “the worst of the worst” actually turned into mass arrests of people without criminal records and even of people with legal papers.

Democrats have said such things as, “We have to rein ICE in because its illegal, out-of-control activities [have] killed individuals … assaulted individuals… incarcerated individuals” (Mississippi Representative Bennie Thompson, likely to chair the House homeland security committee), and “We will rip ICE apart” (incoming US Senator of Minnesota Peggy Flanagan).

But even with House and Senate majorities, enacting legislation will face steep odds without Republicans on board, considering presidential veto power and the Senate filibuster, which requires at least 60 votes to move bills forward.

And not everyone in the Democratic caucus is on the same page. Leaders are initially proposing more modest guardrails, banning masks for ICE officers and requiring body-worn cameras in the field.

In practice, one of the clearest unilateral powers Democrats will have next year is that of greater oversight, conducting investigations to expose the faults of the Trump administration’s immigration policy.

Democratic-led congressional committees will be able to issue subpoenas, and they already plan to call in homeland security secretary Markwayne Mullin, new White House chief of staff Stephen Miller, border czar Tom Homan and former border patrol commander-at-large Gregory Bovino for questioning in public.

They may also hold hearings in cities where they can present evidence of agency misconduct, while continuing congressional visits to ICE detention facilities to check on conditions there and increase public exposure.

Meanwhile, they could consider impeachment. It is unclear whether the US constitution allows for someone like Miller, as chief of staff, to be impeached. But if Democrats lead a second attempt to impeach defense secretary Pete Hegseth – and especially if they succeed in removing him from office – it could curtail Miller’s authority by putting other impeachable officials directing immigration enforcement, such as Mullin, on notice that they could lose their jobs if they follow any White House advice to act lawlessly.

Democrats, both sitting and incoming, are now pushing for comprehensive immigration changes to a system that both parties have long agreed is “broken”, but Congress has not had the will to reform top to tail, balancing security measures at the US-Mexico border with helping immigrants already in the US.

Sufficient bipartisan unity is hard to come by. Republicans largely oppose what they call “amnesty” – giving people in the country unlawfully the chance to legalize their status. Some progressive Democrats, meanwhile, denounce crackdowns on the border and restrictions on seeking asylum that contradict international law.

Yet more targeted fixes may be on the table. Some 81% of Americans endorse a citizenship pathway for undocumented immigrants who came to the US as children, also known as “Dreamers”, according to a recent Gallup poll. Even the Trump administration has indicated renewed openness to this idea since the midterm drubbing.

Lawmakers may be able to get agreement to reinstate temporary protected status (TPS), a program allowing work permits and protection from deportation for nationalities in the US who are unable to safely return to their home countries, especially for Haitians and Afghans. The administration has ended TPS for roughly a million people across more than a dozen nationalities.

Legislation could even create a pathway to a green card for TPS holders, something that does not exist now.

However, once again, with Trump threatening to become “Mr Veto” it’s unclear how he and Senate Republicans will proceed.

DHS, which oversees immigration enforcement and many immigration benefits in the US, has received about a quarter of a trillion dollars in funding during Trump’s second term alone. Taxpayers’ money designated for ICE soared and it is now the highest federally-funded US law enforcement agency.

That includes a roughly $70bn cash infusion in June, meant to bankroll the department through the end of Trump’s presidency. Democrats say they plan to make efforts to claw back or withhold at least some of that funding through legislation once they control Congress.

Very unlikely. The slogan “abolish ICE” became a political liability for Democrats as Americans turned on undocumented immigrants when unauthorized border crossings rose sharply under the Biden administration and Trump and his Maga white nationalist ranks started calling them an “invasion”. Even to many mainstream US voters the notion that you should entirely abolish ICE – like defunding the police – stood for the left being too soft on law and order.

Despite the backlash that Republicans are now feeling given the perceived cruelty of Trump’s mass deportation campaign and ICE violence on the streets, an ideological divide among progressive and more moderate Democrats would probably preclude closing down the agency.

The re-elected centrist Democratic congressman Henry Cuellar, representing a Texas-Mexico border district, last Wednesday said simply: “I’m not going to abolish ICE.”

Although immigration enforcement is broadly a federal responsibility, state and local governments have been deeply involved in recent years – especially through cooperation between police and sheriffs’ departments and ICE, whether because of what’s called 287(g) agreements or other collaborative policies.

Texas, in particular, saw a political earthquake, where Democrats flipped a US Senate seat, the governorship, the attorney general’s office and the state House of Representatives.

This followed decades of Republican dominance statewide and increasingly draconian immigration enforcement. Texas’s laws and policies have required local law enforcement to work with ICE and state penalties have criminalized people who unlawfully crossed the border with Mexico.

Leadership in states that swung heavily blue now have the opportunity to back off such aggressive tactics, likely leading to fewer ICE arrests, less depletion of immigrant-heavy workforces, and the potential for communities to rebuild trust with local law enforcement.

Democrats are now set to hold all 10 of the House seats along the almost 3,000 miles of the US-Mexico border and the four border governorships – California, Arizona, New Mexico and Texas – for the first time since 1979, as well as four states’ top legal offices. Hard-right Texas governor Greg Abbott, for example, outgoing after 12 years, unilaterally bussed migrants to Democratic-led cities and spent an estimated $11bn militarizing the Tex-Mex border with the extreme project, “Operation Lone Star”. Now Democrats will examine what they can and wish to unwind.

Democratic state leaders could help reinstate policies that help immigrants, such as access to in-state college tuition for undocumented students, after those were gutted in some states amid federal collusion in Trump’s second term.

They could also join lawsuits challenging Trump-era policies, and cities, counties and states that are suddenly on the same side of the political debate could pool resources to fight legal battles against the federal government instead of against each other.

The label “sanctuary city” has somewhat gone out of vogue in recent years. But in a similar vein, Democratic city and county leaders, as well as state legislatures, may devise new laws and strategies to block cooperation with ICE, at least when it comes to immigrants who do not pose a public safety risk.

For federal congressional seats that have flipped in favor of Democrats, immigrants may discover a new ally. Congressional offices often help their constituents – including noncitizens – contact federal agencies, get answers from the government and sometimes find solutions. That can mean finally receiving a work permit stuck in limbo, helping a family member overseas with their visa processing or getting a loved one out of detention.

Ultimately, the president and his subordinates have given no signs that policies will be easing - and they plan to continue deportations.

Despite Trump telling 60 Minutes after the midterm losses that maybe immigration enforcement was “too tough”, he appointed the ferociously anti-immigration zealot and longtime ally Miller as his chief of staff shortly after that interview was recorded.

While Democrats can shine a spotlight on excesses and racist attitudes and act as a buffer, more transformational change will probably have to wait to see if a Democrat – particularly a progressive – wins the White House in 2028.

articles.title: New Orleans police arrest teen over beating death of homeless man ‘unable to defend himself’
articles.excerpt:
Police say David Hyde, 68, left with shoe prints in face from kicks to head and prescription medication stolen in attack

A man who was unhoused and “unable to defend himself due to health issues” was...
articles.body_text:
Police say David Hyde, 68, left with shoe prints in face from kicks to head and prescription medication stolen in attack

A man who was unhoused and “unable to defend himself due to health issues” was recently beaten to death and had his prescription medication taken outside a pharmacy in New Orleans, according to authorities.

The killing of 68-year-old David Hyde led police to arrest Antonio Myles, 19, on a count of second-degree murder, with investigators alleging that they came to suspect the much younger man after he had bragged to others about fatally beating an unhoused person.

As portrayed in criminal court records summarizing the circumstances surrounding Myles’ arrest, Hyde’s killing is an extreme example of how people experiencing homelessness in the US are at heightened risk of being victimized by violence.

A 2020 US justice department study determined that about half of people experiencing homelessness report being victims of violence – a rate that for the general population is 2%. And in May, amid an affordability crisis in the US, the federal Housing and Urban Development said the most recent available point-in-time estimate calculated that nearly 700,000 people were experiencing homelessness nationwide when the count was conducted on a night in January.

New Orleans police said officers found Hyde down outside a Walgreens in the 4400 block of Claiborne Avenue, on the edge of the city’s Freret neighborhood, at about 6.55am on 8 November “with severe contusions to his face”. He was near numerous prescription medication bottles and pronounced dead at the scene from what investigators ascertained to be kicks to the head, as evident from the shoe prints left on Hyde’s face, police wrote in sworn count documents.

Investigators later secured video from a store surveillance camera that showed Hyde sitting near the pharmacy’s front entrance when his attacker took his backpack, dumped its contents on the ground and picked some of those items up prior to the beating. While the deadly violence evidently happened out of the camera’s view, the man who approached Hyde at one point used his shirt to wipe his shoes and then left the scene.

Police alleged they received a call a day later reporting that Myles had been heard “bragging to unknown subjects that he was responsible for beating a homeless man to death”. Myles was soon interviewed by police, but they released him pending further investigation, according to the sworn statement summarizing the case.

Then, on 10 November, police investigating Hyde’s killing released video from a surveillance camera overlooking a parking lot which depicted a figure described as a “suspect wanted in connection with a brutal beating that left a disabled man dead”.

“The victim … was unable to defend himself due to health issues,” police said in a statement accompanying the video, without elaborating. Police asked anyone who recognized the figure to call them.

An unidentified “known subject” then told police the person in the video was Myles. That person also reportedly alleged Myles was wearing a beanie-style cap at the time of Hyde’s beating. Investigators said they later recovered surveillance footage which established Myles was wearing a beanie-style cap when Hyde was killed.

Furthermore, police said that a detective interviewed an unidentified but known subject who reported that Myles had called hours after Hyde was discovered dead. The sworn police statement accused Myles of telling that person “he loved them, and that he killed a homeless man, and continued to kick him after he was already dead”.

“The known subject also advised … that Mr Myles advised a known subject that he killed the homeless man and took his prescription medication that was inside his backpack,” the sworn police statement said. Police also said that person knew Myles well and identified him as being on the video released to the public.

According to the police statement, investigators believed that information was true because “no specific details of the investigation were released to the media”.

“Only a person who was there when the homicide occurred would know that the victim was kicked to his head repeatedly, and that the victim was in possession of prescription medicine inside of a backpack,” said the police statement, which was not available to the news media until Monday.

A New Orleans criminal court magistrate commissioner gave police permission to arrest Myles on a count of murder on Friday. He soon turned himself over to police and was jailed – and no bond was immediately set for him, court records show.

Myles’ arrest in Hyde’s killing came after he pleaded guilty to a charge of simple battery on 11 August in an unrelated case and was sentenced to about a month in jail, according to court records. He would receive mandatory life imprisonment if eventually convicted of second-degree murder.

articles.title: MICHAEL RUIZ: New York's gutted police unit was more than a protest squad
articles.excerpt:
Terrorists and other criminals choose the path of least resistance, says retired FBI agent James Gagliano, making NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani's decision to disband a fast-acting deterrent group risky.

N...
articles.body_text:
Terrorists and other criminals choose the path of least resistance, says retired FBI agent James Gagliano, making NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani's decision to disband a fast-acting deterrent group risky.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani is dissolving the NYPD's Strategic Response Group — an elite tactical unit criticized for its handling of some left-wing protests while also responding to critical threats including a mass shooting at an office building last year and an attempted bombing attack on dueling demonstrations outside the city's mayoral residence.

"I think it’s one more step towards emboldening the criminals, emboldening the anarchists and emboldening the terrorists," said James Gagliano, a retired FBI supervisory special agent and Fox News contributor who spent years working alongside the NYPD.

Mamdani announced that the group will be dissolved at a news briefing early Monday. He had campaigned on the issue in part due to the unit's role in responding to organized protests — and riots — including those that exploded after George Floyd's death in 2020, demonstrations against Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Israel's war with Palestinian Hamas terrorists.

MAMDANI GUTS ELITE NYPD TACTICAL UNIT, BACKS 'CIVILIAN-LED APPROACH' TO RESPONDING TO PROTESTS

A looter takes an armful of clothing out of a store with a broken window in Manhattan, New York on June 1, 2020, following protests in the aftermath of the death of George Floyd in Minnesota. (J. Conrad Williams Jr./Newsday via Getty Images)

"New Yorkers exercising their constitutional right to protest should not be met with the same police response as a terrorism threat," Mamdani told reporters in a news briefing announcing the changes. "We are establishing a new, civilian-led approach that prioritizes dialogue, engagement and de-escalation."

Emir Balat flees after throwing a homemade explosive device towards police as NYPD Chief Aaron Edwards and Sgt. Luis Navarro take action during a protest in front of Gracie Mansion, New York mayor Zohran Mamdani's official residence, in New York on March 7, 2026. (CHARLY TRIBALLEAU / AFP via Getty Images)

The mayor plans to replace the SRG with several new programs by next spring. First is an unarmed Community Dialogue and De-escalation Division, or CDDD. This civilian team won't have arrest authority. It will work with new First Amendment Support Team, dubbed FAST, consisting of 30 uniformed officers with specialized training in communication and de-escalation, according to Mamdani's office.

Lastly, his overhaul includes the creation of a new Patrol Support Division consisting of officers who will be trained in crowd control but spend most of their time on patrol duties. Counterterrorism duties will be consolidated in the NYPD's Intelligence and Counterterrorism Bureau.

MAMDANI PREPARES TO FULFILL PROMISE TO AXE NYPD UNIT RESPONSIBLE FOR CONTROLLING PROTEST VIOLENCE

18-year-old Emir Balat was tackled by a law enforcement officer after he allegedly threw a bomb. (FNTV)

But the SRG has a varied role. While members are on hand for crowd control at large demonstrations, they also protect the protesters from outside threats. And they are positioned at other events involving large crowds, including the city's many parades, the iconic New Year's ball drop and other large events that take place every year.

"What the Strategic Response Group was designed to do was to be a highly mobile, well-trained, well-equipped group, like a senior SWAT team," Gagliano told Fox News Digital.

Unlike the NYPD's SWAT team, known as its Emergency Services Unit, the SRG also has a public-facing role, Gagliano said.

"Part of that was being on the front lines, the deterrent effect, and I think that's something that we're losing as well," he said.

ALLEGED ISIS-INSPIRED TERROR SUSPECTS LEFT FEDS ‘VOLUMINOUS’ DIGITAL TRAIL, FAMILY BREAKS DOWN IN TEARS

This image from surveillance video obtained by The Associated Press shows Shane Tamura outside a Manhattan office building on Monday, July 28, 2025. Tamura killed himself and four others in an office building housing the NFL headquarters, and the city's medical examiner later said his brain showed "unambiguous" signs of chronic traumatic encephalopathy, also known as CTE. (AP)

Terrorists and other criminals targeting public events tend to pick soft targets and the path of least resistance, he added.

"The Strategic Response Group was a deterrent and it probably caused some people to decide, ‘Yeah, I’m not gonna try that. I’m not gonna do that,'" he said.

POLICE GROUPS CONDEMN MAMDANI OVER AXING ELITE NYPD UNIT

The unit has also been deployed around large public events with the goal of responding rapidly when needed, Gagliano said.

"The uniform folks are there for a deterrent effect," he said. "The uniform folks kept in abeyance like SRG, that are rolled out quickly and mobilized and strategically placed so that they can get to different spots very quickly."

Students and others demonstrate during a protest outside the gates to the Columbia University main campus in New York City on April 21. (Reuters/Ryan Murphy)

MAMDANI’S FIRST 100-PLUS DAYS: FAR-LEFT MAYOR FLUNKS A KEY LEADERSHIP TEST

Vincent J. Vallelong, president of the NYPD Sergeants Benevolent Association, brought up the failed Gracie Mansion bombing Monday.

"When an alleged terrorist attack threatened lives near Gracie Mansion, NYPD Sgt. Luis Navarro and Chief Aaron Edwards ran toward danger," Vallelong said in a statement. "Their decisive actions should be a lesson for Mayor Mamdani."

HAMAS, HEZBOLLAH FLAGS FLY AT ANTI-ISRAEL PROTEST MINUTES AFTER MAMDANI CONDEMNS TERROR PLOT AGAINST JEWS

Two allegedly ISIS-inspired men, Emir Balat and Ibrahim Kayumi, were arrested after federal prosecutors say they threw improvised explosive devices at a crowd outside the mayor's home and at a group of police as left- and right-wing protesters demonstrated across from one another. The bombs failed to explode.

Protesters are arrested on Park Avenue in New York City, June 5, 2020 as they defy the 8 p.m. curfew while protesting the death of George Floyd. (TIMOTHY A. CLARY/AFP via Getty Images)

According to federal prosecutors, Balat allegedly told police he had wanted the attack to be "bigger" than the Boston Marathon Bombing, which killed three and injured hundreds in 2013.

MAMDANI UNVEILS SWEEPING NYPD USE-OF-FORCE REVIEW, BUT STOPS SHORT OF FULFILLING KEY CAMPAIGN PROMISES

The SRG also deployed to help search for the gunman floor-by-floor after the mass shooting inside a Manhattan office building that houses the NFL’s headquarters on Park Avenue.

Shattered glass lies in front of a looted souvenir and electronics shop near Times Square after a night of protests and vandalism over the death of George Floyd early June 2, 2020 in New York City. (John Moore/Getty Images)

Vallelong scoffed at the idea that the unarmed CDDD will protect the public from similar violent plots.

"Unarmed civilians cannot talk a determined attacker out of detonating a bomb," he said. "I fear this approach will embolden violent agitators to infiltrate peaceful demonstrations, putting protesters, police and bystanders at risk."

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

People loot a store during demonstrations over the death of George Floyd by a Minneapolis police officer on June 1, 2020 in New York. (Bryan R. Smith / AFP)

Upcoming events like the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade and New Year's ball drop will not be impacted since the changes aren't slated to go into effect until spring 2027, he said.

NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch said in a statement that the restructuring would not "diminish the NYPD’s ability to protect New Yorkers, or that put our officers in a position where they lack the resources necessary to confront a serious threat."

Fox News' Anders Hagstrom contributed to this report.
