Protesters are arrested on Park Avenue in New York City, June 5, 2020 as they defy the 8 p.m. curfew while protesting the death of George Floyd. (TIMOTHY A. CLARY/AFP via Getty Images)

According to federal prosecutors, Balat allegedly told police he had wanted the attack to be "bigger" than the Boston Marathon Bombing, which killed three and injured hundreds in 2013.

MAMDANI UNVEILS SWEEPING NYPD USE-OF-FORCE REVIEW, BUT STOPS SHORT OF FULFILLING KEY CAMPAIGN PROMISES

The SRG also deployed to help search for the gunman floor-by-floor after the mass shooting inside a Manhattan office building that houses the NFL’s headquarters on Park Avenue.

Shattered glass lies in front of a looted souvenir and electronics shop near Times Square after a night of protests and vandalism over the death of George Floyd early June 2, 2020 in New York City. (John Moore/Getty Images)

Vallelong scoffed at the idea that the unarmed CDDD will protect the public from similar violent plots.

"Unarmed civilians cannot talk a determined attacker out of detonating a bomb," he said. "I fear this approach will embolden violent agitators to infiltrate peaceful demonstrations, putting protesters, police and bystanders at risk."

LISTEN TO THE NEW 'CRIME & JUSTICE WITH DONNA ROTUNNO' PODCAST

People loot a store during demonstrations over the death of George Floyd by a Minneapolis police officer on June 1, 2020 in New York. (Bryan R. Smith / AFP)

Upcoming events like the 100th Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade and New Year's ball drop will not be impacted since the changes aren't slated to go into effect until spring 2027, he said.

NYPD Commissioner Jessica Tisch said in a statement that the restructuring would not "diminish the NYPD’s ability to protect New Yorkers, or that put our officers in a position where they lack the resources necessary to confront a serious threat."

Fox News' Anders Hagstrom contributed to this report.

articles.title: Drinking 6 to 8 cups of tea a day linked to lower risk of serious diseases, massive study finds
articles.excerpt:
Cardiothoracic surgeon Dr. Jeremy London discusses the best lifestyle approach to maintaining good heart health, including the "80/20" rule for eating whole foods.

Drinking six to eight cups of tea a...
articles.body_text:
Cardiothoracic surgeon Dr. Jeremy London discusses the best lifestyle approach to maintaining good heart health, including the "80/20" rule for eating whole foods.

Drinking six to eight cups of tea a day could help lower the risk of vascular disease, according to a recent study published in the Journal of Internal Medicine.

The study, which was conducted in China, involved 485,934 adult participants.

After a median follow-up period of 9.05 years, researchers identified 14,863 cases of cardiovascular disease, cerebrovascular disease, pulmonary heart disease and peripheral artery disease among participants.

LIVING LONGER MAY START WITH 3 FOODS A DOCTOR EATS EVERY DAY

Consistent tea consumption was associated with an 11% lower risk of those diseases.

Drinking tea regularly may lower the risk of developing vascular disease, a recent study suggests. (iStock)

Those who drank approximately six to eight cups of tea each day were found to have the lowest risk of developing vascular diseases.

Smoking and physical activity levels were also taken into account.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Participants who did not smoke, were physically active and drank tea regularly had the lowest risk of developing vascular diseases.

Tea strength also affected the results, as well, researchers found.

Study participants who drank six to eight cups of tea per day were found to have the lowest risk of developing vascular diseases. (iStock)

The study does not specify what exactly "tea strength" means in this case, but it's possible that the term refers to caffeine content.

Moderate-strength tea was linked with the lowest risk of vascular disease, while strong tea was linked to an increased risk of developing vascular disease.

Those who drank black tea had more consistent negative correlations with vascular disease than those who drank green tea.

"Both black and green tea contain polyphenols, including flavonoids, which are plant compounds with antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties," Amy Davis, a San Diego, California-based registered dietitian nutritionist, told Fox News Digital. "These compounds may help support healthy blood vessel function and blood pressure, which are important factors in cardiovascular health."

Participants' physical activity levels and whether they smoked were taken into account, as well. (iStock)

"Drinking unsweetened tea can also help you stay hydrated without any added sugar or artificial ingredients," Davis added.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The study's conclusion states that its findings "support considering multidimensional tea-drinking and lifestyle patterns in vascular health research."

A study published in 2024 examining the correlation between tea consumption and life expectancy found that participants who drank three to five cups of tea daily had a life expectancy increase of 2.24 years.

"Very few long-term studies have looked at the effects of tea on heart disease risk. However, the limited evidence currently available suggests that both green and black tea might have beneficial effects on some heart disease risk factors, including blood pressure and cholesterol," according to the National Center for Complementary and Integrative Health.

Sadie Chafe is a writer on the Lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Robert Pattinson’s James Bond casting could bring 'darker,' 'moodier' twist as fans crave classic 007: expert
articles.excerpt:
Former Bond girl Alison Papworth shares why she wants the next 007 to stay true to the books as speculation swirls over the role.

James Bond may never miss, but Robert Pattinson's casting as the next...
articles.body_text:
Former Bond girl Alison Papworth shares why she wants the next 007 to stay true to the books as speculation swirls over the role.

James Bond may never miss, but Robert Pattinson's casting as the next iconic British secret agent was positively shocking to fans across the world.

Pattinson, 40, called the role "the honor of a lifetime," in a statement released Monday where "Dune" director Denis Villeneuve was also tapped to bring Bond back to the big screen following Daniel Craig's 15-year reign as 007.

Fox News contributor Raymond Arroyo admitted he was "shaken, not stirred" by the casting choice.

Actor Robert Pattinson at the screening of the film Primetime at the 83rd Venice International Film Festival in Italy, on Sept. 5. (Laurent KOFFEL/Gamma-Rapho via Getty Images)

"As a huge fan of the Ian Fleming novels, Pattinson isn’t quite what I envisioned or what I think fans were hoping for," Arroyo told Fox News Digital. "After five Bond films with Daniel Craig in the lead, it was probably time to bring back some of the fun and charm that Pierce Brosnan and Roger Moore brought to the franchise."

He noted how Pattinson was known for his "brooding and dark qualities," a contrast to the more masculine qualities a Bond character usually brings to the screen.

FORMER BOND GIRL SAYS NEXT 007 SHOULD BE 'ANOTHER GORGEOUS MAN' AS JAMES BOND DECISION

"As a huge fan of the Ian Fleming novels, Pattinson isn’t quite what I envisioned or what I think fans were hoping for."

"Fun and a light touch is not the first thing that comes to mind when you think of his filmography," Arroyo said. "His Batman was a pretty dreary affair, the sequel of which I could care less about seeing. Bond also requires a certain physicality and strength – he is an assassin after all."

Arroyo believed Henry Cavill "would have been a much better choice all round."

Sean Connery starred as James Bond 007 in the '64 film "Goldfinger."  (Screen Archives/Getty Images)

"But it sounds like MGM/Amazon wants to give audiences a darker, moodier Bond – just when the public is craving a good, old fashioned escape. We’ll see if audiences wish this new Bond to Live or Let Die."

Amazon MGM Studios announced Pattinson’s casting on social media with a brief snippet of the actor emerging from the shadows with a gun.

PIERCE BROSNAN BACKS 'FANTASTIC BEASTS' STAR FOR NEXT JAMES BOND, PREDICTS FANS WILL BE 'BLOWN AWAY'

"Before anything else, I want to express my deep gratitude to the remarkable actors who joined us on this journey. We were surrounded by extraordinary talent, but there can only be one 007," Villeneuve said in a statement.

"I am overjoyed to welcome Robert Pattinson as our new James Bond. He has the timeless soul of 007 and brings a spirit that is completely new. I cannot wait to begin."

Daniel Craig starred as the British secret agent from 2006-21. (Greg Williams/Eon Productions via Getty Images)

Adrienne Uthe, founder of Kronus Communications, exclusively told Fox News Digital that Pattinson was a "risk" to the franchise.

"He's going in as the underdog, period," Uthe said. "To win over the Connery people, the Brosnan people, the Craig people, he can’t just be good – he has to do it better than what’s been done before. That’s the bar when you take a role this iconic, you have to prove you’re actually worth it."

Pattinson found global fame years ago as telepathic vampire Edward Cullen in the "Twilight" series, which collectively grossed more than $3.3 billion worldwide.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"He can’t just be good – He has to do it better than what’s been done before. That’s the bar when you take a role this iconic, you have to prove you’re actually worth it."

Uthe noted that while a younger audience already knows his face and therein may show up to watch him as Bond, there's still a risk of "watering down the brand."

Pierce Brosnan stars as 007 opposite Denise Richards as Dr Christmas Jones in the '99 James Bond film "The World Is Not Enough." (Keith Hamshere/Getty Images)

"Bond is established, seasoned, it’s got pedigree – so he has to bring pedigree to it too," Uthe said. "He has to prove he can be taken seriously in a role like Bond."

She added, "Now, underdogs can win. People forget Daniel Craig got torn apart when he was cast – too blonde, too rough, wrong guy – and then 'Casino Royale' came out and that was the end of that conversation. So it’s doable. But he has to earn it on screen, nobody’s handing it to him."

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

Seven actors have starred as the legendary British spy over the years, a role which first originated on television with Barry Nelson before Sean Connery was tapped to play the secret service agent in the '62 film "Dr. No."

Brand expert Eric Schiffer explained that the franchise may face a fan exodus with a "painfully boring" 007, a contrast to the previous Bond's played by David Niven, George Lazenby, Roger Moore, Timothy Dalton and Pierce Brosnan.

English actor Roger Moore poses for a portrait in London, England, on July 20, 1979. Moore portrayed James Bond in the Bond series. (Getty Images)

"Pattinson as Bond is a slap in the face to James, to 007's character, and largely because of his prior history and the Bond character himself," Schiffer told Fox News Digital.

"He failed as Batman. It was a horror show, and prior to that he was the 'Twilight' guy with too much makeup. We're now James Bond? Well, what happened?"

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

He added, "This whole James Bond quest has been, it started with the DEI bake-off. That was where it was going, right? And it looks like we haven't progressed that much further if this is the final choice."

"Pattinson as Bond is a slap in the face to James, to 007's character, and largely because of his prior history and the Bond character himself."

Robert Pattinson starred alongside Kristen Stewart in the "Twilight" series. (Franco S. Origlia)

For Pattinson to get the spy element just right, Schiffer noted that the actor has to prove "that he can be a bada--, and that he can authentically pull off the character in a way that's believable and credible as someone who can get things done under immense pressure and with a refined toughness and cool."

Tracy Wright is an entertainment reporter for Fox News Digital. Send story tips to Tracy.Wright@fox.com.

articles.title: Jim Gaffigan, New York lawmakers push Gov Hochul to axe 'unnecessary tax' hitting comedy clubs
articles.excerpt: Comedian Jim Gaffigan joined New York lawmakers and club owners in calling on Gov. Kathy Hochul to sign legislation eliminating the state sales tax on comedy club tickets, arguing the added cost could...
articles.body_text:
Comedian Jim Gaffigan joined New York lawmakers and club owners in calling on Gov. Kathy Hochul to sign legislation eliminating the state sales tax on comedy club tickets, arguing the added cost could discourage audiences from attending live shows.

New York’s comedy clubs are demanding an end to an "unnecessary" sales tax on comedy tickets that they say threatens to price out everyday fans, and comedian Jim Gaffigan helped lead the charge on Thursday.

The New York State Legislature unanimously passed a bill in June that would exempt comedy performances from the state’s sales tax on admissions, a break already enjoyed by Broadway theaters, concert halls and even bowling alleys.

The legislation now awaits action by Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul, and advocates are calling on her to sign it before the end of the year, arguing the tax is putting additional financial pressure on the state’s comedy industry.

BILL MAHER RIPS CALIFORNIA TAXES, SAYS STATE TAKES BIGGER CUT THAN A 'SKEEZY' DRUG DEALER

Comedian Jim Gaffigan joins comedy club owners, lawmakers and other advocates at The Stand comedy club in Manhattan on Nov. 12, 2026, to urge New York Gov. Kathy Hochul to sign legislation eliminating the sales tax on comedy club admissions. (Fox News Digital)

"It really comes down to comedians need people to be able to afford to go to a show," Gaffigan exclusively told Fox News Digital during a rally at The Stand comedy club in Manhattan on Thursday.

"And [not having] this unnecessary tax that Broadway shows don't have to deal with makes it more palatable for someone to pay," he added. "And particularly given the economic times, people might come out, but if they see the sales tax, even if it moves the bill up a little bit, that might dissuade them from coming back."

Club owners and supporters of the legislation argue that the tax is a legal oversight, dating back to a time when New York City's comedy industry was less established and stand-up performances weren't treated the same as other performing arts.

JOHN RICH WARNS NASHVILLE'S FAMED BROADWAY COULD GO DARK AS BUSINESSES FACE TAX ‘DEATH NAIL’

New York Gov. Kathy Hochul speaks during a Democratic election-eve rally at Brooklyn Bowl in the Williamsburg neighborhood on Nov. 2, 2026, in Brooklyn, N.Y. (Shuran Huang/For The Washington Post via Getty Images)

Paul Italia, co-owner of The Stand and the newly-opened The Stand West, pointed to the difference in how the same comedy performance can be taxed depending on the venue. He argued that if Gaffigan performed at his club and then delivered the same set at a venue classified as a theater later in the week, customers at The Stand would have to pay sales tax, while those at the theater would not.

"There was a gray area, and a lot of us have not been collecting sales tax. And recently, the state decided to come — I don't want to say come after us — but in audits, this has come up many times," Italia told Fox News Digital.

"We are being asked to pay for money that we never collected, because we never charged the sales tax, some of us, and that hurts a great deal," he added. "In fact, if it continues to go that way, I think it would cause a bit of a strain on some of our businesses, comedy clubs, that we may not be able to overcome."

HOLLYWOOD STAR SOUNDS ALARM OVER DISAPPEARING JOBS AS PRODUCTIONS FLEE CALIFORNIA

New York Assemblymember Keith Powers, D-Manhattan, speaks at a podium during a rally at The Stand comedy club in Manhattan on Nov. 12, 2026, urging Gov. Kathy Hochul to sign legislation eliminating the sales tax on comedy club admissions. (Fox News Digital)

Movie theaters, the circus and even singles networking events can all claim tax-exempt status, while comedy clubs cannot, according to New York Assemblymember Keith Powers (D), who sponsored the Assembly version of the bill.

Powers told Fox News Digital that vague rules have left small venues vulnerable to surprise tax audits and a "gigantic financial liability" that could force clubs to shut their doors.

"I can't defend why comedy clubs would be left out of it if everyone else is receiving it, so why not now?" Powers said.

New York state Sen. Kristen Gonzalez (D), a self-described democratic socialist who sponsored the Senate bill, called the measure "common sense" and joked about the irony of a democratic socialist pushing to eliminate a tax. She urged Hochul to "sign the bill, please."

FORGET PAYING YOUR ‘FAIR SHARE’ OF TAXES. HERE ARE 5 WAYS POLITICIANS WANT EVEN MORE

Paul Italia, co-owner of The Stand comedy club, speaks at a podium during a rally in Manhattan on Nov. 12, 2026, urging Gov. Kathy Hochul to sign legislation eliminating the sales tax on comedy club admissions. Italia warned that tax audits and unexpected financial liabilities could threaten small comedy clubs. (Fox News Digital)

"As much as I'm a democratic socialist, and I was able to make that joke… I also think it's fair to support our small businesses, our artists, and that, as a state representative of a district that has so many of them, this is part of my job and duty to my constituents," Gonzalez told Fox News Digital.

Gaffigan added that New York City is an "artistic community" where comedy plays an important role, and said he believes Hochul recognizes its significance.

"New York City is very important for stand-up comedy, so I selfishly want that to be fed and supported," Gaffigan said. "I think that Governor Hochul understands that."

COMEDIAN DES BISHOP ON HOW AMERICA MADE HIM FUNNIER AND HIS 'HEALTHY COLLABORATION' WITH WIFE HANNAH BERNER

Comedian Jim Gaffigan performs during the 5th Annual UO x Katz's Deli Comedy Show at Katz's Delicatessen on Nov. 12, 2026, in New York City. (Astrida Valigorsky/Getty Images)

A spokesperson for Hochul told Fox News Digital, "The Governor will review the bill."

Madison Colombo is a writer for Fox News Digital’s Flash, Media, and Culture team, covering daily breaking news and trending topics with an award-winning background in broadcast and digital journalism.

articles.title: Who is behind Habibi UK, an X account that targeted critics of Israel?
articles.excerpt: The anonymous X account Habibi UK branded opponents of Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza “racists”, “hate marchers” and “anti-Semites”, singling out politicians, broadcasters and campaigners for online a...
articles.body_text:
The anonymous X account Habibi UK branded opponents of Israel’s genocidal war in Gaza “racists”, “hate marchers” and “anti-Semites”, singling out politicians, broadcasters and campaigners for online attacks.

A six-month investigation by the British publication Byline Times has now identified the person behind the account as Benjamin Tait, a 61-year-old former United States Foreign Service officer who went on to run a British energy research company.

The news website and newspaper said that since the initial part of its investigation was published on Thursday, the account has stopped posting.

The account, which joined what was then Twitter in April 2015, used a coronation portrait of Queen Elizabeth I as its profile picture, gave its location as “The Realm” and quoted a line attributed to the monarch in its bio: “If thy heart fails thee, climb not at all.”

An analysis of nearly 300,000 X posts placed @habibi_uk at the centre of a network of 13 anonymous accounts. It found that Habibi UK had posted more than 42,000 times.

The investigation also documented campaigns against 12 public figures in Britain over 10 months. Among those targeted were former BBC presenter and professional footballer Gary Lineker, photographer and outgoing chairman of London’s Southbank Centre arts centre Misan Harriman, documentary filmmaker Louis Theroux, actor and television panellist Nadia Sawalha and Green Party leader Zack Polanski. All of them had spoken out against Israel’s actions against Palestinians.

Tait, a British-American grandson of philosopher Bertrand Russell, graduated from Georgetown University’s School of Foreign Service in Washington, DC. According to his LinkedIn profile, which has now been taken down, Tait spent two years as a US Department of State officer overseas with experience in political-military diplomacy and “counterterrorism research”.

Tait and his wife ran Prospex Research for about three decades. It was a firm that produced energy market reports for clients, including banks, consultancies, government officials and law firms. Reuters, The Wall Street Journal and Dow Jones quoted Tait on energy markets. The company entered voluntary liquidation in September.

Tait was writing under the name Habibi by at least 2008 on Harry’s Place, a British political blog that began as a centre-left forum. His early posts focused on alleged “Islamist extremism”, including pieces about campaigner Ismail Patel and the Palestinian aid charity Interpal, according to the investigation.

Before the United Kingdom’s 2019 general election, Tait was the sole director and controlling owner of MTCAE Ltd, according to Companies House records cited by the Byline Times. The company ran Mainstream, a campaign registered to spend money during the elections independently of a political party.

Mainstream was founded and chaired by Ian Austin, a former Labour MP who quit the party under Jeremy Corbyn and has served as Britain’s trade envoy to Israel under five prime ministers. Austin said the group was set up to oppose “extremism” on the far left and hard right. But the Byline Times found that the Facebook advertisements it examined all attacked the Labour Party, including one that portrayed Corbyn as a national security threat.

Electoral Commission returns showed the company spent £134,457 pounds ($171,715) on the campaign, including 6,880 pounds ($8,786) paid to Tait for overhead costs and administration. The returns listed no donor.

In March 2021, a High Court official ordered Twitter to disclose details behind the account to Professor David Miller, who had brought a legal claim. The operator’s name remained out of the public record. Despite this, the account went on to gain influence, particularly after Elon Musk took over Twitter in October 2022.

Links between the account and the Labour Party establishment run deep, according to the investigation. Austin, who is connected to Tait via Mainstream, shared posts from Habibi UK at least 34 times. John Woodcock, a former Labour MP who sits in the House of Lords, amplified the account 32 times, according to the investigation. It also found that David Toube, general counsel at the Jewish Leadership Council, amplified its posts hundreds of times.

The Henry Jackson Society, a British foreign policy think tank, cited Habibi UK nine times in a 2022 report on Hindu-Muslim unrest in Leicester.

articles.title: Ukraine hails attack on vital Kerch bridge linking Russia and Crimea – Europe live
articles.excerpt:
Zelenskyy praises ‘unprecedented attack’ as the Kremlin says bridge will be restored and will be ‘better than ever’ following strike

Ukraine has critically damaged the Kerch bridge linking occupied C...
articles.body_text:
Zelenskyy praises ‘unprecedented attack’ as the Kremlin says bridge will be restored and will be ‘better than ever’ following strike

Ukraine has critically damaged the Kerch bridge linking occupied Crimea with Russia in an overnight missile attack, in what Ukrainian officials say is a symbolic blow to the Kremlin.

Photos suggest that a 227-metre road arch span has fallen into the Kerch strait, which connects the Sea of Azov with the Black Sea. The adjacent railway arch span has also sustained damage.

Ukrainian commentators say the massive steel arch cannot easily be replaced. The closure of the bridge means that traffic from Crimea can travel out of the peninsula only via a land corridor through occupied southern Ukraine, vulnerable to Ukrainian drones.

But Russian officials, quoted by Reuters, insisted that damage was only minor, and would be quick to sort out.

“We have already gathered together the resources, designers, and builders ‌for repair work. We are sorting out logistics issues with the regional leadership,” Russian deputy prime minister Marat Khusnullin wrote on Telegram.

The bridge has in the past been a key supply route for Russian forces in Ukraine ​and is widely viewed as one of Russian president Vladimir Putin’s signature infrastructure projects.

The overnight strike followed ‌an intensification of ​Russian attacks in the ​past few months on bridges in Ukraine, including in the capital Kyiv.

Elsewhere, EU defence ministers are meeting in Brussels this morning for their latest discussions on Ukraine, followed by the Ukraine defence contact group.

Meanwhile, Germany’s chancellor Friedrich Merz is hosting Finland’s influential Alexander Stubb, two days before a major meeting of the coalition of the willing in Berlin.

They will no doubt offer their reaction to today’s events in Ukraine. I will bring you all the latest.

It’s Tuesday, 17 November 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.

In Kyiv, Russian ballistic missiles hit the Northern and Southern bridges – two major transport arteries that cross the Dnipro river.

Traffic was also suspended, causing gridlock early on Tuesday morning.

Russia’s army confirmed it had hit both bridges in a “massive attack” on Ukraine’s infrastructure, AFP reported.

Hungary will suspend rail traffic between Hungary and Ukraine for two days after a Russian drone struck just hundreds of meters from a railway station in western Ukraine, Hungarian prime minister Péter Magyar said.

“Recently, in Transcarpathia, a Russian drone struck 300 meters from the Mukachevo railway station.

The Hungarian crew of the train arriving from Hungary has been taken off the train.

We are suspending rail traffic between Hungary and Ukraine for today and tomorrow.”

Mukachevo is just across the Hungarian-Ukrainian border on the Ukrainian side, in an area inhabited by many ethnic Hungarians.

Hungary’s foreign minister Anita Orbán – no link with that Orbán – offered a bit more detail on the incident.

“At around 10am Hungarian time, Russian Geran-2 drones attacked Transcarpathia in three waves, primarily targeting the areas around Mukachevo and Uzhhorod.

Ukrainian air defence forces responded effectively and shot down several of the attacking drones. Unfortunately, reports have also come in of multiple drone strikes, and the extent of the damage is currently being assessed.

This is not the first air attack against Transcarpathia, and unfortunately it is unlikely to be the last. As Russia intensifies its attacks against Ukraine’s civilian population, we can expect further attacks of this kind against Transcarpathia as well, which until now has been relatively protected due to its geographical location.

Ukraine’s civilian population is likely to face the most difficult winter of the war so far. The electricity grid and district heating systems are already in critical condition, particularly in Kyiv, Kharkiv and southern Ukraine. Russia is expected to intensify its attacks on power generation. Without electricity, water supplies in cities are also disrupted, millions of people are left without heating and power, and everyday life becomes increasingly difficult.

I express my solidarity with the Hungarian community in Transcarpathia and with the entire Ukrainian people, who have now had to face the horrors of war every day for nearly five years and are making extraordinary efforts simply to get through daily life.”

Let’s quickly go back to Ukraine for some news from Hungary’s prime minister, Péter Magyar.

French ⁠far-right leader Marine Le Pen vowed to ​repeal President Emmanuel Macron’s pension ⁠reform if she is elected ⁠next spring and ​bring ‌down the retirement ‌age to 60 ‌to 62.

She also set out plans to create a fund worth €900bn ($990.54bn) to help fund ​pensions in the long term, she added. It ⁠would take a generation ​to ​build up ​the fund, ​she added.

Reuters noted that pensions are France’s largest public ‌spending item, due to reach ‌more than €430bn ($474bn) next year. Successive governments have struggled to contain costs without provoking fierce public ‌opposition.

RN President Jordan ​Bardella has said ​the party wants to tighten the rules governing pension contribution periods and encourage employers to keep older workers in jobs for longer.

On Friday, we reported on crisis talks aimed at saving Rob Jetten’s three-party minority government in the Netherlands.

The crisis erupted late last week when lawmakers from D66 and the Christian Democrats brokered a deal with center-left opposition parties in parliament to pass a contentious tax package, angering the third coalition partner. AP reported.

But it looks like they have managed to agree on a new way forward, with Jetten announcing a fresh start for the coalition bitterly divided by last week’s tax plans.

“We realise that we have tested the patience of the entire nation, but we are also relieved that, following several days of constructive discussions within the Cabinet and the coalition, trust has been restored,” Jetten said. “In doing so, we have laid the foundation to continue working together in this current composition.”

Let’s take a quick look at other news from across Europe.

Meanwhile, the Kremlin said its bridge linking occupied Crimea to Russia will be “even better” after it is rebuilt following a large-scale Ukrainian attack that caused significant damage.

“There is, of course, no doubt that the bridge will be restored and will be even better than before,” Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said, quoted by Russian state media.

Finland’s highly influential president Alexander Stubb has arrived in Berlin this morning for talks with Germany’s Friedrich Merz.

The pair meets just two days before the highly anticipated threeway talks between US president Donald Trump, China president Xi Jinping, and Russia president Vladimir Putin in Manila and an ‘unprecedented’ meeting of the coalition of the willing in Berlin on Thursday.

The Berlin meeting is expected to bring together over 30 national leaders, including Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelenskyy, and the two US peace envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, who will be able to brief European partners on the Manila talks held a few hours earlier, Politico Berlin Playbook reported.

Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelenskyy has hailed the strike against the Kerch Bridge as “an unprecedented operation” with direct consequences “for the primary military supply route connecting Russian territory to our Ukrainian Crimea.”

He said it was “the seventh phase of an operation that has been under way for several weeks,” with “systematic” destruction of air defence systems, radar and other electronic warfare assets.

“We have repeatedly proposed de-escalation measures to Russia, yet every such proposal has been met only with emphatic rejection. Russia strikes our infrastructure daily – including bridges – in Zaporizhzhia, Dnipro, Kyiv, and the Odesa region.

We are restoring our infrastructure, but we also remind Russia that war will always return to where it began. Ukraine’s defensive capacity is and will remain high, and we will never leave terror against our cities and our people unanswered.”

I am also keeping an eye on an incident in the Czech capital of Prague where two commuter trains collided near the main train station, leaving 46 injured, including four seriously.

The two passenger trains collided on an overpass while travelling at a low speed around 7am this morning, according to the Czech media.

Czech transport minister called it “a very serious” incident, but said the focus was on caring for all affected.

At 10am Czech time, the city’s emergency services said the situation was contained, with all injured transported to hospitals.

Danish defence minister Jeppe Bruus has warned that “Europe needs to wake up” as “the price, if Ukraine falls, will be lot higher than the amount we are now delivering for Ukraine.”

“Ukraine has the most efficient and also modern army in all of Europe. We are gaining a lot of advantages [from] the cooperation with the Ukrainians,” he said.

But he added that “the cost of Ukraine losing will be a lot higher” than any current aid given to Kyiv.

German defence minister Boris Pistorius has warned that Ukraine is facing “an exceptionally difficult winter” amid intensifying Russian attacks on critical infrastructure as he confirmed Germany will fund a new package of air defence systems for Kyiv.

“Ukraine is facing an exceptionally difficult winter as Russia is doing everything in its power - and will continue to do so – to destroy Ukraine’s water, electricity and energy infrastructure,” he said.

Pistorius said that Russia was “intensifying its aerial assaults because its if failing to make progress on the battlefields.”

“For us, as nations supporting Ukraine, this means one thing clearly: we must continue to provide effective and rapid support for Ukraine’s air defence,” he said.

Germany will contribute $300m for another round of defensive weapons purchases from the US, with Norway also expected to join.

“Supporting Ukraine is not an act of charity. It is about far more than solidarity or assisting a nation under attack; it is about the security of Europe – and, by extension, about stopping Putin and keeping him in check.”

During the Ukraine defence contact group, which Pistorius co-chairs, the EU ministers will be joined by the US undersecretary of defence, Elbridge Colby.

“This is important, as we have several matters to discuss – for instance, the upcoming Force Posture Review, as well as cooperation on defence equipment and various other topics.”

Ukraine has critically damaged the Kerch bridge linking occupied Crimea with Russia in an overnight missile attack, in what Ukrainian officials say is a symbolic blow to the Kremlin.

Photos suggest that a 227-metre road arch span has fallen into the Kerch strait, which connects the Sea of Azov with the Black Sea. The adjacent railway arch span has also sustained damage.

Ukrainian commentators say the massive steel arch cannot easily be replaced. The closure of the bridge means that traffic from Crimea can travel out of the peninsula only via a land corridor through occupied southern Ukraine, vulnerable to Ukrainian drones.

But Russian officials, quoted by Reuters, insisted that damage was only minor, and would be quick to sort out.

“We have already gathered together the resources, designers, and builders ‌for repair work. We are sorting out logistics issues with the regional leadership,” Russian deputy prime minister Marat Khusnullin wrote on Telegram.

The bridge has in the past been a key supply route for Russian forces in Ukraine ​and is widely viewed as one of Russian president Vladimir Putin’s signature infrastructure projects.

The overnight strike followed ‌an intensification of ​Russian attacks in the ​past few months on bridges in Ukraine, including in the capital Kyiv.

Elsewhere, EU defence ministers are meeting in Brussels this morning for their latest discussions on Ukraine, followed by the Ukraine defence contact group.

Meanwhile, Germany’s chancellor Friedrich Merz is hosting Finland’s influential Alexander Stubb, two days before a major meeting of the coalition of the willing in Berlin.

They will no doubt offer their reaction to today’s events in Ukraine. I will bring you all the latest.

It’s Tuesday, 17 November 2026, it’s Jakub Krupa here, and this is Europe Live.

articles.title: Bob Dylan's hooded Vatican visit with Pope Leo shows he's still knockin' on heaven's door
articles.excerpt:
Pope Leo meets Bob Dylan at the Vatican, November 4, 2026. (Vatican Media/Handout via REUTERS)

I was not surprised to see legendary singer and songwriter Bob Dylan (born Robert Zimmerman) visiting Po...
articles.body_text:
Pope Leo meets Bob Dylan at the Vatican, November 4, 2026. (Vatican Media/Handout via REUTERS)

I was not surprised to see legendary singer and songwriter Bob Dylan (born Robert Zimmerman) visiting Pope Leo XIV at the Vatican a few weeks ago, dressed in what looked to be nomadic garb. He reportedly insisted on keeping his hood up, and the pope agreed. Perhaps Dylan was channeling his apocalyptic song "All Along the Watchtower," which describes the fall of Babylon prophesied in the eighth century (Isaiah 21) before taking place in 539 B.C. Or perhaps he was taking on the role of a hooded healer to the pope, who had just recovered from lung cancer surgery.

It is no secret that Pope Leo, who hails from Chicago, is a longtime fan of Dylan’s, another Midwesterner who was born in Duluth, Minnesota. In July 2026, the pope wrote the preface for a Vatican book called "Disarmed and Disarming: Peace Is a Gift." In it, he quoted from Dylan’s unreleased 1963 Cold War protest song, "Go Away You Bomb": "I hate you cause yer man-made and man-owned, an’ man-handled."

At the meeting with Dylan, the pope pointed to his Augustinian background (he is the first Augustinian friar to be elected pope) and introduced himself as a "son of St. Augustine." This was no doubt a direct reference to Dylan’s 1967 song, "I Dreamed I Saw St. Augustine."

POPE LEO VISITS SITE OF MIRACLE CURES, MEETS PEOPLE WHOSE UNEXPLAINED HEALINGS STUNNED DOCTORS

According to Dylan’s longtime Chabad rabbi, Manis Friedman, Dylan is a spiritual seeker. "The answer is blowin’ in the wind," Friedman told me for my new book, "The Angels Among Us," "but Dylan hasn’t found it yet. He’s knockin’ on heaven’s door, but can’t get in."

Pope Leo meets Bob Dylan at the Vatican, November 4, 2026. (Vatican Media/Handout via REUTERS)

Indeed, Dylan’s deep spiritual journeys and investigations reflect this "seeking" as he ranges from Orthodox Judaism to evangelical Christianity (he famously saw Jesus in a hotel room in 1978 and studied the New Testament intensely with his then-girlfriend, Mary Alice Artes, from 1978 to 1980).

DR. MARC SIEGEL: 'THE ANGELS AMONG US' -- A DYING WOMAN, THE SHOFAR AND THE MIRACLE THAT FOLLOWED

During this born-again Christian period, Dylan produced his celebrated album "Slow Train Coming," including the hit song "Gotta Serve Somebody," followed by "Every Grain of Sand" on his album "Shot of Love."

An image of  Fox News contributor Dr. Marc Siegel's new book 'The Angels Among Us' (Fox Books)

But while Dylan was studying the New Testament, he was introduced to Rabbi Friedman as well as the famed Rebbe (Rabbi Menachem Schneerson), and Dylan then refocused his studies to include the Old Testament. As I write in my new book, he asked Rabbi Friedman, "What does infidel mean? He liked the word, kept asking about it. Infidel? What did I think of it?"

CAN FAITH HELP PATIENTS HEAL? VETERAN DOCTOR REVEALS WHAT HE'S WITNESSED FIRSTHAND

Dylan was once again questioning and reforming his spiritual identity, this time more toward Orthodox Judaism. The album "Infidels" followed in 1983, including the song "Jokerman," about a worker of blasphemous magic, more of an Antichrist than a godlike figure.

One of Dylan’s best friends from childhood was Larry Kegan, who was paralyzed in a cliff-diving accident at age 16 but managed to survive as he said a prayer directly to God. He spent the rest of his life as a psychotherapist giving back to God and humanity, and he became Bob Dylan’s angel, often appearing with him at concerts in a wheelchair. As I describe in "The Angels Among Us," when Dylan, Larry and a third friend visited the Rebbe, with thousands in the room, everyone ignored the famous Dylan as the Rebbe had eyes only for Larry. The Rebbe raised a glass and wished Larry Kegan a long life. Dylan was humbled, saying he needed to work on his soul so he could become more worthy of recognition.

POPE LEO WELCOMED BACK AS HE DELIVERS ANGELUS PRAYER DAYS AFTER LUNG CANCER SURGERY

This meeting with the pope wasn’t Dylan’s first. In 1997, he nearly died of a severe infection known as pericardial histoplasmosis, especially difficult for a smoker to recover from. Coincidentally, Dylan recorded his near-death song, "Not Dark Yet," months before he got sick. A few months after he recovered, Dylan met with Pope John Paul II in Bologna, Italy, a meeting that Cardinal Joseph Ratzinger (the future Pope Benedict XVI) tried to block because, as he wrote later in his memoirs, he considered rock stars like Dylan to be the wrong kind of "prophet" for Christian youth. But Pope John Paul II overruled him, and Dylan performed several songs, including "Knockin’ on Heaven’s Door."

After the performance, the pope addressed the crowd and took on the very question that Dylan raised in "Blowin’ in the Wind" that Rabbi Friedman mentioned.

The pope had a definitive answer: "A representative of yours has spoken for you, saying that the answer is 'blowin' in the wind.' It is true! But not in the wind that blows things away in a whirlwind of nothingness. The wind that is the breath and voice of the Spirit, a voice that calls and says: 'Come!' You asked me: how many roads must a man walk down before you can call him a man? I answer you: one! There is only one road for man, and it is the road of Jesus Christ, who said, 'I am the way.'"

CLICK HERE TO READ MORE FROM DR MARC SIEGEL

Marc Siegel, M.D. is a professor of medicine and medical director of Doctor Radio at NYU Langone Medical Center. He is Fox News Channel's senior medical analyst. His forthcoming book is "The Angels Among Us: How God's Messengers Play a Role in Healing." (Fox Books, November 17, 2026). His previous book "The Miracles Among Us: How God's Grace Plays a Role in Healing" (Fox Books, November 18, 2025)  debuted at #1 on both the New York Times and Publisher’s Weekly bestseller lists. He is also the author of "COVID: The Politics of Fear and the Power of Science." Follow him on X @drmarcsiegel.

articles.title: Ed Miliband announces first sanctions on Israeli firms working in West Bank
articles.excerpt:
Move is designed to hinder building of more illegal settlements, which Foreign Office says Israel has ‘refused to clamp down on’

Ed Miliband has announced the first set of sanctions against Israeli c...
articles.body_text:
Move is designed to hinder building of more illegal settlements, which Foreign Office says Israel has ‘refused to clamp down on’

Ed Miliband has announced the first set of sanctions against Israeli companies planning to build illegal settlements in the West Bank, after he pledged to try to prevent settlements that destroy the chances of a two-state solution.

The UK foreign secretary also announced he was placing sanctions on a rightwing activist Israeli group involved in trying to block aid into Gaza as recently as last month.

Miliband announced the measures just before tenders for the large E1 West Bank settlement were due to be allocated by the Israeli government, while saying he wanted to work with a new Israeli government in a more cooperative way.

Israel’s possible new prime minister, Gadi Eisenkot has said that, if appointed, he will take a tougher approach than Benjamin Netanyahu to settler violence.

The sanctions are designed to stop the flow of finance to eight identified construction firms, although in practice the extent to which any of the firms are dependent on British finance is yet to be tested.

On 8 September, Miliband announced an expansion of its Global Human Rights sanctions regime, as well as a complex set of measures, yet to be implemented, designed to ban the trade in goods from illegal settlements. The Foreign Office said that it welcomed and encouraged trade with “green line Israel” and firmly distinguished this with activity in settlements.

The Foreign Office said the current Israeli government had “not only refused to clamp down on illegal settlement, but has facilitated and encouraged them”. More settlements had been approved under the four years of this Israeli government than in the previous 20 years.

The entities targeted by sanctions are Israeli construction, property development and architectural businesses that have helped to plan, build, supply or market housing and public infrastructure in Israeli settlements in the occupied West Bank.

Miliband – who was criticised by some for broadening the sanctions criteria and planning a ban on trade with illegal settlement – said: “Protecting the two-state solution is the north star of this government’s approach.

“That is why my message on E1 is clear: do not bid, do not build, and do not profit from the destruction of the two-state solution. And we will not stand by while those blocking desperately needed aid deepen the intolerable suffering of civilians in Gaza. The status quo in the West Bank and Gaza is unacceptable.”

But he added in a potential olive branch: “We are committed to working productively with a new Israeli government and the Palestinian Authority to advance lasting peace and security for Israelis and Palestinians alike.”

Miliband and his Middle East minister, Stephen Doughty, have repeatedly highlighted the Israeli government’s refusal to let a variety of dual-use goods into Gaza. The Foreign Office said civilians in Gaza were in desperate need of winter supplies, with catastrophic floods leaving nearly 4,000 households without shelter and 1.4 million people living in tents or makeshift shelters.

According to the UN, more than 150,000 tents and 300,000 tarpaulins bought by humanitarian partners and donors are outside Gaza ready to go in, but are being held by the Israeli authorities. The Israeli authorities also continue to block timber from entering, leaving no emergency shelter kits available in Gaza.

The Israeli government claims the blockage of some goods is necessary to prevent Hamas obtaining items that could be used to attack Israel. The dispute over dual-use goods and closed entry points into Gaza has lasted for more than two years.

articles.title: Milburn calls for welfare state ‘revolution’ as landmark youth unemployment report to be published – UK politics live
articles.excerpt:
Alan Milburn says his plan could cut the welfare bill before the next election, but overall savings will take years

Milburn urges Burnham to spend billions on ‘new deal’ for young people

Alan Milbur...
articles.body_text:
Alan Milburn says his plan could cut the welfare bill before the next election, but overall savings will take years

Milburn urges Burnham to spend billions on ‘new deal’ for young people

Alan Milburn told Sky News this morning that Labour MPs have so far welcomed his proposals.

When Keir Starmer’s government proposed cutting disability benefits last year, there was a huge backbench rebellion and it was forced to back down.

As Pippa Crerar explains here, Milburn has learned lessons from this debacle. He has spent months making a moral and welfare argument for his plans (unlike Starmer and Rachel Reeves, who tried to justify their cuts principally on cost-cutting grounds), and all the signs so far suggest this has paid off.

Milburn said he received an “incredibly positive” response at the meeting with Labour MPs because they recognised there was a “moral imperative” to act, as well as the economic benefits.

Labour MPs “have to vote for it”, he said.

double quotation markLabour is what it says on the tin. It’s the party of work. It’s not the party of welfare and of benefits.

Defending his plan to cut some benefits to fund much better employment support instead, he said:

double quotation markThere will be some young people who are worse off at least initially as a consequence of benefit changes. But in the end, the best thing for people is to get them into work.

There’s so many young people, for example, who come into the welfare system who frankly shouldn’t be there. It’s not inevitable that if somebody has got anxiety or depression or moderate ADHD, that somehow we should be saying to them, ‘What can’t you do?’

Why aren’t we asking them, ‘What could you do? What could we help you do? What is the opportunity that we can provide for you?’

And so that’s what we should do. And that’s why we need this revolution in the welfare state.

More than 300,000 children across Britain are no longer defined as living in poverty, following the government’s decision to scrap the two-child limit for one of the main types of welfare, figures show. The Press Association says:

double quotation markUnder previous rules, families could only receive the child element of universal credit for their first two children.

Universal credit (UC) is the main form of means-tested social security in the UK and is intended to help with living costs for people in work who are on low incomes, as well as those who are unemployed or cannot work.

The decision to scrap the two-child limit for UC was announced by former chancellor Rachel Reeves at the budget in November 2025 and came into effect in April 2026.

Analysis published today by the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) estimates that 301,720 children in Britain are no longer living in households below the poverty line, due to the removal of the UC cap.

Households where income is less than 60% of the median national average, after housing costs, are considered to be living in poverty.

The figures also show 118,630 adults are no longer defined as living in households in poverty, because of the lifting of the two-child rule.

Overall, 1.57 million children are in families that have seen a rise in UC payments since April, including those no longer below the poverty line.

Commenting on the figures, Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, said:

double quotation markThis is about changing the story of children’s lives.

Children who grow up in poverty are more likely to have mental health difficulties, to be Neet and to earn less as adults.

We want to give every child a genuine shot at life – to do well at school, stay healthy, succeed at work – ultimately contributing to their community as adults.

Removing the two-child limit is the most cost-effective way to drive down child poverty rates and is an investment worth making – for those children, for their families, and for the whole country.

This is what the opposition parties have been saying about the Alan Milburn proposals. The full report has not formally been published yet, but it has been circulating in Westminster on an embargoed basis since yesterday and so the parties all know what it says.

The Conservatives says Milburn should be cutting welfare more aggressively. This is from Helen Whately, the shadow work and pensions secretary.

double quotation markConservatives agree with Alan Milburn on the problem, and we want his review to succeed. Where Milburn gets it right, we’ll back him. Especially where he adopts our proposals like shifting from cash sickness benefits to support for milder conditions and cutting national insurance for young people.

Alan Milburn is right to criticise the tax and regulation burdens Labour have imposed on businesses. But his review is too cautious on reversing that damage and too often his answer is the big and expensive hand of the state. Overall, it fails to bring down the welfare bill, proposes billions more in government spending and won’t make the slightest difference for young people stuck on welfare now - because nothing will happen for at least three years.

The Liberal Democrats say they would prefer a proper plan for growth, including joining the single market. Ed Davey, the party leader, says:

double quotation markSuccessive governments have allowed a generation to fall through the cracks. Nearly a million young people are now out of work or training, which is more than there are job vacancies in the entire country. ‘Work not welfare’ means nothing when the work simply isn’t there.

If ministers want to halve the number of Neets by 2036, they need a plan for growth. That means scrapping Labour’s jobs tax, joining the EU single market and cutting the cost of doing business, so firms can afford to hire young people again. No target or guarantee can conjure up jobs that don’t exist.

Reform UK says Milburn is admitting Labour’s policies have failed. Suella Braverman, the party’s education spokesperson, says:

double quotation markAlan Milburn’s call to cut the cost of hiring for employers is a glaring admission Labour’s jobs tax has failed. It destroyed opportunities for workers, and particularly youngsters. Huge amounts of damage could have been avoided if Labour listened to the warnings.

Waiting 10 years to fix the youth jobs crisis is a huge missed opportunity. We would be consigning another generation to the scrap heap.

Reform UK would act now to axe Labour’s jobs tax, double the number of apprenticeships and end university scam courses that laden students with debt.

The Green party says its Youth Jobs guarantee is a much better offer for young people. Mothin Ali, its co-deputy leader, says:

double quotation markWhat we’ve seen so far from the Blair-era minister and adviser to private equity firms is extremely concerning. There is an alternative to threatening vulnerable people with benefits they need, an alternative to unsuitable short-term work.

Andy Burnham promised an end to 40 years of neoliberalism, but this is more of the same tired proposals. The Green party’s true alternative is proper work and training for proper pay, so young people can reach their full potential without the threat of poverty and homelessness.

The Greens have also posted this on social media.

Ed Miliband has announced the first set of sanctions against Israeli companies planning to build illegal settlements in the West Bank, after he pledged to try to prevent settlements that destroy the chances of a two-state solution, Patrick Wintour reports.

Alan Milburn told Sky News that his report recommends paying small businesses £5,000 if they take on a young person who is Neet (not in education, employment or training). He said:

double quotation markWhat we need to do is make it more worthwhile for employers to take on more young people. So we say in this report, if you’re a small business, for example, the government should give you a £5,000 payment for taking on a young person who is Neet to help you absorb the costs of their hiring.

Alan Milburn told Sky News this morning that Labour MPs have so far welcomed his proposals.

When Keir Starmer’s government proposed cutting disability benefits last year, there was a huge backbench rebellion and it was forced to back down.

As Pippa Crerar explains here, Milburn has learned lessons from this debacle. He has spent months making a moral and welfare argument for his plans (unlike Starmer and Rachel Reeves, who tried to justify their cuts principally on cost-cutting grounds), and all the signs so far suggest this has paid off.

Milburn said he received an “incredibly positive” response at the meeting with Labour MPs because they recognised there was a “moral imperative” to act, as well as the economic benefits.

Labour MPs “have to vote for it”, he said.

double quotation markLabour is what it says on the tin. It’s the party of work. It’s not the party of welfare and of benefits.

Defending his plan to cut some benefits to fund much better employment support instead, he said:

double quotation markThere will be some young people who are worse off at least initially as a consequence of benefit changes. But in the end, the best thing for people is to get them into work.

There’s so many young people, for example, who come into the welfare system who frankly shouldn’t be there. It’s not inevitable that if somebody has got anxiety or depression or moderate ADHD, that somehow we should be saying to them, ‘What can’t you do?’

Why aren’t we asking them, ‘What could you do? What could we help you do? What is the opportunity that we can provide for you?’

And so that’s what we should do. And that’s why we need this revolution in the welfare state.

The UK unemployment rate has unexpectedly fallen as the government prepares to release the Alan Milburn report on the youth jobs crisis, Phillip Inman reports.

Good morning. Few government reports have been as long-awaited and well-trailed as the Alan Milburn report into youth unemployment, or Neets (young people not in education, employment or training), that is finally being published this morning. The title, From a Welfare State to a Working State, gives a clue as to the extent of Milburn’s ambition and, if it gets implemented in full, it will be remembered as one of the landmark social reforms of the 21st century (so far).

And even if Milburn only achieves 50% of what he wants (which, sadly, is probably quite a good success rate for the authors of independent government reports), he will change Britain significantly, as Polly Toynbee argues in a must-read column about the report today. She says:

double quotation markThere will, no doubt, be protest from right and left. But never has a policy been so pitch-rolled to flatten critics and sceptics with undeniable evidence that it will be to the good. There is a cornucopia of plans for schools, colleges, the NHS, councils and early years education. Ideas come from visits to see what works elsewhere, notably the Netherlands and Denmark. Seeing proportionally far fewer Neets in those countries, Milburn asked what they did about school and college drop-outs. “They didn’t understand that term,” he tells me. In those countries, if children start to struggle with school attendance, “they go straight round to find them and work out their problem. Here they disappear.”

Politically, this duty will fall on local mayors (or councils, where mayors have not yet been introduced). Their colossal task is to pull together schools, FE colleges, jobcentres, NHS services and local employers. Heaving them out of their silos to collaborate will test mayoral devolution to its limits. With extra funding comes accountability for creating a continuous decline in the number of Neets in their area.

Everywhere, this will be delivered through youth hubs – welcoming places, “not jobcentres where they’re met by security guards, but places only for young people,” Milburn tells me. Last week he visited a model hub in Liverpool, Merseyside Youth Association. Hiring and training a new cohort of work coaches and advisers has begun, so hubs can offer supported internships, short flexi-jobs to ease people into work and experience for those with none on their CVs. Incentives to employers to hire them may include cuts to employers’ national insurance contributions for those aged 21-24 in retail and hospitality. Ordinary earners under 21 are already NI-free …

It’s for Labour and Milburn, who will remain in post to oversee all of this, to prove, with falling Neet numbers, the value of good social investment. If even half these plans work, that will be a great social advance – a generational shift from appeasing the old to finally directing hope and resources towards the young. And it will be about time.

The full report is being published this morning. But it won’t contain any surprises – Milburn has been talking about his proposals for weeks now, and all the main ideas are already in the public domain. Here is our overnight story by Richard Partington, Kiran Stacey and Aletha Adu.

So far, none of the reaction from the charity sector has been particularly hostile. The opposition parties have generally welcomed the bits of the plan that overlap with their own policies, while criticising the rest. But, for the government, the reaction that matters the most will come in the Commons, when Labour MPs get the chance to say what they think.

Milburn has been giving interviews this morning. And he has claimed that, under his plan, the government could start to save money from the welfare budget before the end of this parliament. This is an important pledge because John Healey, the chancellor, was criticised recently by the Tories for failing to propose cutting benefits before the next election.

double quotation markWe should be doing that. We can get the benefits bill down. And by the way, we can do that quickly. We can start in this parliament to get savings from welfare. But what we’ve got to do is start creating opportunities and support for young people.

But those savings would not at first offset the extra government spending his plan would require. Milburn says his proposals would require “an immediate upfront payment” of £500m in the next financial year.

On the Today programme, Milburn argued that, over time, his plan would save money. He explained:

double quotation markWe can either get the benefits bill down through crude cuts. And when that happens, all that then happens is more young people are in destitution and poverty and frankly will show up somewhere else on the ledger in more housing costs or health costs or crime costs.

Or we can do it through more jobs. And my view is that it’s got to be more jobs.

And over time then, what happens by the time the 10-year programme gets to a conclusion, we will have saved about £13.8bn in welfare.

Milburn was referring to the amount saved from the welfare budget. His plans would require extra spending in other areas, and his plan would involve around £5.8bn a year of funding by 2036-37, offset by £3.6bn of welfare savings and £2.4bn of extra tax revenue from people in work.

When it was put to him that in the short term, his plan “costs, doesn’t save”, Milburn replied: “Correct.” And when it was put to him that the “crossover point” when overall savings would overtake overall costs would only happen after 10 years, Milburn replied: “That’s when it happens.”

9.30am: Andy Burnham chairs cabinet, where Alan Milburn will speak about his youth unemployment report.

9.30am: The Department for Work and Pensions publishes quarterly universal credit figures.

Morning: Kemi Badenoch and Helen Whately, the shadow work and pensions secretary, are on a visit in London.

10.30am: Marsha de Cordova MP and Sandro Gozi MEP, co-chairs of the UK-EU Parliamentary Partnership Assembly, hold a press conference after its meeting in London.

11.30am: Milburn holds a press conference to mark the publication of his report.

11.30am: Miatta Fahnbulleh, the energy secretary, takes questions in the Commons.

Noon: Downing Street holds a lobby briefing.

After 12.30pm: Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, is due to give a statement to MPs about the Milburn report.

I’m afraid we are no longer able to have comments open below the line every day on this blog. If you want to contact me, please email politics.live@theguardian.com. You can use this email to flag up corrections, comments for publication, questions or complaints.

articles.title: Crimean Bridge partly collapses as Zelensky hails 'unprecedented' attack by Ukraine
articles.excerpt:
Footage shows Ukrainian missile approach Crimea bridge

Ukraine has severely damaged a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, in what Volodymyr Zelensky says was an "unprecedented operatio...
articles.body_text:
Footage shows Ukrainian missile approach Crimea bridge

Ukraine has severely damaged a critical bridge linking Russia to occupied Crimea, in what Volodymyr Zelensky says was an "unprecedented operation" weeks in the making.

Images shared by Ukrainian officials show a section of the Crimean Bridge - also known as the Kerch Bridge - has collapsed into the water, dealing a logistical and symbolic blow to Russia's war effort.

A Kremlin spokesperson insisted the bridge would be rebuilt "better than before".

Elsewhere, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said the Northern and Southern bridges, both important crossings over the Dnipro River, were closed after Russia targeted the Ukrainian capital overnight.

Ukraine has long targeted the Crimean Bridge, which provides a road and rail route for Russian soldiers heading towards the front line, but has struggled to close it for good.

The damage reported on Tuesday appeared to be far more severe than previously, with a large arched section of the bridge apparently destroyed.

Video footage appeared to show critical damage to the road section, with remnants of the support arch and road deck seen protruding from the water below.

Zelensky said the overnight strike was the result of a seven-stage operation by the military and security services, which saw Ukrainian forces "gradually destroy air defence systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment, and other designated targets on the way to the final objective".

He said the rail section parallel to the bridge's road had also been hit by a wave of drones, though images showed its supporting arch was still standing and a Russian-backed official said some rail services were operating.

The bridge was built by Russia after it invaded and annexed the peninsula in 2014, and was personally opened by Russian President Vladimir Putin in 2018.

While Ukraine has been trying to increase the cost to Russia of waging war economically, by hitting oil refineries and depots, striking the bridge is an attempt to increase the political cost on Putin.

The timing of the strike comes at a significant moment, ahead of Putin meeting the leaders of China and the US. This could cloud his moment back in the spotlight.

Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the bridge would "be restored following Ukrainian strikes, and it will be even better than before", and did not rule out the possibility the strikes were linked to Putin's visit to china.

Russia's Investigative Committee confirmed structural damage and said it had opened a "criminal case... on terrorism charges" after attacks by "Ukraine's armed formations".

For the second day in a row, Russia recorded the biggest Ukrainian drone attack since the war began, with 2,256 drones downed, according to the defence ministry.

The Northern Bridge (pictured in October) is closed after being targeted again by Russia

Zelensky had warned of major attacks in the days leading up to a meeting between Putin, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in China's Shenzhen on Thursday.

Loud explosions were heard in Kyiv just before midnight on Tuesday, with Klitschko saying shortly after that the city had suffered "damage to critical infrastructure systems" and disruption to heating and water.

Some of Kyiv's above-ground subway services were damaged in the overnight attacks, officials said, after civilians were told to go to civil defence shelters.

Eight major bridges span the Dnipro River connecting the western and eastern parts of Kyiv, and an estimated three million residents rely on the bridges to travel across the city.

Strikes on the busy Northern and Southern Bridges will cause major disruption to people's daily lives.

Elsewhere, three people have been injured in a Russian missile attack in the Cherkast region, according to local officials.

The long-term impact of the Crimean Bridge strike is still not fully clear though the risk of a serious transport and logistics crisis for the Russian military has increased significantly.

The collapse of the arched section of the Crimean Bridge has cut off the peninsula's direct road and rail links with Russia – at least until the crossing can be repaired.

However, there is still a land corridor running through the occupied parts of the Zaporizhzhia and Kherson regions - though Ukraine has been systematically striking transport routes across northern Crimea, as well as bridges and other crossings in the area around Chongar.

This has already caused problems with the delivery of fuel and other supplies, including military cargo.

There is a ferry crossing across the Kerch Strait. It could partly compensate for the loss of the bridge, but its capacity is very limited and it is also vulnerable to attack.

Russia could also supply Crimea by sea, but this route is also risky, as Ukrainian naval and aerial drones operate extensively in the area.

In addition, debris from the Crimean Bridge – particularly its enormous arch – may have blocked the shipping channel.

This would make it harder for larger vessels to pass through and create further problems for ports in the Sea of Azov, including Mariupol and Berdiansk.

Russia's launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Approximately one-fifth of Ukraine is now under Russian occupation and Kyiv has refused Putin's demand to give up areas of Ukraine's eastern Donbas that remain under its control.
