articles.title: Ukraine holds peace talks with US, Europe as conflict escalates
articles.excerpt:
Ukraine has held new talks with United States and European officials on ending the war with Russia, hours before Kyiv’s mayor reported strikes on two bridges in the capital.

Ukrainian President Volod...
articles.body_text:
Ukraine has held new talks with United States and European officials on ending the war with Russia, hours before Kyiv’s mayor reported strikes on two bridges in the capital.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy described Monday’s online discussions with US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner and European representatives as “not easy”. But he said participants had agreed to meet in Berlin with the “Coalition of the Willing”, a group of countries supporting Ukraine, as the US and Europe step up peace talks this week.

“Diplomatic processes are actively underway and we hope that these efforts will not be in vain,” Zelenskyy said in his nightly address.

He also warned that Ukrainian intelligence indicated Russia was preparing major strikes that night and throughout Tuesday.

Later on Monday, Kyiv Mayor Vitali Klitschko said preliminary reports indicated that the North and South bridges across the Dnipro River had been hit. Air defence units were operating, and Reuters news agency witnesses heard a series of loud explosions.

Ukraine on Monday struck a key bridge and targeted oil refineries in what Russian defence ministry data indicated was the biggest overnight drone attack on Russia since the start of full-scale war in 2022. The Crimea Bridge was again struck overnight, with nearly 200 drones intercepted near Moscow, according to Telegram statements.

Kushner, US President Donald Trump’s son-in-law, said Washington was making progress towards an agreement in coordination with Russia, Ukraine and Europe.

“Important challenges remain, and a final agreement will require difficult decisions,” he wrote on X.

He said he and Witkoff had also spoken with Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov about the next steps. Their discussions included how to arrange direct engagement between Europe and Russia so each could hear the other’s concerns and proposals.

The exchanges followed last week’s talks in Abu Dhabi, where US, Ukrainian and Russian officials met together for the first time in nine months. Those negotiations produced an agreement on a prisoner exchange but no breakthrough on ending the war.

Witkoff and Kushner later met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow and said European representatives would join the next round. On Monday, Moscow disputed that assertion.

Zelenskyy said representatives from France, Germany, Britain, Italy and Poland had participated fully in Monday’s discussion and would have the same representation in future meetings with Russian negotiators.

Ushakov said Russia had not agreed to expand the talks beyond the existing Russian, Ukrainian and US delegations. No date had been agreed for the next round, he added.

European governments, meanwhile, were preparing their negotiating team while maintaining pressure on Moscow.

Irish Foreign Minister Helen McEntee welcomed renewed talks and the agreement on EU representation following diplomatic meetings in Abu Dhabi and Dublin last week. But she said, “Russia has clearly not changed its position.”

Speaking ahead of Monday’s meeting of EU foreign ministers in Brussels, McEntee said 113 new sanctions on Russia were intended to maintain pressure on Moscow “as it intensified attacks on civilians and critical infrastructure during the winter”.

“We are also working to ensure Ukraine has the finance and the military support it needs while advancing Ukraine’s path to EU membership,” she said.

Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said Russia wanted a lasting peace rather than a temporary ceasefire that would allow Ukraine to recover from the damage inflicted by Russian forces.

He said Moscow sought peace lasting “years, even centuries”, adding that negotiations were complex and could take considerable time.

Separately, Trump said he would discuss the war with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Putin in China, saying he believed Putin wanted to end the war.

“I think he’s backing down a little bit,” Trump told reporters. “Frankly, I think he’d like to see it finish.”

The planned Berlin meeting would allow Ukraine and its supporters to agree on their next negotiating steps. Russia had yet to accept their proposed representation in the talks that would follow.

articles.title: UK seeks closer ties with EU after Brexit fail
articles.excerpt: British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the Brexit promise failed to deliver for the United Kingdom and that the country needs to reset its relationship with the European Union to combat growing ...
articles.body_text:
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham has said the Brexit promise failed to deliver for the United Kingdom and that the country needs to reset its relationship with the European Union to combat growing global isolationism.

During a speech at the Lord Mayor’s Banquet in London on Monday, Burnham compared the outcome of Britain’s divorce from the EU, triggered by a 2016 referendum, to the Hans Christian Andersen fairy tale “The Emperor’s New Clothes”, in which no one is willing to tell the ruler that he is, in fact, naked.

“I do try to say things as I see them,” Burnham said. “And to be frank, we have lost more than we have gained in the last 10 years. The hard Brexit we were given is not good enough for Britain.”

The remarks come ahead of a UK-EU summit in Brussels on Friday, which Burnham said could deliver “real improvements in people’s everyday lives in areas of the country that have felt neglected for too long”.

Any deal, he said, would have to pass three tests: it would have to be consistent with Labour’s manifesto and red lines, improve the Brexit deal to align with what people voted for in 2016 and pass his Makerfield Test, his benchmark for ensuring real improvements for people in parts of the UK that have long felt neglected.

The meeting is a key step in his pledge to reset relations with the 27-nation bloc a decade after the UK voted to leave and six years after its 2020 departure.

The UK is expected to seal a deal on trading food and drink, and make agreements on energy and emissions and a plan to let young people work for limited periods across Britain and the EU.

Burnham said the promise of the pro-Brexit campaign that Britain would “take back control” of its borders, laws and economy had not been delivered. Trade with EU countries has dropped sharply, and estimates of the economic damage range from 4 percent to 8 percent of the UK’s gross domestic product, he said.

Seeking to draw a line under a decade of political turmoil that has made him Britain’s seventh prime minister since 2016, Burnham said the UK was back on the world stage. He argued the country is well positioned to lead in an era of renewed international cooperation because of its experience since 2016.

“Brexit was the first domino to fall in a global move towards more isolationism and protectionism,” he said. “It is exactly what our enemies wanted. Russia wanted disunity within NATO and a weaker Europe.”

Burnham said that he will open a discussion with EU partners on Britain’s long-term relationship with the bloc soon after the Brussels summit. His spokesperson Tom Wells said on Monday that “no assumptions are being made” and “the British public will be the boss of any outcome”.

Until the next national election, Burnham remains bound by the pledge of Keir Starmer, whom he replaced as centre-left Labour Party leader and prime minister, not to rejoin the bloc’s tariff-free customs union or frictionless single market for goods, services and workers.

Erasing that pledge would reignite a subject that split the country: the 2016 referendum vote was 52 percent in favour of leaving the EU and 48 percent in support of remaining.

articles.title: Labor policy backflip will allow more backpackers to work in regional Australia
articles.excerpt:
Number of people allowed to stay for third year on holidaymaker visa to be increased from 5,000 to 25,000 under revised plan

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The federal g...
articles.body_text:
Number of people allowed to stay for third year on holidaymaker visa to be increased from 5,000 to 25,000 under revised plan

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

The federal government has backpedalled on its plan to cut backpacker numbers, arguing the change is the “best possible outcome” for regional industries who had criticised the crackdown because they rely on travellers for labour.

On Tuesday, the Albanese government announced it would lift the proposed cap on third-year working holiday visas, boost regional work requirements and delay the start of a new ballot system.

The home affairs minister, Tony Burke, had announced in a major speech in September plans to cap the number of third-year backpackers to 5,000 from the current level of about 31,000.

Burke said on Tuesday that the cap would now instead be set at 25,000 places. The home affairs minister claimed despite the increase, the net overseas migration (Nom) target would not change, due to a go-slow on approving UK backpacker visas.

“From the day after the [September] speech, myself, the assistant ministers and the department started consultation with industry to work through what’s the best landing place to deliver the total numbers we’re talking about, but to do it in a way that works best for industry,” Burke told reporters.

“There was some slower processing generally happening before the announcement I made, and we have continued the slower processing with UK only since then. That’s provided the space that allowed me to go to the 5,000 to 25,000.”

The major reforms to working holiday visas unveiled in September included a ballot for backpackers seeking to stay a second or third year which would require them to work in the regions.

Under the original proposal, 45,000 backpackers would be allowed to remain for a second year and would be required to work at least three months in a regional area, and just 5,000 places would be allocated for workers for a third year.

The ballot, due to come into effect in November will now be delayed until early next year. From 1 March 2027, backpackers will be required to work in regional areas for four months, instead of three. (The changes won’t apply to travellers who finish their current regional work by the end of February.)

Burke said the government would introduce a new “guarantee” for backpackers granted second- and third-year visas as part of the ballot process.

“From December, people will be able to apply for the guarantee. And from January, every month we’ll be issuing these guarantees. If you receive the guarantee and you do the regional work … then you’ve got the guarantee for the next year,” Burke said. “We’ll be issuing those every month.”

The minister said the extra requirement was “the best possible outcome” for regional areas.

Making backpackers do 120 days of regional work instead of 88 meant that even with the reduction in visa numbers there was a boost in the overall workforce, Burke said.

The changes followed months of consultation with industry, regional and agricultural groups who warned of worker shortages.

The Nationals leader, Matt Canavan, said the initial policy announcement had done “massive damage” to small businesses and farmers in regional areas.

“The damage has been done to confidence in the sector and we still haven’t seen a cut to migration,” Canavan told reporters on Tuesday.

“Having slightly increased these backpacker number caps in this announcement today, the question has got to go to the government, surely the [net] overseas migration figure is now going up further.”

The government has set a net overseas migration target for 2026-27 of 245,000, and plabs to reduce that to 225,000 in 2027-28.

Workers from the UK are exempt from the caps under a free trade agreement signed in 2021. Sources say the prime minister, Anthony Albanese, is in discussions with his UK counterpart, Andy Burnham, to force British backpackers to also do regional work going forward.

Burke said he was optimistic about negotiations.

“The conversations … have been going very well. But until every detail is landed on, I’m not going to get ahead of an announcement,” he said.

“The United Kingdom have a good understanding of the issues that we need to resolve, so I’m not going to put a timeline on it. But I will say I’m very optimistic.”

The Accommodation Australia chief executive, James Goodwin, said Tuesday’s backflip showed the government had listened to concerns from the sector.

“These are sensible and welcome changes that recognise the important contribution working holidaymakers make,” Goodwin said. “Minister Burke has listened to industry concerns and responded with changes that will make a meaningful difference.”

The government has felt pressure to reduce Nom which has become a contested debate.

In September, ahead of the government’s original announcement, One Nation proposed cutting migration numbers by 750,000 over three years by drastically reducing international student and family visas. That policy has since disappeared from One Nation’s website.

The Coalition has also flagged a reduction in net overseas migration.

articles.title: Ecuador's president denies US operates military base despite reports of troop buildup
articles.excerpt: Dana Perino reports on former President Donald Trump's initiative to combat drug cartels in Ecuador. The U.S. is providing military and intelligence assistance to the South American nation, which is g...
articles.body_text:
Dana Perino reports on former President Donald Trump's initiative to combat drug cartels in Ecuador. The U.S. is providing military and intelligence assistance to the South American nation, which is grappling with significant drug-related violence and has become a major cocaine exporter. This joint effort reflects a broader strategy to reassert U.S. influence and target transnational criminal groups, aiming for enhanced security in the region.

Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa denied that the United States operates a military base in his country after an Agence France-Presse (AFP) investigation signaled an expanded U.S. military presence at an air base near the port city of Guayaquil.

"Sometimes there's a specific mission. Sometimes there's a specific operation," Noboa told the news outlet Altavoz, describing U.S. personnel at Taura Air Base as carrying out "temporary activities" under a bilateral security agreement, including intelligence-gathering drone flights.

"We work together. It's not an American base. It's an Ecuadoran base," he commented.

THE UNLIKELY SOUTH AMERICAN ALLY HELPING LEAD TRUMP'S DRUG CARTEL CRACKDOWN

Ecuadorian President Daniel Noboa denied that the United States operates a military base in his country after an Agence France-Presse (AFP) investigation revealed an expanded U.S. military presence at an air base near the port city of Guayaquil. (Franklin Jacome/Agencia Press South/Getty Images)

Noboa's remarks came about a month after AFP had documented an unusual deployment of U.S. military aircraft, dozens of tents and construction of new infrastructure at the air base.

The investigation identified approximately 20 U.S. military flights arriving at Taura between June and mid-October, along with internal documents confirming the presence of American troops.

Several flights originated from U.S. military installations, including Marine Corps Air Station Cherry Point in North Carolina and Dover Air Force Base in Delaware, with stopovers in Puerto Rico and Panama.

The buildup also raised legal concerns among senior Ecuadorian military officials.

AFP cited a September letter in which then-Air Force commander Gen. Mauricio Salazar asked military leaders to clarify the legality of the deployment. Salazar was subsequently removed from his post and reassigned to a less senior role, the report said.

The increased U.S. military presence comes after Ecuadorian voters rejected a Noboa-backed referendum in November 2025 that would have amended the country's constitution to lift its ban on foreign military bases.

US MILITARY BOARDS, SEARCHES AND SINKS VESSEL ALLEGEDLY SUPPORTING LOS CHONEROS NARCO-TERRORISTS

U.S. and Ecuadorian forces launched joint operations Tuesday targeting suspected narco-terrorists in Ecuador, according to U.S. Southern Command. (U.S. Southern Command)

Despite the referendum's defeat, Quito and Washington have deepened security cooperation to combat drug trafficking and transnational organized crime.

Human Rights Watch has described the United States as Ecuador's primary security partner in its crackdown on organized crime, providing equipment, training, intelligence and direct military support.

The watchdog characterized the partnership as "perilous," warning that "both governments have engaged in serious human rights violations fuelled by their insistence on framing their confrontations with organised crime groups as a kind of war."

Since returning to the White House in January 2025, President Donald Trump has designated several Latin American cartels as foreign terrorist organizations and authorized military strikes against vessels in international waters suspected of drug trafficking.

WHITE HOUSE HIGHLIGHTS 'STEEPEST' EVER DECLINE IN US CASUALTIES FROM CARTELS AMID BOAT STRIKES

Ecuador FM Roberto Kury and Ecuadorian police forces during counterdrug mission. (Fox News Digital)

Ecuador has also emerged as a key ally in Trump's crackdown on drug cartels and narcoterrorism, with U.S. and Ecuadorian forces working together to intercept narcotics shipments and dismantle transnational criminal networks, the country's foreign minister told Fox News Digital in September.

Roberto Kury said closer cooperation with Washington had delivered "a lot of positive results" in recent months, citing drug shipments intercepted through U.S. intelligence and joint operations.

"There is an intelligence (sic) and cooperation from the United States, but there is also always the presence of Ecuadorian military or police. They work together," Kury told Fox News Digital on the sidelines of the U.N. General Assembly.

"Most of the drugs go to the United States. So that’s why the United States shares the problem," Kury said.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio has also praised Ecuador as the United States' most "aggressive" partner in its Western Hemisphere crackdown.

Fox News Digital has reached out to Southcom for comment.

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

articles.title: Trump admin opens civil rights probes into 15 colleges over DEI grants
articles.excerpt:
The Department of Education announced a civil rights probe Friday into over a dozen colleges over their teacher preparation programs. (AP Photo/Evan Vucci)

The U.S. Department of Education announced ...
articles.body_text:
The Department of Education announced a civil rights probe Friday into over a dozen colleges over their teacher preparation programs. (AP Photo/Evan Vucci)

The U.S. Department of Education announced Monday that it has opened federal civil rights investigations into several teacher preparation programs following complaints alleging race and sex-based discrimination.

According to a department press release, the Office for Civil Rights (OCR) formally opened the probes on Friday, Nov. 13, targeting programs "designed to recruit, retain, and support future educators" that allegedly "provide sex or race-specific recruitment, support, and financial opportunities for candidates in violation of civil rights laws."

The initial four entities under investigation are the City University of New York (CUNY), the University of Maryland College of Education, the Minnesota Department of Education, and the Minnesota Office of Higher Education. The department noted that OCR is also opening investigations into 11 additional universities over similar allegations.

DEPT OF ED PUSHES AHEAD WITH EFFORTS TO DISMANTLE FEDERAL BUREAUCRACY AFTER BLUE WAVE

A Department of Education sign is displayed outside the Federal Student Aid office on July 17, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Kevin Carter/Getty Images)

The department said OCR will examine whether the programs violate Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964, which prohibits discrimination based on race, color or national origin, or Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972, which prohibits sex-based discrimination in federally funded education programs.

Specifically, federal investigators are examining:

* City University of New York (CUNY): Under investigation over its NYC Men Teach program for alleged discrimination on the basis of both race and sex.

* University of Maryland: Under investigation for alleged racial discrimination in its administration of the Maryland Higher Education Commission Teacher Quality and Diversity Grant Program and the EdTerps CARES Network.

* Minnesota Department of Education: Under investigation for alleged racial discrimination through its Education Tuition Assistance Program, which provides scholarships and stipends to students in teacher preparation programs.

* Minnesota Office of Higher Education: Under investigation for alleged racial discrimination in its administration of the Minnesota Aspiring Teachers of Color Scholarship Pilot Program and the Underrepresented Student Teacher Grant.

A NEW YORK UNIVERSITY FACES JUSTICE DEPARTMENT INVESTIGATION OVER 'BLACK MALE INITIATIVE'

An aerial view of the University of Maryland campus in College Park, Maryland on Nov. 14, 2009. (G Fiume/Getty Images)

A spokesperson from the Minnesota Office of Higher Education told Fox News Digital: "The Minnesota Underrepresented Student Teacher Grant (USTG) was established by the Minnesota Legislature in 2021. OHE is implementing this program in accordance with State law,"

"The Minnesota Aspiring Teachers of Color Scholarship was a pilot program also established by the Minnesota Legislature in 2021. This scholarship is no longer available to Minnesotans as funding ended after the 2024-25 academic year," the spokesperson added.

The investigations stem from complaints filed by the Equal Protection Project (EPP), a legal advocacy group founded by Cornell Law School professor William Jacobson as part of the Legal Insurrection Foundation.

"The Equal Protection Project welcomes the U.S. Department of Education's Office for Civil Rights' decision to open investigations into complaints alleging violations of Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964," Jacobson told Fox News Digital, adding that his organization will cooperate fully with the investigations.

"The opening of these investigations reflects OCR's determination that the allegations warrant further review and underscores the importance of ensuring that all students have access to educational environments free from discrimination based on race, color, or national origin," Jacobson added.

MINNESOTA YANKS RACE-BASED GRANT AFTER DOJ INITIATED CIVIL RIGHTS REVIEW, DOJ REVEALS

The U.S. flag and Department of Education flags whip in the wind outside the department's headquarters on March 6, 2025, in Washington, D.C.  (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

EPP chief counsel Maureen S. Riordan echoed that sentiment, calling the decision "an important step toward addressing serious concerns regarding compliance with federal civil rights protections and ensuring that educational institutions uphold their obligations under Title VI."

A Department of Education spokesperson told Fox News Digital, "The Department will open investigations across the nation based on credible reports that universities with education programs withhold opportunities for recruitment and financial support from candidates based solely on race," adding, "Teachers are the heartbeat of our schools, and the Trump Administration will ensure a future where students are [judged] based on their merit and grit, not the color of their skin."

The enforcement push aligns with President Donald Trump’s effort to eliminate diversity, equity, and inclusion (DEI) initiatives since he returned to office in January 2025. Shortly after his inauguration, Trump signed executive orders aimed at ending DEI programs across the federal workforce and federal contracting, directing agencies to enforce civil rights laws in alignment with the Supreme Court’s 2023 Students for Fair Admissions v. Harvard ruling, which struck down race-based affirmative action in college admissions.

TRUMP ADMINISTRATION PROPOSES STRIPPING TAX-EXEMPT STATUS FROM SCHOOLS USING RACE-BASED PROGRAMS

The Department of Education exclusively told Fox News Digital it will be doubling down on its efforts to enforce federal civil rights violations. (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images)

Department officials previously told Fox News Digital that the administration, led by Education Secretary Linda McMahon, plans to intensify efforts to dismantle federal bureaucracy, strengthen parental rights, and enforce federal civil rights laws against higher education institutions following Democratic victories in key midterm elections earlier this month.

A CUNY spokesperson told Fox News Digital: "CUNY is proud of its role educating the teachers of tomorrow and our programs are open to all students regardless of race, gender or national origin."

The University of Maryland declined to comment. The Minnesota Department of Education did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Joshua Q. Nelson is a reporter for Fox News Digital.

Joshua focuses on cultural trends, education, and public policy. He extensively covered reparations developments across the U.S., the Department of Education, and immigration issues.

Joining Fox News Digital in 2019, he previously graduated from Syracuse University's Maxwell School of Citizenship and Public Affairs and received the University of Pennsylvania's Wharton Public Policy Certificate.

Story tips can be sent to joshua.nelson@fox.com and Joshua can be followed on Instagram, Twitter and LinkedIn.

articles.title: Ethiopia Moyale clashes disrupt livelihoods as territorial dispute deepens
articles.excerpt: Moyale, Ethiopia – Fighting involving police and armed groups affiliated with Ethiopia’s Oromia and Somali regional administrations has disrupted daily life and trade in the southern Borana Zone, as e...
articles.body_text:
Moyale, Ethiopia – Fighting involving police and armed groups affiliated with Ethiopia’s Oromia and Somali regional administrations has disrupted daily life and trade in the southern Borana Zone, as efforts to resolve a longstanding territorial dispute have yet to produce a lasting settlement.

The violence, which escalated in the border town of Moyale in October, has spread to surrounding areas, including the neighbouring districts of Arero and Wachile, leaving communities insecure and uncertain when normal life will resume.

The disruption has affected livelihoods across several parts of the zone, particularly the livestock trade – a major source of income for rural communities. Residents have reported interruptions to business activities and transport services.

A resident of Moyale town, who asked not to be named for security reasons, told Al Jazeera that people remained fearful as tensions persisted between forces affiliated with the two regional administrations.

The resident said gunfire, especially at night, had heightened personal safety concerns, while violence had restricted movement around the town and made routine activities increasingly difficult. Businesses, people raising livestock and transport operators had also been affected, leaving residents uncertain about when the situation would return to normal.

According to Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED), the latest escalation began on October 18, when Somali regional police clashed with ethnic Oromo militia members following the opening of a Somali regional administration office and the raising of its flag in a disputed locality of Moyale.

The conflict monitor’s East Africa senior analyst, Jalale Getachew Birru, reported that a 13-year-old Oromo girl was killed during the confrontation. However, accounts of how she died differ: some people said she was caught in crossfire, while others claimed she was killed after trying to remove the flag.

Members of the Ethiopian National Defence Force intervened and stopped the initial fighting, according to ACLED. The following day, Oromo residents staged a demonstration against the office opening and the girl’s death, blocking the main road and forcing businesses to close.

Elders and security officials from both sides later agreed to remove the Somali regional flag and suspend the office’s opening. However, the agreement did not prevent further confrontations. ACLED reported that Somali residents also demonstrated against the arrangement on October 20, closing the main road and disrupting transport services.

Fighting escalated again on October 22, when Somali regional police clashed with Oromia regional police and Oromo militia members in several locations in Moyale. ACLED also reported clashes involving Oromo and Somali militias in parts of Arero and Wachile districts.

The violence is rooted in longstanding disagreements over administrative boundaries, political representation and access to land and natural resources. These disputes have repeatedly fuelled tensions between Borana Oromo and Somali communities along the regional border.

A security official familiar with the situation in Moyale told Al Jazeera that clashes were continuing and that attempts to broker an agreement between representatives of the Oromia and Somali regional administrations had failed. He said resolving the crisis required direct and immediate involvement by the federal government.

The federal government’s role has consequently become a central question in efforts to contain the violence. Although members of the Ethiopian National Defence Force intervened during the initial October 18 confrontation, ACLED documented further clashes involving regional police and militia members from October 22 onwards.

The crisis has also drawn attention beyond Ethiopia’s borders. On November 9, Kenya’s Prime Cabinet Secretary Musalia Mudavadi said he had spoken with his Ethiopian counterpart and urged the government in Addis Ababa to help restore stability so that people who had fled into Kenya could return home.

Reporting by Kenya’s The Star newspaper said Mudavadi put the number of Ethiopians who had crossed into Kenya at approximately 40,000 at the time. He said the Ethiopian government had assured Kenya that it would work towards restoring normality.

Cameron Hudson, a political and security analyst and former director for African affairs at the US National Security Council, said the crisis reflected wider challenges facing Ethiopia’s federal system and its management of regional disputes.

Hudson said federal forces were already preoccupied with security challenges elsewhere in the country. He also pointed to a perception among Somali communities that Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed and his Prosperity Party favour the Oromo, Abiy’s ethnic group.

Hudson said previous mediation efforts had largely failed because the territorial dispute along the regional border remained unresolved.

The historical background includes a referendum organised on October 24, 2004, to determine the administration of 463 small communities along the Oromia-Somali regional border, according to Ethiopia’s National Election Board.

However, research by Boku Tache, published in a doctoral thesis at the Norwegian University of Life Sciences in 2008, found that the referendum was conducted in Liban and parts of Arero, while the Moyale case remained unresolved.

The research also examined how displacement, competing claims over grazing land and access to traditional resources contributed to tensions between Borana and Somali communities. These historical disputes continue to provide important context for the current confrontation.

Hudson added that successive Ethiopian governments had failed to engage local communities to address the underlying causes of territorial tensions, instead responding after violence had erupted.

The humanitarian consequences have extended beyond Ethiopia. On October 28, the United Nations refugee agency (UNHCR) said local authorities estimated that up to 50,000 people had crossed into Kenya since October 22 to escape the fighting. The agency said registration and verification were continuing, meaning the figure remained provisional.

Many of those arriving in Kenya were women and children, according to the UNHCR, which identified food, drinking water, emergency shelter, sanitation and healthcare as urgent needs.

For residents in the affected areas, immediate priorities remain the restoration of security and the resumption of livelihoods. With the territorial dispute unresolved and the two regional administrations yet to reach a lasting agreement, uncertainty continues over when affected communities will be able to return to normal life.

“The federal government is ultimately responsible for addressing violence, even along regional borders,” Hudson told Al Jazeera.

articles.title: Netflix's 'Untold' series tackles the New York Giants' miracle Super Bowl XLII upset of the Patriots next
articles.excerpt:
Lane Kiffin has failed to live up to the promise LSU fans had when he was hired, and Dakich points out how Brian Kelly faired better in SEC play, despite not having a $50 Million roster.

Christmas ca...
articles.body_text:
Lane Kiffin has failed to live up to the promise LSU fans had when he was hired, and Dakich points out how Brian Kelly faired better in SEC play, despite not having a $50 Million roster.

Christmas came early for Giants fans. It's not Jaxson Dart's return, though all of New Jersey is eagerly waiting for that day.

Netflix announced on Monday that a new installment in the Untold series will drop Dec. 21. Titled One Giant Upset, the documentary focuses on the miracle New York Giants team that upset the Patriots in 2008.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Netflix's Untold has previously unpacked the wildest sagas in sports, from Manti Te'o's catfishing scandal and the Malice at the Palace brawl to Johnny Manziel and Urban Meyer's Florida Gators. Now, Big Blue gets the spotlight.

ELI MANNING FINALLY REVEALS WHY HE WRIGGLED HIS WAY OUT OF PLAYING FOR CHARGERS

Are they going to retell stories we've all heard in the nearly two decades since the G-Men won that ring? Of course. Will it be sweet to revisit the night Eli Manning and company broke New England's team of destiny? Absolutely.

Quarterback Eli Manning of the New York Giants poses with the Vince Lombardi Trophy after the Giants defeated the Patriots by a score of 21-17 in Super Bowl XLVI at Lucas Oil Stadium on Feb. 5, 2012 in Indianapolis, Indiana. (Rob Carr/Getty Images)

New York Giants wide receiver Plaxico Burress caught the game-winning touchdown in the fourth quarter as the Giants beat the New England Patriots 17-14 in Super Bowl XLII at University of Phoenix Stadium in Glendale, Ariz., on Sunday, Feb. 3, 2008. (MediaNews Group via Getty Images)

For Giants fans, that 2007 squad remains unforgettable because of how ugly things started. New York opened 0-2 with head coach Tom Coughlin on the hot seat before rattling off 11 straight road wins, including playoff upsets in Tampa, Dallas, and minus-one-degree Green Bay.

SUPER BOWL CHAMPION PLAXICO BURRESS COMPARES PLAYING FOR JETS TO HIS TIME IN PRISON: 'A F—KING LOSER'

After trading haymakers with New England in a 38-35 Week 17 loss, defensive coordinator Steve Spagnuolo unleashed his four-end NASCAR pass rush in the rematch: Super Bowl XLII. Michael Strahan, Justin Tuck, and Osi Umenyiora sacked Tom Brady five times, holding the historic offense to 14 points.

Then came the legendary fourth quarter: Manning slipping out of three jerseys, David Tyree pinning the football to his helmet, and Plaxico Burress — playing on a torn ankle ligament — hauling in the winning score.

TOM BRADY ADMITS TO MORE MOTIVATION AFTER DEFLATEGATE SUSPENSION, REVEALS WHAT HE DID WHILE AWAY FROM PATRIOTS

Manning and Strahan lead the documentary's Giants lineup alongside Coughlin, Spagnuolo, Tuck, Shaun O'Hara, Antonio Pierce, Sam Madison, Burress, and Tyree, joined by Brady.

New York Giants defensive end Osi Umenyiora (72) hits New England Patriots quarterback Tom Brady (12) on the final drive of Super Bowl XLVI at Lucas Oil Stadium on Feb. 5, 2012. (TYSON TRISH/USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Image)

Hearing Brady get honest about the toughest loss of his career adds real juice to the show. Still, watching Netflix celebrate one of the landmark games in NFL history highlights a total joke.

DREW BREES GIVES HIS STANCE ON ELI MANNING'S PRO FOOTBALL HALL OF FAME CANDIDACY AMID STRONG DEBATE

Super Bowl XLII defined an era, and Manning owns two Super Bowl MVPs against the Belichick-Brady dynasty, yet the Pro Football Hall of Fame has passed him over twice. Make it make sense. Leaving the architect of football's biggest upset out of Canton is a Giant mistake.

Send us your thoughts: alejandro.avila@outkick.com / Follow along on X: @alejandroaveela

Alejandro Avila is a longtime writer at OutKick, living in Southern California.

articles.title: Democratic judge under fire for releasing violent offenders calls bail law a ‘direct assault’ on rights
articles.excerpt:
Birmingham Mayor Randall Woodfin tells community that "It’s your time to step up and we need you." (Credit: WBMA)

A Democratic Alabama judge facing mounting scrutiny over past decisions to release vi...
articles.body_text:
Birmingham Mayor Randall Woodfin tells community that "It’s your time to step up and we need you." (Credit: WBMA)

A Democratic Alabama judge facing mounting scrutiny over past decisions to release violent offenders is criticizing a state law that allows defendants charged with certain violent crimes to be denied bail.

Circuit Court Judge David Carpenter called Alabama’s Aniah’s Law a direct assault on constitutional rights, arguing that defendants should not be held indefinitely based solely on criminal charges, citing the constitutional presumption of innocence.

In a social media post, Carpenter argued that critics of government overreach involving license plate cameras, such as Flock cameras, are not equally concerned about expanded pretrial detention laws.

"Can someone explain to me why the people who are so alarmed that a flock camera might spot their car on a public road, and they call that government overreach, are silent on the fact that voters across the country keep overwhelmingly passing new laws to empower the government to hold you in jail indefinitely on the basis of a charge only," Carpenter said.

THE SURVEILLANCE CAMERA ON YOUR STREET CORNER: LAWFUL SPYING OR CONSTITUTIONALLY PROBLEMATIC?

Damien McDaniel, 22, is connected to more than a dozen murders in the Birmingham, Alabama, area since July 2023, according to city police. Carpenter approved a plea deal for McDaniel before his alleged shooting spree left 18 dead.  (Alabama Department of Corrections / Birmingham Police Department)

"These laws, like Alabama’s Aniah’s Law, are a direct assault on the Constitutional guarantee of the presumption of innocence. But no one is talking about this at all, much less expressing the hysteria associated with having a camera see a license plate," he said.

Although Aniah’s Law was originally passed in 2022, Alabama voters approved a major constitutional amendment this year expanding the law to cover additional offenses. The expansion added attempted murder, solicitation or conspiracy to commit murder, and discharging a firearm or explosives into an occupied dwelling, building or vehicle.

"We are all one accusation away from being a criminal defendant," Carpenter said in a post on Facebook.

WHITE HOUSE CALLS DC POLICIES 'INSANITY' AFTER 19-YEAR-OLD GUNMAN GETS PROBATION IN SHOOTING

Carpenter has faced controversy over several judicial decisions over the years. Local outlet 1819 News reported that he previously described himself online as a "far left, liberal, progressive, democratic socialist."

In April 2023, Carpenter approved a plea deal for Damien McDaniel, who was arrested in 2019 for shooting two people in a car when he was 17 years old, 1819 News reported. After being released from jail, McDaniel allegedly went on a 14-month shooting spree across Alabama, killing 18 people and injuring more than 30 others.

Carpenter approved a plea deal for Damien McDaniel, 22, who was later linked to multiple shootings over 14 months. (Birmingham Police Department / WBRC)

Carpenter also granted bond to Raukeem Cunningham in connection with the 2022 shooting death of a teenage girl, the outlet reported. While out on bond, Cunningham was arrested and charged with fatally shooting three people at a Bessemer gas station in 2024, prompting the revocation of his original bond.

In addition, Carpenter reportedly dismissed a 2015 rape charge against Fredrick Terrenda Hampton in 2019, according to reports. The dismissal came just two days before Hampton met Paighton Houston, who later disappeared. Her body was found buried behind a home after she died of an accidental overdose.

CONVICTED SERIAL RAPIST ORIGINALLY SENTENCED TO 124 YEARS WALKS FREE AFTER 20, SPARKING OUTRAGE

Frederick Hampton, 50, was wanted in the disappearance of Paighton Houston, left, last seen leaving a Birmingham, Alabama, bar on Dec. 30. Her body was found two weeks later.  (Jefferson County Sheriff's Office)

Hampton pleaded guilty to abuse of a corpse in connection with Houston’s death, and Carpenter gave him a 20-year split sentence with only three years to serve in custody, the outlet said.

Houston’s mother ultimately asked Alabama Attorney General Steve Marshall to investigate Carpenter over his decision to release Hampton, whom critics described as a repeat sex offender.During his campaign for judicial office, Carpenter said one of his major goals was to "reform the criminal justice system in Alabama."

"If elected, I will work to reduce the number of repeat offenders while addressing the expensive problem of prison overcrowding in Alabama," he said.

Bonny Chu is a Breaking and Trending News Writer for Fox News Digital

articles.title: Democratic judge under fire for releasing violent offenders calls bail law a ‘direct assault’ on rights
articles.excerpt:
Birmingham Mayor Randall Woodfin tells community that "It’s your time to step up and we need you." (Credit: WBMA)

A Democratic Alabama judge facing mounting scrutiny over past decisions to release vi...
articles.body_text:
Birmingham Mayor Randall Woodfin tells community that "It’s your time to step up and we need you." (Credit: WBMA)

A Democratic Alabama judge facing mounting scrutiny over past decisions to release violent offenders is criticizing a state law that allows defendants charged with certain violent crimes to be denied bail.

Circuit Court Judge David Carpenter called Alabama’s Aniah’s Law a direct assault on constitutional rights, arguing that defendants should not be held indefinitely based solely on criminal charges, citing the constitutional presumption of innocence.

In a social media post, Carpenter argued that critics of government overreach involving license plate cameras, such as Flock cameras, are not equally concerned about expanded pretrial detention laws.

"Can someone explain to me why the people who are so alarmed that a flock camera might spot their car on a public road, and they call that government overreach, are silent on the fact that voters across the country keep overwhelmingly passing new laws to empower the government to hold you in jail indefinitely on the basis of a charge only," Carpenter said.

THE SURVEILLANCE CAMERA ON YOUR STREET CORNER: LAWFUL SPYING OR CONSTITUTIONALLY PROBLEMATIC?

Damien McDaniel, 22, is connected to more than a dozen murders in the Birmingham, Alabama, area since July 2023, according to city police. Carpenter approved a plea deal for McDaniel before his alleged shooting spree left 18 dead.  (Alabama Department of Corrections / Birmingham Police Department)

"These laws, like Alabama’s Aniah’s Law, are a direct assault on the Constitutional guarantee of the presumption of innocence. But no one is talking about this at all, much less expressing the hysteria associated with having a camera see a license plate," he said.

Although Aniah’s Law was originally passed in 2022, Alabama voters approved a major constitutional amendment this year expanding the law to cover additional offenses. The expansion added attempted murder, solicitation or conspiracy to commit murder, and discharging a firearm or explosives into an occupied dwelling, building or vehicle.

"We are all one accusation away from being a criminal defendant," Carpenter said in a post on Facebook.

WHITE HOUSE CALLS DC POLICIES 'INSANITY' AFTER 19-YEAR-OLD GUNMAN GETS PROBATION IN SHOOTING

Carpenter has faced controversy over several judicial decisions over the years. Local outlet 1819 News reported that he previously described himself online as a "far left, liberal, progressive, democratic socialist."

In April 2023, Carpenter approved a plea deal for Damien McDaniel, who was arrested in 2019 for shooting two people in a car when he was 17 years old, 1819 News reported. After being released from jail, McDaniel allegedly went on a 14-month shooting spree across Alabama, killing 18 people and injuring more than 30 others.

Carpenter approved a plea deal for Damien McDaniel, 22, who was later linked to multiple shootings over 14 months. (Birmingham Police Department / WBRC)

Carpenter also granted bond to Raukeem Cunningham in connection with the 2022 shooting death of a teenage girl, the outlet reported. While out on bond, Cunningham was arrested and charged with fatally shooting three people at a Bessemer gas station in 2024, prompting the revocation of his original bond.

In addition, Carpenter reportedly dismissed a 2015 rape charge against Fredrick Terrenda Hampton in 2019, according to reports. The dismissal came just two days before Hampton met Paighton Houston, who later disappeared. Her body was found buried behind a home after she died of an accidental overdose.

CONVICTED SERIAL RAPIST ORIGINALLY SENTENCED TO 124 YEARS WALKS FREE AFTER 20, SPARKING OUTRAGE

Frederick Hampton, 50, was wanted in the disappearance of Paighton Houston, left, last seen leaving a Birmingham, Alabama, bar on Dec. 30. Her body was found two weeks later.  (Jefferson County Sheriff's Office)

Hampton pleaded guilty to abuse of a corpse in connection with Houston’s death, and Carpenter gave him a 20-year split sentence with only three years to serve in custody, the outlet said.

Houston’s mother ultimately asked Alabama Attorney General Steve Marshall to investigate Carpenter over his decision to release Hampton, whom critics described as a repeat sex offender.During his campaign for judicial office, Carpenter said one of his major goals was to "reform the criminal justice system in Alabama."

"If elected, I will work to reduce the number of repeat offenders while addressing the expensive problem of prison overcrowding in Alabama," he said.

Bonny Chu is a Breaking and Trending News Writer for Fox News Digital

articles.title: James Comer launches bid for Kentucky governor
articles.excerpt:
House Oversight Committee chairman Rep. James Comer, R-Ky., discusses Democrats’ intention to pursue legal action against President Donald Trump and his allies on ‘The Big Weekend Show.’

House Oversi...
articles.body_text:
House Oversight Committee chairman Rep. James Comer, R-Ky., discusses Democrats’ intention to pursue legal action against President Donald Trump and his allies on ‘The Big Weekend Show.’

House Oversight Committee Chairman James Comer, R-Ky., is launching a campaign for governor on Monday night.

"Serving this state is a calling for me," Comer said during a tele-townhall. "Kentucky needs a leader whose policies will lead to growth and good-paying jobs. We need a leader whose priority will be to reduce taxes so Kentuckians can keep more of what they earn."

Comer teased a "major announcement" for Monday night earlier in the day. A source familiar with his plans told Fox News Digital it would be his long-awaited campaign to lead the commonwealth of Kentucky.

REDISTRICTING EFFORTS BLOW UP IN REPUBLICANS' FACES AMID HISTORIC HOUSE LOSSES

House Oversight Committee Chairman James Comer, R-Ky., speaks at a press conference at the U.S. Capitol on Oct. 21, 2025 in Washington, D.C. (Tasos Katopodis/Getty Images)

Comer spent the majority of his announcement fielding questions from Kentuckians on topics like education, small business, and high prices.

Among the policies he advocated for was reducing Kentucky's income tax to zero.

"We all talk about attracting new businesses and new industry to Kentucky," Comer said. "If we can get that existing income tax to zero, people are going to have more money to spend, and we're going to be able to attract more good-paying jobs to Kentucky, which will be able to keep our best and brightest in the state and help our state grow into the future."

Kentucky's gubernatorial election will take place in November 2027, with the primaries set for May of that year.

Gov. Andy Beshear, who is widely considered a potential contender for the Democratic presidential primary in 2028, is term-limited.

Andy Beshear, governor of Kentucky, speaks during a campaign event with Rob Sand, then-Democratic gubernatorial candidate for Iowa, not pictured, at The River Center in Des Moines, Iowa, US, on Sunday, June 7, 2026. (KC McGinnis/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Comer ran for Kentucky governor in 2015 but narrowly lost the GOP primary to former Gov. Matt Bevin.

But this election cycle will likely see the House lawmaker enter as the frontrunner for his party's nomination.

Comer has served in the House of Representatives since November 2016, when he won a special election for Kentucky's 1st congressional district. Since then, his profile has skyrocketed as the top Republican on the House Oversight Committee for the better part of the last six years.

FOX NEWS VOTER POLL: HOW DEMOCRATS TOOK CONTROL OF THE SENATE

As committee chairman since Republicans took back the House majority in 2023, he's launched investigations into former President Joe Biden's use of autopen and the federal government's handling of Jeffrey Epstein's case, among others.

Rep. James Comer, R-Ky., chairman of the House Oversight and Accountability Committee, left, and Rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, attend a hearing in Washington, D.C., on March 4, 2026. (Graeme Sloan/Bloomberg/Getty Images)

And despite Beshear's popularity as the state's two-term Democratic governor, Kentucky has historically been seen as a red state.

President Donald Trump defeated former Vice President Kamala Harris by roughly 30 points there in 2024. He beat former President Joe Biden there by 25.9% in 2020.

Elizabeth Elkind is a politics reporter for Fox News Digital leading coverage of the House of Representatives. Previous digital bylines seen at Daily Mail and CBS News.

Follow on Twitter at @liz_elkind and send tips to elizabeth.elkind@fox.com

articles.title: Illegal alien accused of attempted murder at large after Rikers release despite ICE detainer: DHS
articles.excerpt:
NYC ICE official Kenneth Genalo blasts Mayor Zohran Mamdani and sanctuary policies, warning they force agents into dangerous street arrests and put public safety at risk.

A Guyanese citizen living in...
articles.body_text:
NYC ICE official Kenneth Genalo blasts Mayor Zohran Mamdani and sanctuary policies, warning they force agents into dangerous street arrests and put public safety at risk.

A Guyanese citizen living in the United States illegally remains at large after being released from custody in New York City earlier this month, despite facing multiple violent felony charges and an active federal immigration detainer, according to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS).

DHS officials stated that Delon Raymond Jaundoo was arrested in Brooklyn on charges including attempted murder, first- and second-degree assault, criminal use of a firearm, and multiple counts of criminal possession of a loaded weapon.

His prior criminal record also includes an arrest for third-degree assault.

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) lodged an immigration detainer for Jaundoo on April 29, which the New York City Department of Correction declined to honor, allowing him to be released from Rikers Island.

MANHUNT UNDERWAY FOR VIOLENT ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT WHO WAS RELEASED UNDER NYC SANCTUARY POLICIES

Delon Raymond Jaundoo, an illegal immigrant from Guyana, has multiple violent crime arrest, including for attempted murder. He remains at large after he was released from Rikers Island Jail in New York City under the city's sanctuary policies, the Department of Homeland Security said. (Department of Homeland Security; Getty Images)

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin criticized New York’s sanctuary policies following the release, arguing that state and local laws prevent cooperation with federal immigration authorities even in cases involving violent offenses.

Jaundoo lawfully entered the country during the Obama administration but overstayed his authorized stay, which expired in January 2015, according to DHS.

"Despite these violent charges, sanctuary politicians in New York refused to honor ICE’s detainer and released this criminal back onto the streets to put more American lives in danger," Mullin said in a statement. "Under Governor Kathy Hochul, New York has become a hotbed of illegal alien crime."

DHS SECRETARY BASHES NEW YORK LEADERSHIP AFTER ANNOUNCING THOUSANDS OF ARRESTS IN SWEEPING OPERATION

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani signs executive orders with campaign volunteers during an appearance at Grand Army Plaza in Brooklyn on January 2, 2026, in New York City. (Spencer Platt/Getty Images)

"The sooner we put an end to these reckless sanctuary policies, the sooner we can all work together to make America safe again," he added.

Jaundoo's release comes amid ongoing restrictions on local cooperation with federal immigration enforcement.

HOCHUL BOASTS 'I JUST BANNED IT' AS NEW YORK OUTLAWS LOCAL POLICE PARTNERSHIPS WITH ICE

Upon taking office, New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani signed an executive order limiting city coordination with ICE, and a state law signed by Gov. Kathy Hochul took effect in August barring local authorities from cooperating with federal immigration officials.

DHS stated that several other illegal immigrants arrested for or convicted of violent crimes, including murder, arson, assault, and rape, have similarly been released from custody under the state's current policies.

"Governor Hochul has been clear: New York State is not and never will be a sanctuary for violent criminals," a spokesperson for Hochul told Fox News Digital. "By law, New York State always notifies federal immigration enforcement of any non-citizen serving a State prison sentence. Any assertion otherwise is a blatant mischaracterization of the facts meant to distract from the cruelty and violence we’ve seen from Secretary Mullin’s ICE agents."

Fox News Digital has reached out to Mamdani's office for comment.

Louis Casiano is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to louis.casiano@fox.com.

articles.title: Ukraine hits Putin's prized bridge in record drone blitz as Kremlin tells lawmakers to prepare for 'victory'
articles.excerpt: The upcoming trilateral summit in China between President Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin faces critical global challenges. Alexandria Hoff reports on key agenda items, while retired Navy Captain...
articles.body_text:
The upcoming trilateral summit in China between President Trump, Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin faces critical global challenges. Alexandria Hoff reports on key agenda items, while retired Navy Captain Brent Sadler analyzes strategic threats from Iran. Discussions are expected to address nuclear talks, international trade and the potential inclusion of tech leaders.

Ukraine launched what Russia described as the largest overnight drone attack of the war Monday, striking President Vladimir Putin's prized Crimea bridge and setting industrial facilities ablaze, as separate reports revealed a covert French military mission in Ukraine and preparations in Moscow for a possible return of Russian troops.

The developments came days before President Donald Trump is expected to meet Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping in China, amid renewed U.S.-brokered efforts to end the nearly five-year conflict.

"The sheer scale and effectiveness of these drone attacks are remarkable," retired Air Force Lt. Gen. Richard Newton told Fox News Digital. "Ukraine has developed the capability to produce large numbers of drones and strike targets once considered a safe haven deep inside Russia."

UKRAINE TARGETS RUSSIA WITH OVER 1,000 DRONES, KILLING 2 AS MOSCOW HOLDS LAST DAY OF ELECTIONS

Flames engulf industrial structures as a massive fire lights up the night sky in Nizhnekamsk, Russia, Nov. 15, 2026. (Reuters)

Russia's Defense Ministry claimed its forces intercepted 1,336 Ukrainian drones across 16 regions, exceeding the previous overnight record of 1,254 on Oct. 29, Reuters reported Nov. 16. The numbers could not be independently verified.

Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said about 600 drones had been launched toward the capital region since Sunday evening, with 191 intercepted.

Russian-installed Crimean governor Sergei Aksyonov confirmed that the Kerch Strait bridge, linking occupied Crimea to mainland Russia, had been struck. The Kremlin characterized the damage as minor. Road traffic was temporarily suspended for repairs, while trains continued running, according to Russian transportation officials.

The bridge is both a strategically important supply route and a symbol of Russia's annexation of Crimea in 2014.

The strikes also hit Russia's energy sector. Rostov regional governor Yuri Slyusar reported fires at four industrial sites in Azov, where three people were injured. Officials in neighboring Krasnodar said a separate fire broke out at an industrial facility in Ilsky. Falling drone debris reportedly injured six people in the Krasnodar region.

ZELENSKYY ACCUSES PUTIN OF DEFYING TRUMP'S CEASEFIRE PUSH, SENDS POINTED MESSAGE TO WHITE HOUSE

Rescuers from the State Emergency Service of Ukraine work at a packaging facility damaged by a Russian attack in Odesa region, Ukraine, on November 16, 2026. The strike destroyed a two-storey administrative and warehouse building, damaged the roof of a production facility and shattered windows. Two people were injured in the attack. (Nina Liashonok/Ukrinform via Reuters)

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy claimed Sunday that strikes had disabled more than half of Russia's refining capacity, a figure Fox News Digital could not verify. Two industry sources separately estimated that recent attacks reduced refining capacity by approximately 30%, Reuters reported.

"Putin has a serious problem on his hands," Newton said. "Russia is enormous in terms of size; there’s simply no way to 100% defend every refinery, airfield, and military installation."

Newton said Ukraine's campaign was designed to strengthen its negotiating position while disrupting Russia's military and logistics networks.

"I don’t believe Ukraine has reached a culminating point yet, by any stretch, to change Putin’s mind, but sustained military and economic pressure just may eventually at some point force him to reconsider his position," he said.

In a separate development, Radio France Internationale reported Nov. 16 that French troops had been operating inside Ukraine since at least summer 2026 as part of a confidential mission codenamed "Volia."

The mission reportedly consists of small teams making short visits to train Ukrainian personnel and maintain equipment. RFI said French lawmakers had not been informed and alleged that an established French training operation in Poland, known as "Gerfaut," provided a gateway for deployments into Ukraine.

An anonymous source familiar with the mission confirmed French personnel's presence to AFP, while stressing that they were not combat troops.

"The rotation of French trainers supporting Ukraine in France, Poland, or occasionally in Ukraine is a reality," the source told AFP. "But this is not a military operation. There is absolutely no intention of engaging in coercive actions."

France's military general staff did not immediately comment to AFP. The number of troops involved remains unknown.

Smoke and flames rise over Moscow on June 18, 2026, following a Ukrainian drone attack that hit the Kapotnya oil refinery and other targets in the Russian capital. (East2West)

Meanwhile, Russian newspaper Vedomosti reported Nov. 16 that Kremlin officials had instructed lawmakers from Putin's United Russia party to prepare for "victory" and the return of personnel from the battlefield.

The message was reportedly delivered during a closed-door seminar attended by senior presidential administration official Sergei Kiriyenko. A source described lawmakers being told to anticipate the possibility of soldiers returning home simultaneously.

The report provided no timetable and did not establish that Putin had ordered a withdrawal or decided to end the war.

The reports emerged after U.S.-brokered talks in Abu Dhabi last week resulted in a major prisoner-exchange agreement but no breakthrough over territory.

Trump, Putin and Xi were due to meet Thursday, Nov. 19, in Shenzhen, China, with Kremlin aide Yuri Ushakov describing the trilateral summit as a potentially significant event.

Newton expressed skepticism about an immediate diplomatic breakthrough. "I don't anticipate a major breakthrough on any issue, including Russia's war against Ukraine," he said.

Left to right: Russian President Vladimir Putin, U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping (Reuters)

"If President Trump has any discussions with Xi and Putin regarding Ukraine I would advise him to look those two leaders in the eye and underscore the U.S. is not backing down in our support to the Ukrainian people as they valiantly defend their homeland," he concluded.

Efrat (Effie) Lachter is a reporter for Fox News Digital with more than 15 years of experience covering conflict, global affairs, human rights and political accountability. She has directed and produced more than 200 documentary segments across more than 40 countries, documenting conflicts, humanitarian crises, corruption, human trafficking, gender-based violence and the human stories behind major world events.

Lachter’s reporting has taken her into conflict zones and crisis areas across the Middle East, Europe, Asia and Africa. Her work has included uncovering human trafficking networks, revealing an ISIS underground torture prison in Syria, documenting the war in Ukraine and interviewing senior political figures and world leaders. She was also among the Western journalists who entered Russia after the war began to bring testimonies from Putin’s opposition. Lachter is the recipient of the 2022 Peres Center for Peace Award and was a 2023–2024 Knight-Wallace Journalism Fellow at the University of Michigan. She also won two Rockower Awards for Excellence in Reporting. She holds a bachelor's degree in communication and a master's degree in political science.

articles.title: Third US aircraft carrier arrives in Middle East as Iran rules out UN nuclear inspections
articles.excerpt: Stakes rise as President Donald Trump prepares for his Asia trip to hold trilateral talks on Thursday. Christian Whiton analyzes the geopolitical implications alongside reports of Jensen Huang weighin...
articles.body_text:
Stakes rise as President Donald Trump prepares for his Asia trip to hold trilateral talks on Thursday. Christian Whiton analyzes the geopolitical implications alongside reports of Jensen Huang weighing an Nvidia comeback 33 years after founding the company.

The USS Roosevelt aircraft carrier on Sunday reportedly entered the region overseen by U.S. Central Command, which means that the American military now has three carriers positioned in the region again.

"The USS Roosevelt aircraft carrier has arrived in the U.S. military central command (CENTCOM) area of responsibility earlier on Sunday, a U.S. official tells me," Israeli journalist Barak Ravid wrote in a Sunday post on X. "The U.S. military now has three air craft carrier strike groups in CENTCOM."

The Pentagon referred Fox News Digital to CENTCOM, which did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment on Monday.

IRAN VOWS 'WE WILL FIND YOU' TO 2 US NAVY OFFICERS THE DAY WARSHIP RETURNS FROM MIDDLE EAST

An EA-18G Growler assigned to Electric Attack Squadron (VAQ) 137 lands aboard the aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt (CVN-71) while the ship is moored in Honolulu, Hawaii, during Exercise RIMPAC (Rim of the Pacific) 2026 on July 17, 2026. (Michelle Bir / AFP via Getty Images)

The news comes as the U.S.-Iran war continues more than eight months after it began earlier this year.

There were previously three carriers positioned in the region earlier this year, as CENTCOM noted in April.

BLINKEN WARNS US GROUND INVASION OF IRAN WOULD BE 'ABSOLUTE DISASTER' AS TEHRAN ESCALATES ATTACKS

A flight deck director signals an F-35C Lightning II on the flight deck aboard the USS Theodore Roosevelt (CVN 71) during Exercise RIMPAC (Rim of the Pacific) 2026 while underway in the Pacific Ocean near Hawaii on July 17, 2026. (Michelle Bir / AFP via Getty Images)

Iranian Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi has reportedly indicated that the nation will not grant the International Atomic Energy Agency access to facilities until the war has concluded.

"We will not grant the IAEA access to the facilities until Iran's conditions are met and the war has permanently ended," he said, according to CBS News.

DHS CHIEF MULLIN SAYS IRAN POSES DAILY THREAT TO TRUMP AND HIS FAMILY AMID DRONE CONCERNS

A Persian-to-English translation from material on Iran's irib-news.ir website indicates that Gharibabadi said that "our current policy with the Agency is that as long as this situation is not resolved, the talk of war is not permanently ended, a diplomatic understanding is not established, and the United States does not establish its own interactions, we cannot establish access to the Agency."

Alex Nitzberg is a writer for Fox News Digital.
