Justus Kelley shares how she practiced with her baby in a carrier, squeezed in workouts during nap time and prepared for the stage around motherhood.

Nearly 70 years ago, a beauty queen lost her Miss USA crown after pageant officials learned she was married and had children. In August, Justus Kelley broke that barrier, becoming the first married woman and mother to win the title during the pageant's 75th edition.

Kelley, 31, is a foster mother who founded the nonprofit Foster Footprints to support children and families involved in foster care.

The historic victory came three years after the Miss USA pageant changed its rules to allow married women and mothers to compete.

Kelley is scheduled to compete in the 75th Miss Universe pageant, which is set to take place Nov. 24 in Puerto Rico.

FORMER MISS USA CONTESTANT MADE A LIFE-CHANGING DECISION AT 26 AFTER CANCER DEVASTATED FAMILY

Justus Kelley (left), the first married mom to win Miss USA, is paying tribute to Mary Leona Gage (right), the former Miss USA 1957, who was stripped of her title after it was revealed she was married and had two children. Kelley will be competing in the Miss Universe pageant on Nov. 24, 2026. (Ivan Apfel/Getty Images; Getty Images)

Kelley paid tribute to Gage by wearing a custom black-and-white coat featuring the former beauty queen's image as she traveled to Puerto Rico for the competition.

"Having the opportunity to represent the United States on the Miss Universe stage, I couldn't help but think about Mary Leona Gage and the circumstances under which she represented this organization," Kelley, 31, told People magazine.

"She was a woman who, in many ways, wasn't allowed to be fully herself or embrace all that she was. Her title was ultimately taken away because society wasn't ready to accept who she was as a wife and mother of two."

Justus Kelley and her husband Tyler have been licensed foster parents in the Commonwealth of Virginia for nearly two years. (Ivan Apfel/Getty Images)

On Aug. 27, the Miss USA Organization held the 75th edition of the national pageant in Miami. Kelley, who held the title of Miss Virginia USA 2026, succeeded 2025 winner Audrey Eckert. The pageant began allowing married women and mothers to compete in 2023.

WATCH: MISS USA 2026 REVEALS HOW SHE TRAINED FOR PAGEANT WITH KIDS IN TOW

In 1957, Gage represented Maryland in the Miss USA pageant and won the title, according to People.

Shortly after Gage's win, rumors circulated about her marital status and children. Gage initially denied the reports. However, it was later revealed that she had married at 14 and given birth to her first child soon afterward. She had her second child at 16, The Baltimore Sun reported.

Leona Gage, ex-Miss USA, disqualified from the Miss Universe contest because she was married rather than single, returned to California to do a television show for NBC. She later headed to Las Vegas for an engagement at the Tropicana Hotel. Gage spent the day in Hollywood with Debbie Reynolds at the Brown Derby. (Bettmann Archive)

Gage also misrepresented her age, telling pageant officials she was 21 when she was actually 18.

Mrs. Mary Leona Gage Ennis, the young lady who won the title of Miss U.S.A. in the Miss Universe contest and then lost it when it was discovered she was married and the mother of two children, is shown in this photo made in 1956 with her husband, Gene and their sons David, left, and Gene Jr. at the time she was 17 years old. (Getty Images)

Following an official investigation, Gage was disqualified and stripped of her Miss USA crown. Runner-up Charlotte Sheffield, who represented Utah, assumed the crown and received the prizes.

Gage, who lost the crown about 24 hours after her win, said she received hate mail following her disqualification.

Actress Zsa Zsa Gabor and Mary Leona Gage in Los Angeles, circa 1957. (Getty Images)

Gage had already competed in the Miss Universe preliminary round and secured a spot among the 15 semifinalists before she was disqualified. Although Sheffield inherited the Miss USA crown, she could not replace Gage in the international competition because preliminary judging had already concluded.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Leona Gage of Maryland was crowned Miss USA. (Bettmann Archive)

According to The Baltimore Sun, Gage later worked as a performer at the Tropicana Hotel in Las Vegas and reportedly dated Frank Sinatra and former Mr. Universe Mickey Hargitay. She also pursued a film career but never achieved widespread success.

Despite losing her crown, Gage continued watching the Miss USA pageant every year. She died in 2010 at age 71.

Justus Kelley married her high school sweetheart. (Ivan Apfel/Getty Images)

Kelley told People that Gage has been on her mind as she prepares for the Miss Universe competition.

Miss USA 2026 winner Justus Kelley and Miss Florida Aileen Cerchiara stand on stage during the 2026 Miss USA Final Competition and Coronation at Adrienne Arsht Center for the Performing Arts in Miami, Florida., on Aug. 27, 2026. (Ivan Apfel/Getty Images)

"I think about how much has changed since then, and how grateful I am that today's American women have the opportunity to represent their country while embracing every part of who they are," Kelley said.

"I hope this moment serves as a reminder that we stand on the shoulders of women who dared to challenge what was expected of them, so that we could have the freedom to be exactly who we are today."

Justus Kelley walks the runway at the Michael Cinco show during New York Fashion Week Powered by Art Hearts Fashion at The Angel Orensanz Foundation on Sept. 12, 2026, in New York City. (Getty Images for Art Hearts Fashion)

The Miss USA pageant began in 1952 in Long Beach, California, with New York's Jackie Loughery becoming its first winner. The competition is separate from the Miss America pageant, which traces its history to a 1921 event in Atlantic City, New Jersey.

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

Miss USA was founded in 1952. (Bettmann Archive)

In an earlier interview with Fox News Digital, Kelley expressed a similar message about motherhood and ambition.

She said she hoped to use her reign as Miss USA to challenge the idea that women must choose between their families, careers and personal dreams.

Designer Marina Safina, Miss USA Justus Kelley and models walk the runway at the Marina Safina show during Los Angeles Fashion Week Powered By Art Hearts Fashion at The Majestic Downtown on Oct. 8, 2026. (Getty Images for Art Hearts Fashion)

"You don't have to choose one part of who you are," Kelley said. "You can be all of who you are. That, to me, is the message. We can embrace every part of who we are. It doesn't take away from the other. It doesn't mean there aren't trade-offs, and there aren't times when we have to lean on our village more heavily to get through all the things that we may be pursuing. But know that we don't have to sacrifice ourselves."

Miss Virginia USA 2026 Justus Kelley is crowned Miss USA 2026 onstage during the 2026 Miss USA Final Competition & Coronation at Adrienne Arsht Center for the Performing Arts on Aug. 27, 2026, in Miami, Florida. (Ivan Apfel/Getty Images)

Kelley said her victory gave her an opportunity to represent mothers and wives who balance family life with their own ambitions.

Miss USA 2026 Justus Kelley wants to raise awareness of providing a loving home to foster children. (Ivan Apfel/Getty Images)

"Knowing that history was made as the first mom, as the first wife, as the first woman in her 30s, my first thought was how amazing it is to get to do this and to represent women from all over the country, from all over the world that resonate with, 'Hey, we're still dreaming,'" she said.

Miss USA 2026 Justus Kelley stands on stage during the Miss USA Final Competition and Coronation at the Adrienne Arsht Center for the Performing Arts in Miami, Florida, on Aug. 27, 2026. (Ivan Apfel/Getty Images)

"We're raising our families, but we still have dreams. We still have things that we want to go after and pursue. But what an honor. I get to do this. I get to represent these women. What an honor."

Stephanie Nolasco is an Entertainment Reporter for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Iran vows ‘we will find you’ to 2 US Navy officers the day warship returns from Middle East
articles.excerpt:
Iran threats against US officers should set off ‘alarm bells’ in Washington, Foundation for Defense of Democracies senior fellow, Behnam Taleblu, warns.

Iran’s embassy in South Africa threatened two ...
articles.body_text:
Iran threats against US officers should set off ‘alarm bells’ in Washington, Foundation for Defense of Democracies senior fellow, Behnam Taleblu, warns.

Iran’s embassy in South Africa threatened two U.S. Navy officers with a "We will find you" message online as their warship returned to San Diego on Friday after a historic 357-day deployment that included combat against Iranian forces.

The warning, posted on X on Nov. 13 alongside images identifying the USS Spruance’s commanding officer and executive officer, prompted a regional expert to warn that Iran’s public targeting of American service members should set off alarm bells in Washington.

The embassy identified Cmdr. Leigh R. Tate, commanding officer of the Spruance, and Lt. Cmdr. Jeffrey E. York, the ship’s executive officer.

IRAN MINES US TROOPS' SOCIAL MEDIA AS MILITARY CONSIDERS SEIZING CELLPHONES

"We will find you," the embassy wrote on X.

The embassy had previously singled out the officers in a March 28 post accusing them of ordering Tomahawk missile launches that killed 168 children at an elementary school in Minab, Iran.

"Remember these two criminals," the earlier post began. "Don’t they have children of their own?" the embassy asked at the time.

Behnam Ben Taleblu, a senior fellow at the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, warned that the rhetoric coming out of Tehran should be taken seriously given Iran’s history of plotting attacks against American officials.

"This should be setting off alarm bells in Washington, in the White House, the Pentagon, and even within CENTCOM," Taleblu told Fox News Digital. "The Islamic Republic has literally identified personnel that they allege are involved in strikes against the regime, and they’re talking about retribution."

"If indeed there is any plot to go after these individuals, it is critical they’re detected, they are disrupted, they are defeated," Taleblu warned.

IRAN-BACKED TERROR SUSPECTS PLOTTED ATTACK ON US TROOPS USING VANS PACKED WITH FUEL, DOJ SAYS

Arleigh Burke-class guided-missile destroyer USS Spruance fires a Tomahawk Land Attack Missile in support of Operation Epic Fury. (U.S. Navy/Handout via REUTERS)

The threat from Iran came a day after President Donald Trump warned Tehran against assassinating senior American officials.

During a Nov. 12 interview with radio host Hugh Hewitt, Trump was asked what would happen if Iran killed a senior U.S. official.

"They will not exist very long, any longer," Trump responded.

His warning also followed reports that Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had relocated from his Washington-area residence to a military base amid Iranian threats against his life.

Bessent confirmed the move during a Friday interview on CNBC, saying he was following Secret Service instructions.

"Why am I going to be afraid when the brave military personnel in the Gulf, President Trump, constantly receive death threats?" Bessent asked.

Bessent described Iran as behaving "like a dangerous cornered animal" and insisted the threats would not derail the administration’s economic pressure campaign against Tehran.

TRUMP ADMIN THREATENS IRAN WITH 'CONSEQUENCES' AS ALLIES CONVENE AMID THREATS OF POST-ELECTION ESCALATION

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent gestures while speaking at the U.S.-China Relations Gala Dinner on Nov. 10, 2026, in New York. (AP Photo/Frank Franklin II)

Secretary of State Marco Rubio, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and senior White House official Stephen Miller have also reportedly moved into military or other protected housing amid security concerns.

In another post on X, the Iranian embassy in South Africa went on to mock senior administration officials over their security arrangements.

"Rubio, Bessent, Hegseth, and other U.S. officials live in constant fear, haunted by the crimes committed, and now confined to military bunkers for their own protection," the embassy wrote, suggesting they should occasionally appear in public.

The threats come as federal authorities have announced developments in alleged Iranian-backed plots targeting Americans.

On Nov. 10, the FBI added Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps operative Shahram Poursafi to its Most Wanted Terrorists list over an alleged assassination plot targeting former senior U.S. officials, including former national security adviser John Bolton.

That same day, the Justice Department announced terrorism charges against three men accused of involvement in nearly 20 attacks and attempted attacks across Europe and the United States, including an alleged plot targeting a British air base housing American forces.

The developments followed an Oct. 23 U.S. intelligence warning that Iranian efforts to target American personnel abroad had substantially increased, with some plots reaching advanced stages.

TRUMP'S TOP OFFICIALS RETREAT BEHIND MILITARY GATES AS EX-FBI DEPUTY POINTS TO WHAT'S FUELING THREATS

The Arleigh Burke-class guided-missile destroyer departed San Diego on Nov. 21, 2025, alongside the USS Abraham Lincoln Carrier Strike Group. Its deployment was extended as American forces conducted Operation Epic Fury against Iran. (Sandy HUFFAKER / AFP via Getty Images)

The embassy’s warning coincided with the Spruance’s return to Naval Base San Diego on Nov. 13, ending the longest deployment by a U.S. Navy destroyer since World War II.

The Arleigh Burke-class guided-missile destroyer departed San Diego on Nov. 21, 2025, alongside the USS Abraham Lincoln Carrier Strike Group. Its deployment was extended as American forces conducted Operation Epic Fury against Iran.

The Spruance traveled more than 88,000 nautical miles during the deployment and launched dozens of Tomahawk land-attack cruise missiles against Iranian military targets between February and August 2026, according to a statement released by the Navy.

The ship also destroyed 12 unmanned aerial vehicles and four anti-ship cruise missiles while operating under persistent threats from Iranian drones and missiles.

"Spruance, in particular, as the alternate air defense commander was, I would say, instrumental in defending the carrier, defending the force from those inbound threats," Tate said Friday in the statement.

CENTCOM COMMANDER TOUTS USS ABRAHAM LINCOLN MENTAL HEALTH RECORD AFTER MORE THAN 260 DAYS WITHOUT PORT CALL

The destroyer also participated in the U.S. blockade of Iranian ports. In April, it intercepted the Iranian-flagged cargo vessel Touska after the ship failed to comply with repeated American warnings. (CENTCOM/Handout via REUTERS )

The destroyer also participated in the U.S. blockade of Iranian ports. In April, it intercepted the Iranian-flagged cargo vessel Touska after the ship failed to comply with repeated American warnings.

U.S. Central Command said at the time that the Spruance ordered the vessel’s engine room evacuated before firing rounds that disabled the ship.

Tate called commanding the ship during the extended deployment an "honor of a lifetime."

"Spruance sailors made a difference," Tate also said in a statement Friday. "They represented their families, their ship and the United States Navy with distinction."

Meanwhile, Iranian officials have also been threatening U.S. military installations overseas.

On Nov. 11, Iranian Supreme National Security Council Secretary Mohsen Rezaei warned that Tehran could strike American bases in Europe if the United States resumed attacks on Iran.

ANOTHER TRUMP HEAVYWEIGHT REVEALED TO BE LIVING ON MILITARY BASE AS CABINET ROSTER GROWS

Mohsen Rezaei was named secretary of the Supreme National Security Council. A foremr Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps general and member of the Expediency Discernment Council, as well as the secretary of the Supreme Council for Economic Coordination and the Iranian government's Economic Committee, attends a ceremony at Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini's shrine in southern Tehran, Iran, on June 4, 2026. (Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto)

"If the Americans make a mistake and attack us, we will not limit ourselves to nearby bases," Rezaei told Al Mayadeen.

Taleblu described the embassy’s latest statements as part of an escalating pattern of threats against American personnel.

"This is an escalation of the course that we’ve been on," he said, pointing to threatening rhetoric from Iranian diplomatic accounts and hard-line commentators during and after the war.

"So this is basically incitement and invective from the world’s foremost state sponsor of terrorism, one which unfortunately has a track record of carrying these things out, even with a delay."

He pointed to threats against U.S. military personnel following the accidental American shootdown of an Iranian civilian airliner in 1988.

"Something like this is not unprecedented in the 47-year shadow war between the Islamic Republic and America," Taleblu said, warning that the conflict has increasingly moved from covert operations into open warfare and increasing public threats on social media.

Fox News Digital has reached out to the Pentagon and the White House for comment.

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

articles.title: Retro burger chain once served up beloved TV character to American diners
articles.excerpt: Culinary storyteller Capri Cafaro shares how postwar development, expanding interstate travel and widespread automobile ownership helped turn ordering meals from behind the wheel into a lasting nation...
articles.body_text:
Culinary storyteller Capri Cafaro shares how postwar development, expanding interstate travel and widespread automobile ownership helped turn ordering meals from behind the wheel into a lasting national phenomenon.

Before Dunkin' became a household name for coffee and donuts, its founder tried to build a fast-food business around a TV puppet.

William Rosenberg, who founded Dunkin' Donuts, launched Howdy Beef N' Burger in New England in 1961. At its peak, the chain had about 30 locations, some of which operated alongside Dunkin' Donuts.

The retro chain was originally called Howdy Beefburger before changing to Howdy Beef N’ Burger, according to reports.

RETRO PIZZA HUT DRAWS CUSTOMERS FROM HOURS AWAY AS 1980S NOSTALGIA SENDS SALES SOARING

The regional chain took its name and mascot from Howdy Doody, the beloved cowboy marionette who starred in a children's show that aired on NBC from 1947 to 1960, according to food website Chowhound.

The show featured the puppet and human characters in skits and songs before a studio audience of children known as the "peanut gallery."

The chain took its name and mascot from the TV puppet Howdy Doody. It launched as Howdy Beefburger before later changing its name to Howdy Beef N’ Burger. (Noah Webster House & West Hartford Historical Society)

Aside from burgers and fries, the chain also served a signature Big "B" burger.

It also served roast beef sandwiches, fried chicken, shakes and New England seafood dishes such as clam strips, chowder and lobster rolls, according to the food history blog Burger Beast.

FAST-FOOD CHAIN THAT ONCE LIT UP AMERICAN ROADS STILL MISSED DECADES LATER

Promotions leaned into the chain’s family appeal. A Boston Globe ad, cited by The Takeout, promised diners could "feed the family on just pocket change."

The chain also offered burger deals and prizes, giveaways and buttons for children, according to reports.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

But Howdy's reportedly faced competition from McDonald’s, plus Rosenberg’s company had other ventures to manage, including seafood, pancakes and deli businesses.

"The Howdy Doody Show," a popular NBC children’s program, aired from 1947 to 1960. (Bettmann)

When his son Robert became company president in 1963, he began narrowing the company’s focus to Dunkin’ Donuts, Chowhound reported.

While Dunkin' continued to grow, Howdy's faded, with some locations sold off to other restaurant chains.

A Quincy, Massachusetts, restaurant became a Wendy’s in 1979, according to Burger Beast.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

By the 1980s, the chain had largely disappeared, according to Chowhound.

Today, the New England burger chain survives in vintage ads, nostalgic memorabilia and diners' memories.

Long before the Dunkin' most Americans know today, founder William Rosenberg launched a regional burger chain. (Jeffrey Greenberg/Universal Images Group via Getty Images)

Howdy Doody wasn’t the only fictional character to inspire a restaurant, though.

Bubba Gump Shrimp Co. draws on the 1994 film "Forrest Gump," while Central Perk Coffee Co. recreates the café from the series "Friends."

Meanwhile, Tony Soprano’s, an East Coast pizza chain, is themed around "The Sopranos," according to The Takeout.

Deirdre Bardolf is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Photos: Pope Leo visits Peru’s Amazon and Andean regions during 12-day tour
articles.excerpt:
Pope Leo XIV has criss-crossed Peru on the penultimate day of his Latin America tour, making stops in the Andean highlands and the Peruvian Amazon.

Sunday marked the last full day of his trip, which ...
articles.body_text:
Pope Leo XIV has criss-crossed Peru on the penultimate day of his Latin America tour, making stops in the Andean highlands and the Peruvian Amazon.

Sunday marked the last full day of his trip, which has seen him visit Uruguay and Argentina already.

The pontiff spent the morning in the Andean city of Cusco, the former capital of the Inca Empire, delivering a speech at the Indigenous fortress of Saqsaywaman.

In his remarks, Leo praised the region’s traditional festivities and processions, which often blend Indigenous and Catholic spirituality.

“The future of these traditions lies not only in preserving what has been handed down, but also in passing it on in a living way,” he said.

Huge crowds also packed Cusco’s central Plaza de Armas to greet Leo. Though born in the United States, Leo acquired Peruvian citizenship in 2015, after living in the country for years and later becoming the bishop of Chiclayo, a major city in the north.

Leo is the first Peruvian citizen to become pope.

The visit to Cusco, a high-altitude city some 3,400 metres (more than 11,000 feet) above sea level, tested the 71-year-old pope’s stamina as he continues to recover from lung cancer surgery.

Leo, however, has shown no sign of fatigue since his 12-day, three-nation South American trip began on November 6.

In the afternoon, Leo flew to Pucallpa, a city near Peru’s eastern border, on the banks of the Ucayali River.

Pucallpa is considered a gateway to the Peruvian Amazon, and during his stay, Leo reinforced his late predecessor Pope Francis’s teachings on protecting the environment.

He also denounced the violence faced by Indigenous land defenders, who use their advocacy to confront deforestation, pollution and the threat of Indigenous expulsion.

“Many Indigenous leaders have been murdered for defending their territories,” Leo said. “The blood of these brothers cries out ⁠to God and demands justice.”

Indigenous communities have long been threatened by illegal mining, deforestation and other forms of exploitation. Mining has also led to a water crisis in Peru, with pollution leading to an increased risk of heavy metal poisoning.

Leo is expected to return to Rome on Monday.

articles.title: FAA ground stop timeline: Weekend chaos grounds planes and postpones games
articles.excerpt: Airlines for America president Chris Sununu joins 'Fox & Friends Weekend' to discuss how thousands of travelers continue to face flight delays and cancellations nationwide following a recent FAA groun...
articles.body_text:
Airlines for America president Chris Sununu joins 'Fox & Friends Weekend' to discuss how thousands of travelers continue to face flight delays and cancellations nationwide following a recent FAA ground stop. They discuss infrastructure challenges and how to go forward.

A communications failure brought departures across the country to a halt Friday, stranding travelers, disrupting professional sports teams and sending federal officials scrambling to restore flights and determine what went wrong.

The longest nationwide ground stop in 25 years ended after more than four hours, but the fallout stretched through the weekend as airlines worked through cancellations and investigators zeroed in on routers tied to the outage.

Here’s a timeline of the shutdown and the federal response. All times are Eastern.

4 CRITICAL TRAVEL ISSUES FOR THOSE DELAYED AND DISRUPTED BY FAA NATIONWIDE GROUND STOP

A view from San Francisco International Airport (SFO) in California as the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a rare nationwide ground stop for all departing flights across the States due to a telecommunications and air traffic control communication outage affecting multiple Air Route Traffic Control Centers on November 13, 2026. (Tayfun Coskun/Anadolu via Getty Images)

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said officials detected instability in radar data and communications at 3:36 p.m., affecting facilities that guide planes approaching airports and traveling between them.

The Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) halted departures nationwide at 3:54 p.m. as controllers and pilots followed procedures to bring aircraft already airborne safely to the ground. About 3,500 flights were in the air.

FAA SAYS AIR TRAVEL SHOULD BE BACK TO NORMAL SUNDAY AFTER NATIONWIDE GROUND STOP

Duffy later emphasized that officials had not lost every radar feed or all telecommunications service. The inconsistent information was enough to trigger the shutdown as a safety precaution.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy, right, with Federal Aviation Administrator Bryan Bedford, left, speaks during a news conference at the U.S. Department of Transportation, Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026, in Washington. (Tom Brenner/AP Photo)

Duffy said the ground stop was necessary because of "a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers."

FAA technicians were investigating, he said.

The disruption also prompted a broader federal response as officials examined whether the failure could have involved malicious activity.

BUTTIGIEG TAKES SWIPE AT TRUMP ADMINISTRATION AMID FAA FLIGHT CHAOS

President Donald Trump brought federal agencies together on a call Friday, including intelligence officials, the FBI and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. Intelligence partners reported they were not detecting the usual signs of a cyberattack, Duffy said.

Steven Cheung, assistant to the president and White House director of communications, later said on X that the White House and administration had acted within minutes of the FAA notice, crediting Trump for the response.

UPDATED START TIMES FOR COLLEGE FOOTBALL GAMES AFFECTED BY FAA GROUND STOP, BROKEN DOWN BY CONFERENCE

"Minutes after the FAA notice posted, the White House and Administration sprang into action. Because of that speed and effectiveness, the ground stop was lifted after just a few hours," Cheung wrote.

"A Herculean effort, only made possible by President Trump's leadership."

NFL OFFICIAL DON WILLARD WILL REFEREE TWO GAMES IN ONE DAY AFTER FAA GROUND STOP DISRUPTS TRAVEL, LEAGUE SAYS

Speaking to reporters outside the White House on Friday, Nov. 13, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication of a nefarious attack and reassured Americans with loved ones traveling.

"There’s no reason for the public to be afraid or scared for your loved ones," Mullin said.

TENNESSEE VOLUNTEERS OVERCOME SLUGGISH OFFENSE, JET LAG TO TAKE DOWN TEXAS A&M AND KEEP CFP HOPES ALIVE

TOPSHOT - Planes wait on the tarmac at Chicago O'Hare International Airport in Chicago, on November 13, 2026. The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has issued a ground stop at all US airports.  (Kamil Krzacynski/ AFP via Getty Images)

The shutdown also left college football teams scrambling to reach Saturday’s games. Texas had already boarded its plane for Baton Rouge to face LSU when the ground stop prevented departure. Tennessee’s scheduled 4 p.m. flight to College Station was also halted.

Teams including Ole Miss, Tennessee and Baylor returned to their athletic facilities as officials weighed alternate travel plans. Some teams sat aboard charter planes for up to two hours.

PRIVATE PLANES AND ROADTRIPS: AEW GOES ABOVE AND BEYOND TO GET TO PHOENIX FOR FULL GEAR DESPITE TRAVEL CHAOS

Passengers wait at boarding gates at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in Washington, DC on November 13, 2026. (Zina Desmazes / AFP via Getty Images))

The shutdown also disrupted travel for professional sports teams ahead of a busy weekend.

The Brooklyn Nets were trying to fly from New Orleans to Memphis when their flight was halted, according to The Associated Press. The Memphis Grizzlies were also in New Orleans for a Friday game against the Pelicans, with plans to depart afterward.

The Cleveland Cavaliers and Chicago Bulls also had planned postgame flights. The San Jose Sharks’ flight to Utah for a Saturday game against the Mammoth did not depart before the shutdown, while the Detroit Pistons had reached Miami earlier Friday.

Travelers check a flight information display board at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport on Nov. 13, 2026, in Arlington, Va. (Li Rui/Xinhua via Getty Images)

The FAA lifted the nationwide order at 8:15 p.m., allowing departures to resume.

Planes began leaving airports including LaGuardia, Los Angeles International and Reagan National. Some travelers at Reagan National had been waiting since around 3:30 p.m. for flights scheduled to leave around 4 p.m.

Duffy warned that reopening the airspace would not immediately get every flight moving. Departures depended on whether airlines had pilots, flight attendants and other crews available.

Lifting the ground stop did not immediately solve the travel problems for college teams. By 9:12 p.m. Friday, Washington, Texas, Tennessee and Oregon State were heading back to airports, but other programs faced crew availability problems.

Utah’s charter crew ran out of available hours, forcing the team to plan a Saturday morning departure for its game at Arizona. The Big 12 moved kickoff to 10:30 p.m. ET Saturday.

Just after midnight Saturday, the Ole Miss-Oklahoma game was moved to 1 p.m. ET Sunday after the Rebels were unable to leave Friday evening.

Oklahoma athletic director Roger Denny said the school objected to the change but was told it would face a forfeit if it refused to play Sunday.

Travelers wait at LaGuardia Airport in New York, Friday, Nov. 13, 2026, after the Federal Aviation Administration grounded flights nationwide. (Ryan MurphyAP Photo)

At a Saturday briefing, Duffy said contractor L3Harris had been replacing aging copper communications lines with fiber-optic connections at a remote FAA location.

The copper line was being discontinued, making the replacement necessary, he said.

During the work, a router began generating more than 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, overwhelming other routers and disrupting communications and radar feeds.

Investigators were examining whether installation error or faulty equipment caused the failure.

"Our contractor didn’t meet the moment or the equipment didn’t meet the moment," Duffy said.

Bedford distinguished the routine maintenance from the administration’s broader air traffic control modernization program. Duffy also said officials would reevaluate when such work should be performed.

FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said "the worst is behind us," with air travel expected to return to normal by the end of Sunday.

The Transportation Department said more than 8,000 flight operations resumed Friday night after the ground stop ended, but passengers continued facing delays and cancellations Saturday.

Airlines still needed to reposition aircraft and crews, leaving travelers scrambling to rebook and check whether their flights would operate.

Officials urged passengers to check directly with their airlines for current flight information.

Planes wait on the tarmac at LaGuardia Airport, New York on November 13, 2026. The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has issued a ground stop at all US airports due to communications problem.  (Charly Triballeau/ AFP via Getty Images)

Duffy said Sunday morning that air travel would improve throughout the day but probably would not return fully to normal until Monday, updating officials’ earlier prediction of a recovery by Sunday night.

Two routers from Texas and Arkansas were undergoing testing as investigators worked to determine the cause.

Duffy said work in El Dorado, Arkansas, was followed by problems involving equipment in Amarillo, Texas, where a system had been replaced about three weeks earlier. Engineers were examining the routers at an L3Harris laboratory in Florida.

"We think it was the installation or the router that was the bad actor," Duffy said.

He said there was no indication of a foreign cyberattack, while leaving open further investigation if new evidence emerged.

Duffy also pressed Congress for additional funding. He said the $12.5 billion already allocated covered specific upgrades, including radar, radios and electronic flight strips, but did not fund a replacement telecommunications network.

By 2 p.m. ET Sunday, 5,280 flights had been delayed and 1,709 canceled within, into or out of the U.S., according to FlightAware.

Dallas Fort Worth, Atlanta and Chicago O’Hare were among the hardest-hit airports tracked in the update, with hundreds of delays at each.

The disruptions continued Sunday afternoon as airlines worked to restore normal schedules.

FORMER TOP FAA OFFICIAL WARNS OF 48-HOUR RECOVERY AFTER AGING TECH 'OVERWHELMED' AHEAD OF GROUND STOP

Scott Kirby, chief executive officer at United Airlines Holdings Inc., during a Bloomberg Television interview at Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) in Newark, New Jersey. (Michael Nagle/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby praised the FAA’s decision to halt flights and thanked employees and customers for their patience during the disruption. He also called for better technology and full staffing to help prevent future outages.

Kirby said he had spoken directly with Duffy, Bedford and aviation leaders from both parties in Congress about the impact on United’s passengers and employees.

"This moment must be a call to action," Kirby said in a statement shared with Fox News Digital.

"It is critical for safety, our passengers, and our economy that we fix our nation’s Air Traffic Control system now."

Kirby said lawmakers from both parties were committed to modernizing the system while holding the FAA accountable.

Fox News' Grady Trimble, Anders Hagstrom, Stephen Sorace, Trey Wallace, and The Associated Press contributed to this report.

Stepheny Price is a Writer at Fox News with a focus on West Coast and Midwest news, missing persons, national and international crime stories, homicide cases, and border security.

(Tayfun Coskun/Anadolu via Getty Images)

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said officials detected instability in radar data and communications at 3:36 p.m., affecting facilities that guide planes approaching airports and traveling between them.

Duffy said the ground stop was necessary because of "a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers."

BUTTIGIEG TAKES SWIPE AT TRUMP ADMINISTRATION AMID FAA FLIGHT CHAOS

President Donald Trump brought federal agencies together on a call Friday, including intelligence officials, the FBI and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency. Intelligence partners reported they were not detecting the usual signs of a cyberattack, Duffy said.

UPDATED START TIMES FOR COLLEGE FOOTBALL GAMES AFFECTED BY FAA GROUND STOP, BROKEN DOWN BY CONFERENCE

"Minutes after the FAA notice posted, the White House and Administration sprang into action. Because of that speed and effectiveness, the ground stop was lifted after just a few hours," Cheung wrote.

"A Herculean effort, only made possible by President Trump's leadership."

NFL OFFICIAL DON WILLARD WILL REFEREE TWO GAMES IN ONE DAY AFTER FAA GROUND STOP DISRUPTS TRAVEL, LEAGUE SAYS

Speaking to reporters outside the White House on Friday, Nov. 13, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication of a nefarious attack and reassured Americans with loved ones traveling.

"There’s no reason for the public to be afraid or scared for your loved ones," Mullin said.

TENNESSEE VOLUNTEERS OVERCOME SLUGGISH OFFENSE, JET LAG TO TAKE DOWN TEXAS A&M AND KEEP CFP HOPES ALIVE

TOPSHOT - Planes wait on the tarmac at Chicago O'Hare International Airport in Chicago, on November 13, 2026. The US Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) has issued a ground stop at all US airports.  (Kamil Krzacynski/ AFP via Getty Images)

Teams including Ole Miss, Tennessee and Baylor returned to their athletic facilities as officials weighed alternate travel plans. Some teams sat aboard charter planes for up to two hours.

Passengers wait at boarding gates at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in Washington, DC on November 13, 2026. (Zina Desmazes / AFP via Getty Images))

Travelers check a flight information display board at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport on Nov. 13, 2026, in Arlington, Va. (Li Rui/Xinhua via Getty Images)

articles.title: USC's latest terrible loss to Indiana Hoosiers might be the final straw for Lincoln Riley in LA
articles.excerpt:
"He didn't lead Indiana to nothing. Indiana won and the kid played."

Where have we ever seen this movie before? The USC Trojans, with their season and hopes of reaching the College Football Playoff o...
articles.body_text:
"He didn't lead Indiana to nothing. Indiana won and the kid played."

Where have we ever seen this movie before? The USC Trojans, with their season and hopes of reaching the College Football Playoff on the line, on the road against another good team, needing to come through late in the fourth quarter to finally get the breakthrough win they need to reach the next level.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

While there's more to Saturday's 27-13 loss to the Indiana Hoosiers than any one play or incident, the embodiment of the Trojans' season, of head coach Lincoln Riley's tenure at USC, came halfway through the fourth quarter.

INDIANA HOOSIERS BOOST COLLEGE FOOTBALL PLAYOFF HOPES WITH 27-13 WIN OVER USC TROJANS

Southern California Trojans head coach Lincoln Riley watches game action against the Ohio State Buckeyes during the first half at the Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum in Los Angeles, Calif., on Oct. 31, 2026. (IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

Down 20-13, SC moved the ball down the field quickly, with Jayden Maiava completing a 34-yard pass to superstar freshman Trent Mosley to set up 1st-and-goal from the Hoosier's 8-yard-line. A quick two-yard run set up 2nd-and-goal from the six with 6:34 remaining. Maiava dropped back to pass and...telegraphed his intentions by staring down receiver Kayden Dixon-Wyatt, ignoring Indiana linebacker Isaiah Jones, and delivering a perfectly thrown and timed interception.

Just like that, a potential tie game became Indiana ball. And just as they so often have, the Trojans defense couldn't get the ball back with the game still in reach. The Hoosiers went 93 yards on just seven plays, with a 42-yard touchdown pass from Grant Wilson to Charlie Becker effectively ending the game. Though it was officially ended when Maiava threw yet another interception on SC's final drive of the game.

Again, to put the entire loss on that one play, 2nd-and-goal from the six, isn't doing SC's collapse enough justice. The Trojans dropped not one, not two, not three, but four interceptions. One thrown directly to a defense back that bounced off his chest. One that went through a defenders hands on a diving try in the end zone. One in which SC actually did catch the ball, miraculously, only to have it knocked away by the slightest bit of contact. And another just for fun.

They missed two field goals, a 51-yard try that hit off the upright, and, somehow, a 27-yard attempt that wasn't even close. To make matters worse, a random Indiana fan nailed a field goal from almost that exact same spot a few minutes later.

The missed attempt came after a 3rd-and-8 with an obvious pass interference on the Hoosiers incorrectly waved off because a linebacker got a fingertip the pass. Per NCAA rules, a tipped ball negates pass interference, but contact before the ball is touched should still be enforced. The contact on the play came before, and after, the tip, but the refs apparently determined otherwise. Though the fact it was even close points to Maiava's poor pass and decision making.

LINCOLN RILEY HAS CONFRONTATION WITH OHIO STATE AD, READS PREPARED STATEMENT TO MEDIA AFTER HUGE USC WIN

USC's two fourth quarter drives, pre-garbage time, resulted in 17 plays for 148 yards, both reaching to the Indiana 10-yard-line, and...zero points. Not three points, zero points. 148 yards on two drives, zero points. That wasn't an aberration; USC drove into the Indiana red zone five times throughout the game and scored just one touchdown. Five red zone opportunities, 13 total points.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Southern California Trojans quarterback Jayden Maiava warms up before a game against the Indiana Hoosiers at Merchants Bank Field at Memorial Stadium in Bloomington, Ind., on Nov. 14, 2026. (IMAGN IMAGES via Reuters Connect)

USC's defense was frequently in the right place at the right time, as evidenced by the four dropped interceptions, but they also gave up their share of trademark back-breaking mistakes too. With the game still tied late in the third quarter, Indiana had a 37-yard run, helped along by an obvious holding on No. 11 against a USC linebacker that wasn't called, that set the Hoosiers up for a go-ahead touchdown.

After Maiava's pick, SC needed a stop to get the ball back. Instead, the Hoosiers went four-yard run, five-yard run, eight-yard run, 12-yard run, two-yard run, five-yard-run, 42-yard touchdown pass. That was the fourth play of 30+ yards the SC defense gave up to an offense run by a backup quarterback.

It was a microcosm of the problems with the Lincoln Riley era in LA. Ten positives, outweighed by five negatives. A defense that isn't good to win games on their own. Missed opportunities on offense, particularly with short fields, missed field goals, and in the post Caleb Williams-era, quarterback play that simply isn't good enough. Especially on the road.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

The loss was eerily reminiscent of the USC-Notre Dame game in 2025, when the Trojans took a 24-21 lead in the third quarter, then immediately gave up a 100-yard kickoff return. Still only down 27-24 after a missed PAT, Maiava threw yet another back breaking interception around midfield. The SC defense held, and the offense got the ball back, drove down to the Notre Dame 37-yard-line and...Makai Lemon fumbled on a trick play. The Irish scored on the ensuing drive, all but ending the game. Though Maiava added another late pick on the final drive of the game, just as he did against Indiana.

Much of the blame for Saturday's loss can be placed on the players; dropped picks aren't Riley's fault, and Maiava's interception was a textbook case of poor quarterback vision. But at some point, the blame has to come back on Riley, doesn't it?

This loss wouldn't have mattered as much if the Trojans had just beaten a very mediocre Wisconsin team on the road. They scored seven points and lost. Or if they'd have been able to hold serve against the Oregon Ducks playing backup QB Dylan Raiola for most of the game, at the LA Coliseum. They couldn't.

Maiava's played in a whopping 29 games for USC and Lincoln Riley now, and hasn't improved much. His footwork is awful, frequently unnecessarily throwing off his back foot. He often makes terrible decisions in pressure situations. His accuracy is atrocious as soon as there's pressure, and despite being a fairly mobile quarterback, he's all but stopped moving up in the pocket or running for free yards. That's a necessity in modern college football, and Maiava no longer even attempts it.

OUTKICK IS NOW AVAILABLE ON THE FOX NEWS APP: CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD

Some of that's on him, yes, but Riley's claim to fame is his work with quarterbacks. Why hasn't Maiava gotten better? Or why did he not evaluate Maiava's weaknesses and hit the transfer portal hard to find someone better?

We're somehow just two weeks removed from SC fans storming the field after a huge win over Ohio State, but with the Trojans once again out of the College Football Playoff, once again suffering a disastrous, self-inflicted loss on the road, once again staring down the barrel of a long offseason of wondering what went wrong, it's once again enough to start the "Lincoln Riley hot seat" conversations. Particularly considering RIley's dismissive pre-written statement after the Buckeyes' win implying that he always knew the Trojans would peak at the right time and get into the tournament.

USC Trojans leave as fans storm the field following the NCAA football game against the Ohio State Buckeyes at Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum on Oct. 31, 2026. Ohio State lost 30-18. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)

Already, reports have suggested the Trojans could put his buyout together. And the crosstown rivalry game on Thanksgiving weekend might be the last try he has of staying in LA. UCLA in year one under Bob Chesney is a near-lock for the playoff, while Riley in year five is once again on the outside looking in. Lose to the Bruins, in a symbolic changing of the guard in LA, and it seems impossible that he's back at the Coliseum in 2027.

It's a roller coaster, and most of the SC fanbase is ready for it to end.

articles.title: 'The Odyssey' actor John Leguizamo demands Democrats 'abolish ICE,' shut down detention centers
articles.excerpt:
Actor John Leguizamo urged Democrats to abolish ICE and shut down immigration detention centers in a social media video outlining his priorities for the next Congress. (Jamie McCarthy/Getty Images)

"...
articles.body_text:
Actor John Leguizamo urged Democrats to abolish ICE and shut down immigration detention centers in a social media video outlining his priorities for the next Congress. (Jamie McCarthy/Getty Images)

"The Odyssey" actor John Leguizamo urged Democrats to abolish Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), shut down detention centers and protect abortion rights and transgender Americans on Friday, while outlining his priorities for the next Congress.

Leguizamo presented a lengthy list of demands in a video he posted on social media, along with an accompanying policy list aimed at lawmakers taking office in January. His immigration proposals also included protecting sanctuary cities, ending family separation and pursuing immigration reform.

"Alright, my project 2027, starting January 3rd: Get it done, Dems, all right? Guarantee affordable healthcare, Medicare for all, strengthen social security, abolish ICE, shut down detention centers, end family separation, immigration reform, protect sanctuary cities, comprehensive gun reform," he said in the video.

Leguizamo called for Stephen Miller to be tried and convicted over what the actor described as "ICE murders." (Grant Buchanan/Dave Benett/WireImage)

JEFFRIES VOWS DEMOCRATS WON’T ‘GIVE A DIME’ TO TRUMP’S DEPORTATION EFFORTS

"Trial, and convict Stephen Miller for ICE murders, impeach Todd Blanche, end Citizens United, so there's no dark money in government," Leguizamo added.

Leguizamo’s agenda also extended to changes in presidential powers, elections and the Supreme Court. He called for eliminating the Electoral College, limiting presidential pardon powers, ending presidential immunity and establishing term limits for Supreme Court justices.

His economic priorities included a $20 federal minimum wage, a billionaire wealth tax, paid maternity leave and a 10% cap on credit card interest rates.

DEMOCRATS’ MIDTERM SWEEP OPENS PATH TO BYPASSING ELECTORAL COLLEGE BY 2028

The actor's demand to close detention centers overlaps with legislation already proposed by Democratic lawmakers, although Leguizamo's list did not provide the implementation details outlined in those bills.

Rep. Delia Ramirez, D-Ill., and Rep. Yvette Clarke, D-N.Y., introduced the Melt ICE Act in January. According to Ramirez’s office, it would remove immigration detention authorities from federal law and terminate existing detention contracts within two years of enactment. Her office outlined how the legislation would redirect the agency’s funding.

"Redirects ICE funding to community-based organizations to provide wrap-around services to communities around the country," her office said in its summary of the bill.

The proposal would also prohibit new detention contracts and require DHS to submit a plan to remove immigrants from ankle monitors within six months. Funding would instead go toward community services, including housing and health care.

Rep. Delia Ramirez, D-Ill., introduced a bill to abolish ICE and Border Patrol while dismantling DHS in its current state. (Jemal Countess/Getty Images for The Service Employees International Union (SEIU); Pat Greenhouse/The Boston Globe via Getty Images)

'SQUAD' DEMOCRAT SLAMMED BY TRUMP ADMIN FOR MOST 'RADICAL' PLAN TARGETING ICE YET

Ramirez subsequently announced a broader proposal, the Reimagining Safety Act, to dismantle DHS and replace it with a Department of Community Safety.

Her office described a plan to abolish ICE and Customs and Border Protection while preserving customs functions and agencies responsible for disaster response, transportation security and cybersecurity.

Support for cutting ICE funding is not universal among Democrats. Rep. Henry Cuellar, D-Texas, previously opposed defunding.

"I don't believe in defunding ICE," Cuellar said, in a previous statement to Fox News Digital.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE OF MEDIA AND CULTURE

In his post, the actor also called out former House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, D-Calif.; Rep. Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y.; and Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., while calling for new Democratic leadership.

"My project 2027 starts Jan 3! If you have the cojones to sign on Dems and reps with wisdom. No more absences (means u Pelosi) no excuses! Enough is enough and if you can’t wrangle your peeps Hakeem then bye! ✌bye anyway you are compromised! And Schumer u too should go away! We need new leadership," the actor posted.

Fox News Digital reached out to the offices of Pelosi, Jeffries, and Schumer for comment, but did not immediately hear back. Leguizamo’s latest demands followed an earlier appeal the actor made to his own audience. In January, he told followers who supported ICE to stop attending his performances and watching his films.

(From L) Colombian-US actor John Leguizamo, South African-US actress Charlize Theron, Kenyan-Mexican actress Lupita Nyong'O, British actor Tom Holland, US actor, screenwriter, producer Matt Damon, US actress Anne Hathaway, US actress and singer Zendaya, British film producer Emma Thomas and British-US film director Christopher Nolan pose during a photocall ahead of the premiere of the film 'The Odyssey' at the Grand Rex in Paris on July 8, 2026.  (JULIEN DE ROSA / AFP via Getty Images)

DEMS SEIZE ON MIDTERM ROUT TO DEMAND ICE REFORM, BUT POLLS REVEAL A TWIST IN WHO PRIORITIZED IMMIGRATION"If you follow ICE, unfollow me, don’t come to my shows, and don’t watch my movies," Leguizamo said.

A DHS spokesperson told Fox News Digital that DHS law enforcement has been delivering on President Donald Trump's promises since day one.

"Since Day One, DHS law enforcement has been delivering on President Trump’s promise to the American people to arrest and deport criminal illegal aliens including murderers, rapists, pedophiles, gang members, and terrorists," the spokesperson said.

"Nearly 60% of ICE arrests are of illegal aliens charged or convicted of a crime in the U.S. More than three million illegal aliens are out of the country and counting. Our message is clear: if you come to our country illegally, we will find you, we will arrest you, and we will deport you," the spokesperson told Fox News Digital.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP"Attacks and demonization of ICE law enforcement is wrong. Because of smears like this, our ICE officers are now facing a 1,600% increase in assaults, a 3,300% increase in vehicle attacks, and an 8,000% increase in death threats," the spokesperson added.

The White House told Fox News Digital that Leguizamo was "out of touch" with Americans.

"This C-list Hollywood actor is out of touch with Americans. To most Americans, our brave ICE law enforcement officers are heroes who put their lives on the line to arrest murderers, rapists, pedophiles, terrorists, and gang members," White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis told Fox News Digital.

"President Trump will never allow criminal illegal aliens to flood into our communities," Bis added.

CJ graduated from Long Beach State University in 2025 with a Bachelor of Arts in Political Science and a minor in Journalism.

articles.body_text:
CMLL star Thunder Rosa talks to OutKick about the company's streaming partnership with MyAEW.

All Elite Wrestling (AEW) may be a relatively young pro wrestling company in the greater landscape, but with a vast roster of wrestlers who bring different styles to the ring, history is bound to be made every now and again.

Kris Statlander and Harley Cameron did just that when the duo known as Wrathlander won the AEW Women’s World Tag Team Championship against Jamie Hayter and Alex Windsor at Full Gear on Saturday night.

Wrathlander dethroned The Brawling Birds at All Elite Wrestling's Full Gear on Nov. 14, 2026. (Photography by Ricky Havlik)

Statlander was being put into a position for Windsor and Hayter’s finishing move. As Hayter bounced off the rope, Cameron tripped her up from outside the ring. Statlander turned the tables on Windsor and nailed Saturday Night Fever. She pinned Windsor for the win as Cameron held back Hayter.

It’s the first reign for Statlander and Cameron as a team. Statlander joined Willow Nightingale as the only AEW stars to hold the world title, TBS Championship and tag team title in their careers.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Harley Cameron nails Jamie Hayter at All Elite Wrestling's Full Gear on Nov. 14, 2026. (Photography by Ricky Havlik)

She became the first woman to hold the tag team titles twice. She and Nightingale were the first-ever AEW women’s tag team champions. Now, she’s the only person to hold the belt twice.

Windsor and Hayter, known as The Brawling Birds, have their reign ended after 77 days. They knocked off Megan Bayne and Lena Kross, who were the champions for 168 days before losing to Windsor and Hayter at All In in August.

Wrathlander now stands alone as the champions and the AEW sickos will have to wait and see who will challenge them next.

articles.title: Iran targets US military base in Bahrain with drone attack
articles.excerpt:
Iran and the US are vying for control of the Strait of Hormuz

Iran launched a drone attack against a US military base in Bahrain on Sunday, its second attempt to target the country in three days.

Th...
articles.body_text:
Iran and the US are vying for control of the Strait of Hormuz

Iran launched a drone attack against a US military base in Bahrain on Sunday, its second attempt to target the country in three days.

The country's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said it targeted the US air defence radar facility at al-Riffa air base in Bahrain using six drones.

Bahrain's military said its air defence systems intercepted and destroyed the Iranian air attacks "before they could achieve their objectives".

It comes after Iran fired drones at Bahrain on Friday, its first attack against Gulf countries since September.

The US and Iran are locked in a stand-off over the Strait of Hormuz. About a fifth of the world's gas and oil supply usually flows through it but shipping has been restricted since the outbreak of war in February.

Iran insists that it should control the strait and has been attacking what it calls "unauthorised" traffic, while the US military is providing protection for tankers shuttling oil through the strait to keep exports flowing from Gulf Arab states.

As sirens sounded across Bahrain on Sunday the interior ministry called on citizens to head to their nearest safe location.

Bahrain's foreign ministry said: "The Kingdom of Bahrain condemns in the strongest terms the continued brutal Iranian attacks on its territory and holds Iran fully responsible for their consequences."

In a statement on the strikes shared by Iran's state broadcaster on Telegram, the IRGC said: "The Strait of Hormuz is closed, and any aggression by the American enemy will be met with an even harsher and more forceful response."

Earlier this week, the IRGC claimed that it struck a US early warning radar system in Bahrain on Friday.

The US military has denied the claim, stating that the IRGC launched two one-way attack drones towards Bahrain and both were shot down by US forces. It added that there were no injuries or damage.

Earlier in the week the US carried out strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, US officials told CBS, the BBC's US partner.

The officials described the strikes as limited and defensive, and said they were in response to the IRGC firing on a US aircraft.

Iranian state news agency Irna reported explosions on Qeshm on Monday. The IRGC did not comment but said its forces had shot down two US MQM-170 drones south of the island and a US MQ-9 drone east of the Strait.

The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated a naval blockade of Iranian ports.

Iranian negotiators had been discussing with mediators a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days if the US meets seven conditions, reportedly including the lifting of the naval blockade and releasing frozen Iranian assets.

However this week Donald Trump said that the US was no longer interested in a deal to end the war with Iran and ordered Vice-President JD Vance, who had been involved in efforts to restart negotiations, to focus on domestic US politics.

articles.title: AI mosquito trap targets deadly dengue outbreak
articles.excerpt: Florida is combatting its largest dengue fever outbreak in decades, with over 290 locally acquired cases reported. Former CDC Director Dr. Robert Redfield breaks down the risks of transmission and ess...
articles.body_text:
Florida is combatting its largest dengue fever outbreak in decades, with over 290 locally acquired cases reported. Former CDC Director Dr. Robert Redfield breaks down the risks of transmission and essential prevention measures. Meanwhile, Hillsborough County mosquito management teams deploy aerial spraying to target the mosquitoes carrying the virus.

You probably aren't thinking much about mosquitoes in November. In much of the country, cooler weather has sent those annoying little bloodsuckers into hiding. But in Florida, mosquitoes are still causing serious trouble. The state is dealing with its largest dengue outbreak in decades, and hundreds of people have caught the virus without leaving the state.

Now, researchers at the University of South Florida have developed an AI mosquito trap that could help health officials find dangerous mosquito species much faster. It can identify mosquito species with more than 98% accuracy in laboratory testing. And with dengue still spreading in Florida, the timing couldn't be more important.

Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the replay and discover 5 ways to travel smarter and save money.

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, 5 Ways to Travel Smarter and Save Money, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five practical ways to protect your phone and personal information, avoid common travel scams, find better deals, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.

Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com.

TROPICAL DISEASE SPREAD BY MOSQUITOES CLAIMS FIRST RECORDED DEATH IN SOUTHERN US STATE

The Digitomy AI mosquito trap uses built-in cameras and artificial intelligence to identify mosquito species that can spread diseases like dengue. (University of South Florida)

If you thought mosquito season ended when summer did, Florida has a different story to tell. According to the Florida Department of Health's latest available weekly surveillance report, Hillsborough County has recorded 407 locally acquired dengue cases in 2026, the county's largest outbreak on record. Across Florida, health officials have reported 524 locally acquired cases through October 31. That means people contracted the virus from mosquitoes in the area rather than while traveling overseas.

The Tampa area has been hit especially hard. In October, the Florida Department of Health confirmed that Hillsborough County was still responding to an ongoing dengue outbreak. Dengue can cause high fever, severe headaches and intense muscle pain. In serious cases, it can lead to life-threatening complications. Health officials continue to encourage residents to take precautions against mosquito bites.

On November 13, Hillsborough County announced that it had extended its state of local emergency through November 19 as mosquito control crews increased aerial and ground treatments to help contain the outbreak. County officials say mosquito surveillance continues to detect dengue virus activity in neighborhoods across the area.

And here's why we're talking about this in November. While mosquitoes have largely disappeared from colder parts of the country, they can remain active in warmer states. Florida's outbreak shows that the threat doesn't disappear simply because summer is over. Meanwhile, a new generation of technology could give communities a better way to respond before mosquito populations get out of control.

The technology comes from Digitomy, a startup founded by researchers at the University of South Florida. Associate Professor Ryan Carney and Professor Sriram Chellappan have been developing the system through research dating back to 2018. Their goal is to help mosquito control teams identify the insects they're catching without spending days examining them under a microscope.

The trap itself looks fairly straightforward. Workers can hang it from a low tree branch or place it on the ground. A light or bait attracts mosquitoes, and a small fan pulls them inside. Once the insects land on a sticky pad, two built-in cameras photograph them. Artificial intelligence then compares those images against a large database to determine which mosquito species have been captured.

But the technology goes further. It can also identify whether a mosquito is male or female and whether it has recently fed on blood. That's useful information because female mosquitoes bite people and can transmit diseases. The researchers say their system achieved more than 98% accuracy in identifying mosquito species during laboratory testing.

GOOGLE WANTS TO RELEASE MILLIONS OF MOSQUITOES

A researcher displays mosquitoes collected by the smart trap, which uses AI to identify potentially dangerous species much faster than traditional methods. (University of South Florida)

Traditional mosquito surveillance can take two to three days because specialists often need to examine captured insects under a microscope. That's valuable work, but when health officials are trying to track a disease outbreak, waiting several days can slow their response. Digitomy wants to shorten that process dramatically. Its system uses AI and cloud computing with the goal of identifying captured mosquito species the same day. That could help mosquito control teams see where potentially dangerous species are appearing and decide where to concentrate their efforts.

This is especially important with Aedes aegypti, the mosquito species primarily responsible for spreading dengue in Florida. There are roughly 3,500 mosquito species worldwide, but only certain species spread particular diseases. Knowing which ones are present can help officials make better decisions. There's one important point to understand. The trap identifies mosquito species capable of carrying disease. It does not automatically prove that a captured mosquito is infected with dengue. Health officials would still need laboratory testing to confirm the presence of the virus.

What I find particularly interesting is what happens after the trap identifies a mosquito. Digitomy can send that information to a mapping dashboard, allowing mosquito control teams to see where certain species are appearing. The goal is to give mosquito control teams access to that information the same day, helping them identify where potentially dangerous species are appearing. Think about how useful that could be during an outbreak. If several traps begin detecting more Aedes aegypti mosquitoes in one neighborhood, officials could investigate that area and consider targeted mosquito control measures. Instead of waiting for more people to become sick, they could use surveillance data to guide their response.

The researchers have already integrated trap information into a private layer of their Global Mosquito Observations Dashboard at mosquitodashboard.org/. That system also incorporates more than half a million citizen science reports. The idea is to combine information from automated traps with observations from people who help track mosquitoes. Digitomy's technology could also complement an existing early warning system developed by Carney for dengue and West Nile virus. Together, these tools could give public health departments a clearer view of mosquito activity across communities. Of course, detecting mosquitoes early doesn't guarantee that an outbreak can be prevented. But faster information could help officials respond sooner, particularly in areas where mosquito control resources are limited.

Digitomy has already tested its technology at the University of South Florida and worked with the Anastasia Mosquito Control District in St. Johns County, which includes St. Augustine. The researchers are also preparing for field validation with Hillsborough County, where Florida's dengue outbreak has been especially severe. The startup is working with USF's Technology Transfer office to license the AI identification system to established mosquito trap manufacturers. That could allow companies to add the technology to equipment they already produce.

Digitomy is working toward commercial availability by licensing its AI technology to established mosquito trap manufacturers. For now, the university has not announced a consumer launch date or retail price. The company also received a $25,000 grant from the USF Research Foundation's Bull Ring Accelerator during summer 2026. The funding is intended to help accelerate the licensing and commercialization of university-developed technology. The team is also developing an online education platform that would allow mosquito control professionals and the public to practice identifying mosquito species using images and AI-generated feedback.

THIRD PERSON DIES AFTER MOSQUITO IS REPORTEDLY TRAPPED ON PLANE TO GERMANY IN 'AIRPORT MALARIA' PHENOMENON

Researchers test the AI-powered mosquito trap in a controlled environment as they work to improve mosquito surveillance and help communities respond faster to disease threats. (University of South Florida)

You probably won't be hanging a Digitomy trap in your backyard anytime soon. But that doesn't mean this technology couldn't eventually affect your community. If mosquito control departments adopt smarter surveillance systems, they may be able to identify dangerous mosquito populations sooner and make better decisions about where to intervene. And even though we're heading into November, people living in warmer areas still need to pay attention to mosquito activity. If you're traveling to Florida or another place where mosquitoes remain active, taking precautions is important.

For now, the best protection is still fairly simple. Empty standing water from flowerpots and other outdoor containers because mosquitoes can breed in surprisingly small amounts of water. Use an EPA-registered insect repellent when spending time outdoors. Wearing long sleeves and pants can also help reduce exposed skin. We've covered some useful products that can help keep mosquitoes away, including repellents and outdoor gadgets.

You can find them in our guide to mosquito and tick repellents at CyberGuy.com

I think this is one of those uses of AI that could make a real difference in people's lives. Most of us see mosquitoes as an annoying part of summer. But Florida's dengue outbreak is a reminder that these tiny insects can cause serious health problems, even late in the year. What interests me about Digitomy is the possibility of giving mosquito control teams information while they still have time to act. The technology looks promising, especially with its reported accuracy in laboratory testing. But I want to see how it performs in real-world conditions before calling it a breakthrough. If it works as researchers hope, communities could have a valuable new tool to help protect people from mosquito-borne diseases. And that's a use of AI I can get behind.

Would you feel safer knowing AI-powered mosquito traps were monitoring your neighborhood? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com

articles.title: Hundreds of thousands of Czechs protest in Prague over media freedom
articles.excerpt:
Hundreds of thousands rally against plan to scrap licence fees and fund broadcasters from state budget

Hundreds of thousands of Czechs are rallying in Prague to protest against what they say is a gov...
articles.body_text:
Hundreds of thousands rally against plan to scrap licence fees and fund broadcasters from state budget

Hundreds of thousands of Czechs are rallying in Prague to protest against what they say is a government attempt to stifle media freedom.

The gathering on Sunday to save the mandatory licence fees that fund Czechia’s public broadcasters could be one of the biggest in the country’s history, organisers say.

It will mark the latest challenge to the prime minister, Andrej Babiš, and his coalition of populist, hard-right nationalist and Eurosceptic parties, and follows weeks of demonstrations in towns and cities and a strike by staff at Czech TV and Czech Radio.

Protesters say the plan to scrap licence fees and fund the broadcasters from the state budget would give ministers more leverage over newsrooms and follow the example of Slovakia, Hungary, Poland and Serbia, where current and previous rightwing populist governments eroded media independence.

The Million Moments for Democracy group that is organising the demonstration said the authorities would see the level of opposition. “Babiš and his government obviously think they will get away with anything … that they can ignore experts, silence critics and treat democratic institutions like their property,” it said.

Organisers said an estimated 350,000 people had come out to join the protest at Letná Plain, which overlooks Prague’s historic centre.

Many protesters wore pointed hats folded out of newspapers as tribute to an animated character who has introduced Czech Television’s nightly children’s bedtime stories for decades. “We do witness here something extraordinary today,” Mikuláš Minář, the lead organiser from Million Moments for Democracy, told Associated Press.

The proposed changes, which would cut state television and radio budgets by about 15%, have drawn fire from international media organisations.

The European Broadcasting Union, the European Federation of Journalists, Reporters Without Borders and the International Press Institute have also criticised the government’s media plan, likening it to controversial moves by Slovakia’s prime minister, Robert Fico, and Hungary’s former premier Viktor Orbán.

Babiš, a billionaire who returned to power last year, said protesters were riling up the public with unfounded claims about threats to media freedom. Last week, he published an op-ed on what he called the “seven lies” being peddled by the opposition over the licence fees, which together add up to 205 koruna (£7) a month.

“Anyone who talks about ‘nationalisation’ [of public media] is deliberately lying,” he wrote, describing the criticism as “hysterical outbursts”. “Under no circumstances will we interfere in editorial work.”

Thousands of people have gathered in central Prague to protest against the Czech government's plans to scrap...
articles.body_text:
Czech radio said it's the largest protest in the history of the independent Czech Republic

Thousands of people have gathered in central Prague to protest against the Czech government's plans to scrap the license fee and use the state budget to fund public media.

Critics say the plans would allow politicians to stifle media freedom.

The coalition government - which consists of the populist ANO party and two right-wing Eurosceptic parties - insists the change will not affect editorial independence, but wants broadcasters to cut costs.

Parliament passed the first draft of the proposal late last month. Since then, thousands of Czechs have taken part in protests.

Czech households currently pay ⁠205 crowns ($9.44, £7.06) a month for Czech TV and Czech radio.

Organisers say the protest in Prague's Letna park has "roughly 400,000" attendees, making it the largest protest since the country's independence in 1993

Sunday's protest was organised by the Million Moments for Democracy association which said "roughly 400,000" people had attended.

It is being described as the largest protest since the Czech Republic's independence  in 1993.

"I know that our entire Czech Television is a guarantee of truth and objectivity," pensioner Milana Rudolfova, 72, told Reuters news agency.

"If we do not have public television and radio then unfortunately we will not be able to believe anything anymore."

Some protesters wore pointed hats folded out of newspapers as a tribute to an animated character, Večerníček, who has introduced Czech Television's nightly children's bedtime stories for decades.

Critics have compared the government's media bill to changes in Hungary under former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán, who tightly controlled state media when he was in power.

Prime Minister Andrej Babis was appointed in December in 2025, and has faced criticism over his coalition's attacks on Czech media.

"Political attacks against private and public media have become one of the hallmarks of Andrej Babis' premiership," said Pavol Szalai, Prague Bureau director of international press freedom organisation Reporters Without Borders, in June.
