articles.title: Millions of Americans use marijuana to sleep, but new study raises troubling questions
articles.excerpt: American Heart Association expert Robert Page warns that cannabis use may increase cardiovascular risks, even in younger adults who don't smoke tobacco. He urges patients to discuss cannabis use with ...
articles.body_text:
American Heart Association expert Robert Page warns that cannabis use may increase cardiovascular risks, even in younger adults who don't smoke tobacco. He urges patients to discuss cannabis use with their doctors.

Marijuana may be making sleep quality worse, despite its widespread use as a sleep aid, a recent Northwestern Medicine study found.

The findings of the study, which included 1,266 participants, showed that both lifetime and recent cannabis users objectively had worse sleep quality, although they did not report their sleep to be worse.

Participants were monitored for almost 35 years, from young adulthood into middle age, with scientists tracking their use of cannabis over time.

AMERICA HITS MAJOR MARIJUANA MILESTONE AS DAILY WEED USE SURPASSES DAILY DRINKING

In middle age, participants wore a sleep monitor on their wrist for a week and filled out surveys about their sleep quality.

This allowed researchers to compare objective and subjective reports of participants’ sleep.

A recent Northwestern Medicine study found that cannabis use does not improve sleep. Instead, it actually worsens people's quality of sleep. (iStock)

"Our data do not support the belief that cannabis is helpful as a sleep aid," said senior study author Mercedes R. Carnethon, Ph.D., as Northwestern Now reported.

"As cannabis becomes increasingly available and accepted, it's important to better understand its long-term associations with health behaviors such as sleep," Carnethon added.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

Among all participants, a greater lifetime exposure to marijuana was linked to worse objective sleep quality.

Those who had a higher cannabis usage over time were generally asleep for a lower percentage of the night and experienced more sleep disruption.

The study found that recent cannabis users had more sleep disruption. (iStock)

Similarly, recent cannabis users were more likely to have more sleep fragmentation and lower sleep efficiency, compared to people who never used the substance.

The study also found there was a much higher chance that recent cannabis users would sleep longer than eight hours per night.

The study discusses the differences between objective and subjective reports of sleep quality.

"What makes this study particularly interesting is that participants who used cannabis demonstrated objectively poorer sleep, yet their own assessments of sleep quality did not reflect those differences," Alfred Joshua, M.D., a board-certified emergency medicine physician based in California, told Fox News Digital. (He was not involved with the new study.)

"In other words, someone may believe marijuana is helping them sleep, while objective measurements suggest otherwise."

Scientists say more research needs to be done to determine the long-term effects of cannabis use on sleep. (iStock)

Researchers considered multiple outside factors including age, race, sex, smoking frequency, alcohol consumption, physical activity and more.

Even with these factors taken into account, the study found a consistent correlation between cannabis use and poorer objectively measured sleep.

The mode of cannabis consumption, such as smoking versus taking edibles, was not considered.

"These findings raise important questions."

"It is not surprising that the actual quality of sleep of these subjects, after chronic marijuana use, is poor compared to those who do not smoke marijuana because people who claim that they need to smoke marijuana before they go to sleep, in order to relax, are only kidding themselves," board-certified psychiatrist Carole Lieberman, M.D., of California told Fox News Digital. (She, too, was not affiliated with the new study.)

Participants in a new study often did not report having poorer sleep quality even though data from their wrist monitors showed they had objectively worse sleep quality. (iStock)

"It is more a psychological addiction than a physical one," she added. "They enjoy the high that they get right away, but the marijuana doesn't help them to sleep better."

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"The researchers found that greater cumulative cannabis exposure was associated with reduced sleep efficiency, increased sleep fragmentation and more time spent awake after initially falling asleep," said Joshua, the board-certified emergency medicine physician.

"These findings raise important questions about whether habitual marijuana use is a sustainable strategy for managing sleep problems," he added.

Fox News Digital recently reported on other cannabis findings.

A study of nearly 450,000 American adults, for instance, linked cannabis use to an increased risk of stroke and cardiovascular disease.

The findings were scheduled for presentation at the American Heart Association’s Scientific Sessions 2026 in Chicago Nov. 6–9. They showed that both casual and heavy marijuana users have higher odds of heart conditions compared to non-users.

Khloe Quill of Fox News Digital contributed reporting.

Sadie Chafe is a writer on the Lifestyle team at Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Private planes and roadtrips: AEW goes above and beyond to get to Phoenix for Full Gear despite travel chaos
articles.excerpt: Rep. Laurel Lee, R-Fla., joins ‘Fox Report’ to discuss congressional efforts to modernize the nation's aging air traffic control system and the need for increased investment and oversight following a ...
articles.body_text:
Rep. Laurel Lee, R-Fla., joins ‘Fox Report’ to discuss congressional efforts to modernize the nation's aging air traffic control system and the need for increased investment and oversight following a nationwide FAA ground stop.

All Elite Wrestling (AEW) dropkicked a nationwide nightmare to make sure its talent and personnel made it to Phoenix for Full Gear on Saturday despite travel chaos that plagued millions across the U.S.

AEW owner Tony Khan brought in some wrestlers and other workers on private planes just to make sure they were going to show up for the fans, who were expected to pack the Mortgage Matchup Center for one of the company’s top pay-per-views on the calendar.

"I know it’s been an incredibly challenging few days for a lot of people," Khan said in a video posted to his social media. "My sympathies to everybody affected by all of the flight cancelations and delays. Yesterday, as you can imagine, was a hectic day as it was for a lot of people with the flights grounded and that applied to all flights yesterday – private and public flights. For AEW, we’re the same as everyone else, we’re not trying to break any rules. Everybody was grounded and we started formulating a plan that has come together really, really well."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK PRO WRESTLING COVERAGE

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

A person looks at a flight information board at LaGuardia Airport in New York on Friday, Nov. 13, 2026, after the Federal Aviation Administration grounded flights nationwide. (AP Photo/Ryan Murphy)

Khan said everyone on the Full Gear pay-per-view card arrived in Phoenix. Khan sent private planes at three "hub locations" to bring the wrestlers and other personnel to the Mortgage Matchup Center. The only thing that changed was the Tailgate Brawl – which will occur on the Full Gear pre-show.

Khan said he believed everyone probably would have made it on their scheduled flights.

"I think it was virtually impossible given how many flights of people who work in AEW have been canceled had I not dispatched the private planes to the three hub locations, I think it’s very unlikely everybody would have made it here. I think there probably would have been some changes to the main card."

Adam Copeland, who battles Kazuchika Okada for the AEW International Championship, said it was "challenging" to get from the East Coast all the way to Phoenix.

"I was going down the runway about to take off for Denver and the pilot came on and said there’s a ground stoppage nationwide. I was like, ‘OK.’ I called Beth (Phoenix) and she came and got me and I went home," he said. "No idea if I was going to make it today. All of my flights started getting canceled one after the other after the other. Everyone else’s flights were starting to take off but mine weren’t.

"Even still, my flight to get out here is tomorrow at 5:37. So, Tony Khan sent a plane to come get us. Poor (Tony) Schiavone got there early so he was sitting there at 9 o’clock. I don’t think we were taking off until 11 so I was like, come have a coffee, come pet my dogs. We had a big dog cuddle-fest this morning and my girls got to meet Tony and we had some coffee – we made the best of it."

Tony Schiavone, one-third of the AEW broadcast team, was set to fly out of Atlanta when he made the last-minute decision to take a smaller plane out of Asheville, North Carolina, because of the uncertainty that he may have been delayed or canceled. He told his wife he wasn’t going to drive all the way to Phoenix, but he would have if he had the time to make the 27-hour trip.

Tony Schiavone is in the ring during AEW Collision on June 15 at the Covelli Centre in Youngstown, Ohio. (Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

LIVE COVERAGE: THOUSANDS OF FLIGHTS CANCELED AFTER LONGEST NATIONWIDE GROUND STOP IN 25 YEARS ROCKS US AIRPORTS

"But that was OK because I waited, got to hang out with Adam Copeland, which was pretty cool," he said. "It was a pretty cool day but it was a very challenging day. I guess I got here around 2 o’clock local time here in the afternoon. My car is still in Asheville. I have no idea how I’m gonna get it but it doesn’t matter. I’m glad I’m here. I would do anything to make it to Full Gear. … I would have driven to Phoenix! I would have, but I didn’t have the time."

Mark Davis and Jake Doyle, the duo known as Davis and Doyle, will challenge for the AEW World Tag Team Championship against The Young Bucks. But it was far from easy for them to get to the arena.

"Tumultuous last 24 hours leading up to Full Gear," Davis said. "For me, I had to run across the great state of Florida. I went from Tampa to Orlando, trying to get a flight – didn’t happen. Thankfully, the big guy had our back and I think he’s pretty excited to see Davis and Doyle take down some Young Bucks here this evening at Full Gear."

Doyle made it clear, "It’s a bad day to be a Buck."

"It was already a bad day to be a Buck but then I had to drive to Detroit, then drive to Chicago, then sit on a private jet, which is pretty awesome, but I had to sit on that jet for eight hours, waiting to get here to tear up these Young Bucks.

"So, Tony Khan, thank you for that jet. Young Bucks, I don’t feel sorry for you."

Matt and Nick Jackson – The Young Bucks – were only in California. They had to make the drive to Phoenix.

"We told each other, we’re blessed, we’re in California. A lot of these guys are coming further than us, but we will do anything – planes, trains and automobiles – we will be here at Full Gear," Matt Jackson said. "We have a big match tonight – Davis and Doyle. Two intimidating meatheads that actually had our number the last couple times when we’ve been in the ring. We talked about it on the drive. We had six hours to really think about it and strategize. Yeah, the travel sucked but we’re ready and we’re gonna rock the house tonight at Full Gear."

Excalibur, Schiavone’s broadcast teammate, said he was at the gym when he got a text about the travel chaos. He said he planned to jump in a car to go from Southern California to Phoenix. He drove five hours to get to the arena but took solace in the fact he got a chance to stop in the desert he doesn’t normally stop in.

"I made it. I wouldn’t miss this for the world. I know people have much tougher travel days than I did. I mean a five-hour drive, it’s doable, but in wrestling terms, it’s nothing," he said. "I wasn’t going to miss this for the world. I know a lot of people in AEW, everybody in AEW, has the same idea, same feeling, if there’s any way possible for them to be here today, they’re gonna be here at Full Gear. … There’s nothing that can keep me from Full Gear today."

Nigel McGuinness, the third person on the broadcast team, got to Phoenix from Los Angeles. He jumped in his car when he learned about the travel woes.

"There was no way I was gonna miss Full Gear," he said. "There’s something about being in professional wrestling where you make the show no matter what. I’ve never missed a show and there was no way I was going to miss Full Gear."

AEW President Tony Khan during AEW Dynamite at Footprint Center in Phoenix, Ariz., on Feb. 22, 2023. (USA TODAY Sports)

The main pay-per-view card begins at 8 p.m. ET and can be seen on HBO Max.

Ryan Gaydos is a senior editor for Fox News Digital.

articles.title: Hundreds of men march in Switzerland to protest violence against women
articles.excerpt:
Hundreds of men have led a demonstration in Switzerland’s capital, Bern, to denounce misogyny and violence against women, saying men need to take a more effective role in fighting both.

The “Men Agai...
articles.body_text:
Hundreds of men have led a demonstration in Switzerland’s capital, Bern, to denounce misogyny and violence against women, saying men need to take a more effective role in fighting both.

The “Men Against Violence Against Women” rally outside parliament on Saturday follows persistent concerns that misogyny is too prevalent online among teenage boys and young men and that other men need to build a stronger counter-narrative.

The misogynistic views are pushed by the right-wing “manosphere” – a loose network of online forums and influencers that promote male supremacy and hostility to feminism. Such influencers were emboldened after Donald Trump won the US presidential election in 202 to justify and amplify misogynistic derision and threats online.

“We men are part of the problem – the problem being violence against women and queer people,” said Christoph Gosteli, a 42-year-old social worker who co-organised the rally with a group called maenner.

“That is why it is important for us to take a stand and say, ‘We no longer want to be part of the problem; we want to be part of the solution.’”

An academic and advocacy group survey released in June by the University of Zurich and MenCare, an umbrella group of Swiss men’s and fathers’ organisations, found that half of male respondents aged 18 to 24 held a “restrictive and dominance-based view of masculinity”, expressing concerns that “real men are increasingly marginalised in society”.

The study called for “a systematic and society-wide debate about ideals of masculinity that promote violence”, beginning in schools.

Swiss Justice Minister Beat Jans attended a conference earlier this month on the dangers of violent online abuse of women.

In a speech on November 2, he said that men commit four-fifths of violent crimes and that in rape cases, the share is “as high as 99 percent”.

“It is not all men. But we must also admit: It is almost always men,” Jans said. “Violence by men does not begin with the first blow; it begins with a disparaging remark. We men all have a duty.”

articles.title: Michigan loses again and the noise around Kyle Whittingham's job grows as Oregon keeps playoff hopes alive
articles.excerpt:
Dylan Raiola found Dakorien Moore for a 59-yard TD that extended the Oregon Ducks' lead over the Michigan Wolverines.

If you close your eyes and listen closely, you can hear the faint heartbeat of th...
articles.body_text:
Dylan Raiola found Dakorien Moore for a 59-yard TD that extended the Oregon Ducks' lead over the Michigan Wolverines.

If you close your eyes and listen closely, you can hear the faint heartbeat of the Oregon Ducks' College Football Playoff hopes.

On the other hand, for Michigan coach Kyle Whittingham, the noise surrounding his job is deafening. No. 16 Oregon (7-3) beat Michigan (5-5) 31-7 on Saturday. The outlook for both teams couldn't be more different.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

The loss for Michigan makes the possibility of Whittingham being a one-and-done head coach all the more real, while Oregon keeps it playoff hopes alive.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Michigan head coach Kyle Whittingham watches the first half of an NCAA college football game against Oregon on Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026, in Eugene, Ore. (AP Photo/Lydia Ely)

The Ducks came out flying, scoring touchdowns on two of their first three possessions of the game. Ducks quarterback Dylan Raiola opened the scoring when he connected with wide receiver Jeremiah McClellan on a deep ball for a 60-yard touchdown, putting Oregon up 7-0.

The Ducks' second touchdown of the opening quarter came with less excitement, but the points still counted the same. Raiola hit running back Da'Juan Riggs in the flat for his first career receiving touchdown to put Oregon up 14-0.

It looked like the Ducks were on their way to an easy win, but Michigan running back Savion Hiter got the Wolverines on the board with a 70-yard rushing touchdown to cut the deficit in half, making it 14-7.

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

Oregon Ducks wide receiver Jeremiah McClellan ran after the catch for a 60-yard touchdown in the first quarter during a college football game against the Michigan Wolverines on Nov. 14, 2026, at Autzen Stadium in Eugene, Ore. (Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

Michigan looked like it was going to go into halftime down one score, but instead it had a complete coverage breakdown with seconds remaining in the first half. Raiola scrambled outside the pocket and connected with Dakorien Moore for a 59-yard touchdown after Moore got behind the defensive backs to put Oregon up 21-7.

Coming out of the half, Michigan benched quarterback Bryce Underwood for Tommy Carr, looking for a spark.

It looked like Michigan was going to cut into the deficit at the beginning of the fourth quarter, but the Oregon defense slammed the door with the Wolverines on the Ducks' 3-yard line, forcing a turnover on downs. With the game out of reach, Oregon tacked on another score with a 49-yard touchdown from Dierre Hill Jr. off a screen pass.

Brandon Finney Jr. #4 and Devon Jackson #9 of the Oregon Ducks celebrate after a play during the first half of a game against the Michigan Wolverines at Autzen Stadium on Nov. 14, 2026, in Eugene, Ore. (ISI Photos via Getty Images)

With just over four minutes left, Whittingham went back to Underwood to end the game.

Oregon's next game is against Michigan State, and beating the Spartans is paramount to staying alive in the playoff race.

For Michigan, its next two games are against ranked opponents. Next week, the Wolverines play No. 4 UCLA and then end their season against No. 20 Ohio State. Losses to either or both of those teams could spur changes in Ann Arbor.

articles.title: UK government to consider changing age of consent after allegations against Russell Brand
articles.excerpt:
Deputy prime minister says change would be a massive step but ‘deserves proper consideration and scrutiny’

The government has said it will consider calls to change the age of consent after a woman wa...
articles.body_text:
Deputy prime minister says change would be a massive step but ‘deserves proper consideration and scrutiny’

The government has said it will consider calls to change the age of consent after a woman waived her right to anonymity to publicly claim she was raped by Russell Brand as a 16-year-old schoolgirl.

Mia Latter, now 37, alleged she had been orally raped by the jailed comedian when she was a teenager and he was 30 years old.

In an interview with the Sunday Times, she called for the introduction of a staggered age of consent – which would make relationships between adults and teenagers aged 16 and 17 illegal.

Louise Haigh, the de facto deputy prime minister, told the newspaper that Latter’s “heart-breaking story” meant a law change deserved consideration.

She said: “We need to listen to Mia and other victims like her who have been through these experiences because it’s really important that as lawmakers their experience is at the heart of what we consider.

“It clearly would be a massive step to change the age of consent, but it deserves proper consideration and scrutiny. I can absolutely understand why she is calling for it.”

Under UK law, adults of any age are legally able to have sex with 16 and 17-year-olds.

Latter said: “It’s shocking to me time and time again that whenever the news comes up again about him, it’s always in the comments about the relationship with a 16-year-old.

“That’s not the most heinous bit. But why is that the thing that everybody collectively gets stuck on? I think we all sort of agree that … adults shouldn’t be allowed to have sexual relationships with children, with somebody under the age of 18. That really doesn’t seem like a gigantic leap to take.”

Latter was referred to under the pseudonym of Alice in previous reporting by the Sunday Times, the Times, and Channel 4’s Dispatches documentary.

She was 16 when she first met Brand in Leicester Square, central London, while she was on her way home from a shopping trip.

He took her number and later messaged her, asking if she wanted to go for dinner, she said.

She told the newspaper that Brand – who was working at MTV at the time – still asked her to meet after she had confessed her age to him.

Latter alleges Brand orally raped her towards the end of their three-month relationship.

Brand denied all of the allegations made against him by Latter when they were first reported in 2023 by the Times.

She spoke to the police after the documentary, but the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) decided not to include her case in Brand’s trial at Southwark Crown Court.

He was convicted of attacks against four of the six women who gave evidence against him, and is now serving a 10-and-a-half-year prison term for one count of rape and three sexual assaults.

Earlier this week, it was announced that a series of “serious” sex offence allegations against comedian David Walliams are being probed by the Metropolitan police after an investigation by the Guardian and ITV News.

One woman described her alleged encounter with Walliams when she was 15 as “sexual assault”.

Haigh went on to say that, in light of news that one of Walliams’s accusers was asked to sign a non disclosure agreement (NDA), the government should also look at banning them in cases of alleged sexual assault and harassment. She said: “When we consider the allegations against David Walliams, teenagers who were fans wouldn’t come under the current consultation.

“I do think there is a very strong case to look at banning NDAs in all circumstances where they relate to harassment or discrimination, to make sure that no victim, regardless of where it happened or what their relationship was with the perpetrator, should ever be silenced.”

It is believed MPs outside Labour may support a bill to change the age of consent laws, with Jess Brown-Fuller, the Liberal Democrat justice spokesperson, coming out in favour of reviewing them.

Commending Latter for the “extraordinary bravery” it took to waive her anonymity, Brown-Fuller said: “I think we must go further to increase protections for young women and girls, and looking at a staggered age of consent is an important step.

“We already have rules that recognise power imbalances in professions: between teachers and students, or barristers and junior colleagues. It’s time for the government to recognise the implicit power imbalance held by older men over teenage girls.”

Latter’s decision to come forward was also praised by Bridget Phillipson, the minister for women and equalities, who said she “and thousands of others across the country will be in awe of her courage and determination”. She added that it is “up to all of us to send a message to women and girls who experience sexual violence: the shame is not yours. Women like Mia are leading the charge, but we can and must do more to make this a moment of change.”

Latter’s allegation was reported to the Met police, who said the investigation into the alleged rape remains ongoing.

A Met Police spokesperson said: “Officers launched an investigation in January 2026 after receiving an allegation of rape.

“Detectives sought advice from the Crown Prosecution Service to determine how best to proceed, and officers were advised that further information was needed before a charging decision could be made.

“This investigation remains ongoing. We understand the delay has been distressing for this victim-survivor. However, our focus has been on putting forward the best possible evidence.”

The CPS said: “The Crown Prosecution Service will continue to work closely with investigators to provide advice and make sure cases progress as quickly as possible.”

articles.title: SpaceX’s Starship captured by launchpad arms in dramatic first
articles.excerpt:
SpaceX’s Starship ‌spacecraft has returned to Earth, caught midair by giant mechanical arms where its journey began 22 hours earlier.

The spaceship emerged from a cloudy sky on Saturday, descending s...
articles.body_text:
SpaceX’s Starship ‌spacecraft has returned to Earth, caught midair by giant mechanical arms where its journey began 22 hours earlier.

The spaceship emerged from a cloudy sky on Saturday, descending slowly over Starbase before slipping smoothly between mechanical “chopstick arms” above Launch Pad 2 in Texas – the first-ever capture of a Starship flying back from space.

Soon afterwards, SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk congratulated his “incredible team”.

SpaceX officials said Saturday’s catch demonstrates Starship’s full reusability, crucial for rapid, low-cost recycling.

However, with the first-stage booster exploding shortly after Friday’s liftoff from Texas, the company fell short of its desired double catch.

Separating neatly from its booster before things went awry, the upper-stage spacecraft soared into orbit and released 26 advanced Starlink satellites.

SpaceX’s Kate Tice said its engines stopped firing too soon on the way back down. The booster’s guidance system sensed it was not in the right position and automatically initiated the watery detour and self-destruction. Engineers are still investigating the cause.

Although Friday’s booster recovery failed, the company had already made three previous booster catches, validating the technique.

NASA, which is paying billions of dollars for Starship to land Artemis astronauts on the Moon later this decade, welcomed the achievement.

“It was almost magic,” NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said on X.

Starship completed 14 laps around the Earth, 265km (165 miles), outshining the previous mission’s one to two laps.

SpaceX reported that everything on the spacecraft, including its vital heat shield, appeared to work well.

It was SpaceX’s 15th flight of a full-scale Starship since 2023 and its only second trip to orbit.

Starship, a 124-metre (407ft) behemoth, is the world’s largest and most powerful rocket, intended for Moon and Mars travel.

SpaceX expects to begin launching Starships from Florida’s Kennedy Space Center within the next few months.

articles.title: My mother told me I would die if I sought treatment for Ebola - I am proof you can survive
articles.excerpt: When Dr Raymond Kasereka Kamwanga told his family he suspected he had Ebola and was going to a treatment centre in the city of Butembo in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, his family were horrifie...
articles.body_text:
When Dr Raymond Kasereka Kamwanga told his family he suspected he had Ebola and was going to a treatment centre in the city of Butembo in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo, his family were horrified.

They regarded the specialised unit as a "death house" as not many patients do recover - especially those admitted in the late stages of the illness. His 50-year-old mother was in tears, pleading with him not to go there.

"Why are you choosing to die at the Ebola treatment centre?" Masika Ndungo had asked him.

But as a doctor at Butembo's Katwa Hospital, he knew that if stayed at home, he was unlikely to survive.

This was in July, two months after the World Health Organization (WHO) had declared the Ebola outbreak in DR Congo a public health emergency of international concern. Since then 5,400 people have died and 11,000 have been infected, making it the second-most deadly outbreak ever recorded.

Butembo is in North Kivu province, the epicentre of the crisis, with the highest number of reported cases, according to the Congolese health ministry.

Dr Kamwanga is one of 3,031 people who have survived - and is evangelical about sharing his story in an effort to help stop the spread of infections devastating his community.

After staring death in the face and overcoming ostracisation, he has even started writing a book about his experience.

"As someone who has recovered, I am living proof that the disease exists, but also that it is possible to recover from it," he tells the BBC outside Katwa Hospital where he still works.

The 30-year-old medic believes he contracted the virus through contact with a patient in a setting where protective measures are not always adequate.

Raymond Kasereka Kamwanga uses his book to help convince sceptics that Ebola is real

The first symptoms appeared gradually: a bitter taste in his mouth, headaches and a general feeling of malaise. He contacted the Ebola response team.

After an initial consultation and some tests, he returned home, but his condition did not improve.

Butembo does not have the equipment to quickly test for Ebola - samples need to be sent to the city of Beni, 54km (33 miles) north.

This delays diagnosis as the condition of roads in this war-torn and underdeveloped part of DR Congo means it can take between 48 and 72 hours to travel even this relatively short distance.

After three days at home, Kamwanga felt extremely weak and experienced muscle pain. On the fourth day, he began vomiting and had diarrhoea.

This is when he gathered his family members - including his mother - to tell them he had to go to the Ebola treatment centre.

"She had started crying, along with my sisters. I told them everything would be alright, that I was a doctor and that I was confident. But they weren't reassured," he says.

Around 18:00, he set off on foot to the nearby centre but refused to use the main entrance.

He called his colleagues and asked them to put on their protective gear before they approached him and isolated him. The virus spreads from one person to another by contact with infected bodily fluids.

Dr Kamwanga's mother says his experience has helped dispel some of the misinformation she had heard about Ebola

The current outbreak is caused by the Bundibugyo species of the virus for which there is no approved vaccine or treatment.

"The treatment given to Ebola patients is symptomatic - meaning that doctors treat the symptoms the patient presents," says Kamwanga, explaining that in his case it was severe vomiting and diarrhoea.

In some patients these symptoms can lead to organ failure and then some develop internal and external bleeding.

Kamwanga lost a lot of fluid and struggled to stay hydrated - he was terrified.

"I was afraid for myself. Every day, patients were dying right before my eyes. But I stayed positive," he explains.

Over 13 days lying in his hospital bed, he tried to keep his spirits up by watching movies and TV shows on his phone, reading and scrolling through TikTok.

The day he learned he had recovered, Kamwanga felt immense relief. He thanked the healthcare workers who had cared for him.

However, even a certificate showing he was Ebola-free did not initially dispel the unease those around him felt after he was discharged.

What is Ebola and why is stopping the latest outbreak so difficult?

'I buried my parents one day after the other' - Ebola mourners learn how to grieve safely

"We welcomed him home warmly. But because of our fear, we didn't get close to him any more," Ndungo, his mother, tells the BBC.

For 21 days - the incubation period of the virus - the doctor lived separately in another part of the family home, which was crowded at the time with at least 18 people living there, including several children and people displaced by recent fighting in the region.

He would only see them from afar when he went to pick up his meal, while other family members kept their distance.

Neighbour Kavugho Sifa shared these concerns.

"We were really afraid, but we prayed to God to protect him at the treatment centre. With God's help and the doctors' efforts, we saw him return in good health," she tells the BBC.

They all agree the experience changed their perception of Ebola.

Some do not believe the disease even exists - Ndungo says that witnessing Ebola first-hand helped to dispel some of that misinformation.

After his recovery, Kamwanga threw himself into community outreach - sharing his story as a way of combatting rumours and mistrust.

"I started writing my book - The Price of Saving Lives - one week after recovering and leaving the hospital," he says. "However, it is not finished yet. What I currently use during my awareness-raising activities is the draft, and it is already making a significant impact."

During these sessions, he also distributes photos taken while he was sick to help convince residents that Ebola is real.

But in Butembo, this mission remains difficult. Kamwanga explains that some people view awareness campaigns as a way for humanitarian organisations to profit from donor funding.

Such mistrust, which is also levelled at healthcare professionals, is often fuelled by poverty and trauma related to years of armed conflict, he says.

"Ebola has come alongside the war," he says, explaining that some even interpret it as a way for those in authority to threaten a vulnerable population "to finish off those whom the war failed to exterminate".

He also believes that the number of deaths observed during epidemics - compared to recoveries, which are sometimes less visible - reinforce fear and suspicion.

But putting himself on the front line also comes with risks - and Kamwanga says he receives death threats on his phone.

Some residents accuse him of being paid to spread information about Ebola. He also reports that outreach workers have been attacked by members of the community.

He feels the authorities do not work effectively to address all these problems: "Our government is taking things lightly."

He agrees too with the recent report by Médecins Sans Frontières (MSF) that Ebola funds are going missing.

"The money allocated to the Ebola response is being misappropriated by the government. We do not have enough protective equipment," the medic says.

The BBC has asked the Congolese government for comment.

Despite the intimidation and the obstacles he and other medics face, he remains determined - his goal is to help put an end to the disease.

"Should we give up the fight against Ebola? No. We continue to do what we can with the resources available to us, which are unfortunately very limited."

'They said it isn't real': Ebola rumours fuel attacks on health workers

Recovery of Ebola patients offers rare moments of joy at epicentre of outbreak

Questions remain over Ebola patient who travelled across three nations undetected

articles.title: Judo champion shakes up French  presidential race with surprise candidacy
articles.excerpt:
Five-times Olympic champion Teddy Riner is one of France's most popular athletes

Apart from an overwhelming urge to pin one's opponent to the floor of the house, there is no obvious connection betwee...
articles.body_text:
Five-times Olympic champion Teddy Riner is one of France's most popular athletes

Apart from an overwhelming urge to pin one's opponent to the floor of the house, there is no obvious connection between politics and the world of top-level judo.

That has not stopped France's much-garlanded world heavyweight champion Teddy Riner from throwing his hat into the ring for next April's presidential race.

The Guadeloupe-born 37-year-old may have no experience of public office, no party behind him, and as yet no manifesto. All so far is a slogan La France qu'on aime (The France we love), a declaration on social media, and a campaign visit to a hospital in the Seine-Saint-Denis suburb of northern Paris.

But it would be a foolhardy pundit who would totally write off his chances.

Riner is, after all, one of the most popular figures in modern-day France, regularly topping the polls for embodying the nation's "values". He is a proven winner, with five Olympic golds and 11 world championships under his belt, as well as a successful career in business.

More than 28 million people have watched his election broadcast on Instagram and X, shot with proper presidential decorum against a backdrop of books and a French flag. Some 22% told an Ifop poll within 24 hours they "could" vote for him.

Teddy Riner's video has attracted 14.5 million views on Instagram alone

Actors and television personalities have become presidents in other countries. The ex-leader of Liberia – George Weah – was formerly a professional footballer.

So why not a judoka in the Élysée Palace?

"Anyone who thinks that being out of the political in-crowd disqualifies Riner from running for the Élysée would be very wrong," says Guillaume Tabard of Le Figaro.

"But [Riner] too would be wrong if he thinks not belonging to the in-crowd is all it takes."

For now the whole of the French political world has decided to take the Riner candidacy seriously – or at least to pretend to. That is partly because he is such a popular personality that mocking his political hopes could easily rebound badly.

But it is also because the state of French politics – outside of the burgeoning forces of the hard left and hard right – is one of total disarray.

The centre-ground is floundering, with no candidate yet emerging who can inspire anything like the sense of mission of hard-right leader Marine Le Pen and Jean-Luc Mélenchon on the hard left, who for now look set to face off in the final round of the presidential election in May.

So when a popular figure like Riner enters the race - proclaiming himself "neither left, nor right", wanting to "unite the country" and "put money back in people's pockets", railing equally against "racists" and "yobs who scare people off our streets" – politicians have to take note.

Hard-right leader Marine Le Pen currently leads the polls in the race to be France's next president

It is perfectly possible, probable even, that Riner's campaign will fizzle out after a brief period of hype, and that the judoka will after all be a joker in the pack. But it is also possible that it won't, in which case the pre-election arithmetic will need a hasty readjustment: and it won't be the centrists who are smiling.

Thus far, Riner has shown himself a master of the codes required for this kind of out-of-nowhere candidacy, the first of which is to press home the message: "Don't Worry! I'm NOT a Politician!"

In this day and age in France, anyone who smacks of the "system" is automatically downgraded in voters' eyes, so it is important to emphasise that you are only running for office because, one, you have experienced real life (unlike those loafers in Paris); and two, you have discovered that there are solutions out there for the country's many problems. Solutions that are invisible to those same blinkered apparatchiks.

All this Riner was able to express in last Monday's social media broadcast by using sophisticated rhetorical devices.

"People say I am a fool for wanting to run for the presidency," he said.

"Am I a fool? Well, if refusing to see France sink under the weight of debt; refusing to see mothers and fathers grit their teeth every time they do their weekly shop, and tremble with fear when their kids go out on the street… if all that means being a fool, then yes call me a fool."

It was a promising oratorial start for the sportsman, and certainly attracted the viewers.

Are student protests being manipulated ahead of France's presidential election?

France's Marine Le Pen, fighting court conviction and running for presidency

But if he is serious – and Riner says he never does anything half-heartedly - that's not how he became an Olympic champion – then the hard work begins now.

What does Riner actually want to do? Who will be on his team? Where does he position himself on the all-consuming matters of the day: pension-reform,  investment in education, the cost of living, public debt, the rise of populism or Russia's war in Ukraine?

In short, how does he intend to transform his undeniable popularity as a sporting figure into a political mandate?

Protesters have for weeks taken to the streets in France over wages, the cost of living and public services

Broadly, Riner appears to be on the right on economic matters and law and order, but being black and of Caribbean background he is also very strong on racism. When he says he is anti-extremism, he is referring mainly to Marine Le Pen.

In other words his pitch is somewhere in the centre, and against the extremes.

The trouble is, this is already an extremely crowded area, with important figures like ex-prime ministers Edouard Philippe and Gabriel Attal signally failing to take off.

Currently there are a dozen or so candidates in the area between centre right and centre left, stretching from the Socialist-backed Raphaël Glucksman to the Republicans' Bruno Retailleau on the right.

The latest possible addition is Christine Lagarde, who steps down as head of the European Central Bank next February.

President Emmanuel Macron is among the few politicians who appears genuinely pleased by Riner's decision to run

The addition of yet another contender will dilute their polling numbers even further, making a second-round qualification for Mélenchon more likely.

So no wonder the leader of France Unbowed (LFI) seemed so happy about Riner's decision to run. "We know how it goes: neither right nor left means not left," Mélenchon told reporters on Friday.

The only other politician who seems genuinely pleased, rather than putting on a fixed smile, is President Emmanuel Macron, who said Riner was a "great champion" and that politics "did not belong to the professionals".

That could be explained by the president's cool relations with his former prime ministers, Philippe and Attal, both of whom are doing all they can to distance themselves from their unpopular one-time boss.

Riner said he viewed Macron's praise as a "poisoned chalice", telling reporters on Saturday that he was "not the president's envoy, I'm not a Macronist".

Politics and judo have very little in common, but of the two, as Riner will soon discover, the more vicious is not the one that is fought out hand-to-hand after mutual acknowledgement on the tatami mat.

In Japanese, judo actually means "the gentle way".

If he starts looking like a serious candidate, Riner must know his life will be turned upside down, not just his physical form.

In politics you do not bow in respect to your opponent. You give him a metaphorical headbutt.

French wartime resistance heroine Solange Alexandre dies aged 104

Inside the French drug gangs recruiting children to kill

French protests see numbers surge as unions join strikes over high cost of living

articles.title: Tennessee Volunteers overcome sluggish offense, jet lag to take down Texas A&M and keep CFP hopes alive
articles.excerpt:
Craig Carton calls out the debut College Football Playoff rankings, exposing glaring SEC brand bias and demanding to know how Alabama landed at No. 5 despite a loss to No. 13 Tennessee.

Last week, th...
articles.body_text:
Craig Carton calls out the debut College Football Playoff rankings, exposing glaring SEC brand bias and demanding to know how Alabama landed at No. 5 despite a loss to No. 13 Tennessee.

Last week, the Tennessee Volunteers needed a fourth quarter explosion to put the Kentucky Wildcats away.

History repeated itself seven days later in College Station, as the Vols overcame a sluggish first half and a quarterback injury to vanquish Texas A&M on the road and keep their College Football Playoff hopes alive.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Before we go any further, it's important we address the elephant in the room, and that is the FAA ground stop.

FAA GROUND STOP LIFTED ON FRIDAY NIGHT, BUT SOME COLLEGE FOOTBALL TEAMS STILL SCRAMBLING TO TRAVEL

Tennessee head coach Josh Heupel at the Vol Walk before the Orange & White spring game, Saturday, April 12, 2025. (IMAGN)

Although Tennessee coach Josh Heupel likely won't admit it, his team's late arrival in the Lone Star State may have contributed to their sleepy start on offense.

The Vols arrived at the team hotel just before 1 a.m. local time, likely offering an explanation for the lack of fireworks on offense.

Luckily for Heupel, his defense was up for the challenge, harassing Aggies quarterback Marcel Reed all afternoon to the tune of just 71 yards passing.

The Aggies could only muster one touchdown the entire game and were held to only 179 total yards.

UPDATED START TIMES FOR COLLEGE FOOTBALL GAMES AFFECTED BY FAA GROUND STOP, BROKEN DOWN BY CONFERENCE

KJ Edwards No. 0 of the Texas A&M Aggies rushes during the first quarter against the Tennessee Volunteers at Kyle Field in College Station, Texas, on Nov. 14, 2026. (Getty Images)

It's been a hard fall for Texas A&M, who began the season as a top-10 team before falling out of the AP top-25 entirely.

Saturday's loss has the Aggies in danger of missing a bowl game, and they still have a showdown with a surging Texas squad to end the season.

For the Vols, a letdown almost surely would have meant the end of their CFP aspirations, as a third loss could have put those dreams on life support.

Things looked bleak until, ironically, Tennessee was bit with the injury bug when starting quarterback George MacIntyre went out midway through the third quarter.

From that point, the Vols remembered they could run the ball and run it quite well at that, rushing for 196 yards on the day and holding the ball for over 42 minutes.

Arion Carter No. 7 and Jeremiah Telander No. 22 of the Tennessee Volunteers react to a play during the first half at Kyle Field on Nov. 14, 2026, in College Station, Texas. (ISI Photos via Getty Images)

If Tennessee can replicate this formula of salty defense and controlling the time of possession, they will be a hard out in December and beyond.

With that in mind, the Vols have a date with the LSU Tigers next Saturday before a road game in Nashville against rival Vanderbilt.

If they can navigate that stretch undefeated, they will be a shoo-in to make the CFP.

Once they make it, I doubt anyone will want to play this version of Tennessee.

articles.title: Netanyahu says only a unity government can guarantee Israel’s security
articles.excerpt:
Israeli caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has renewed his call for a national unity government with his rival, Gadi Eisenkot, saying only such a government can guarantee Israel’s security.

...
articles.body_text:
Israeli caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has renewed his call for a national unity government with his rival, Gadi Eisenkot, saying only such a government can guarantee Israel’s security.

In a video statement on Saturday, Netanyahu said a meeting with Eisenkot on Thursday “only strengthened the conviction that it is essential to form a national unity government”.

The prime minister said such a government could “eliminate the Iranian threat once and for all”, claiming Tehran would “not hesitate to use nuclear weapons against us”.

“Let’s meet in one room, without preconditions,” he said.

Within minutes, however, Eisenkot dismissed the appeal as a ploy.

A former army chief, Eisenkot said Netanyahu “knows he lost the election”.

“Netanyahu is calling for negotiations while they are already underway,” he said. “These tricks don’t work on me.”

Neither side won a majority in the October 27 election. Netanyahu’s right-wing and religious bloc took 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, Eisenkot’s four-party bloc got 48 seats, and Arab-led parties won a record 19.

President Isaac Herzog last week tasked Eisenkot with forming a government, after 67 lawmakers, including those from Arab-led parties, endorsed him, while 46 backed Netanyahu.

Eisenkot has 28 days, with a possible 14-day extension. He has ruled out including Arab-led parties in his government.

Under Eisenkot’s plan for a minority “national emergency government”, his bloc’s 48 lawmakers would vote in favour against the 46 Netanyahu supporters, while the 26 lawmakers from Arab and ultra-Orthodox parties could abstain. It would allow his government to be approved without an absolute majority in the Knesset.

Netanyahu has warned that such a government would lead to Israel’s “collapse”.

Netanyahu’s version would include Jewish parties from the centre and the right and exclude Arab parties. He and his allies have made unsubstantiated claims that Arab-led parties “stole” the election.

On Friday, Eisenkot called Netanyahu’s campaign against them “racist”.

Eisenkot has said he could work with members of Netanyahu’s Likud party and with Bezalel Smotrich’s Religious Zionism if their commitment to unity is “sincere”, but he insisted on a “break with the extremists”, notably supporters of far-right minister Itamar Ben-Gvir.

The Knesset will elect its speaker on Tuesday. The post is currently held by Netanyahu ally Amir Ohana, and the opposition has put forward Matan Kahana, a former military officer, in his place.

articles.title: Kathy Ireland’s husband escapes burning boat after engine explodes 20 miles offshore
articles.excerpt:
Kathy Ireland described the working dynamic between herself and her husband while working together on his commercial fishing boat.

Kathy Ireland is thankful after her husband narrowly escaped a fire ...
articles.body_text:
Kathy Ireland described the working dynamic between herself and her husband while working together on his commercial fishing boat.

Kathy Ireland is thankful after her husband narrowly escaped a fire that engulfed his boat while he was alone at sea.

In a recent Instagram post, the 63-year-old actress shared video of husband Dr. Greg Olsen's boat, the 4th Watch, engulfed in flames. Ireland said Olsen was out alone on the water while she was away on business.

"Life is really hard and really beautiful. God is great," she wrote. "Engine exploded and a fire quickly melted all navigation equipment and survival raft!"

She then thanked everyone "who prayed and continue to pray" for her husband, as well as all "those who aided in the rescue," including "@towboatus_ventura and the entire community" for their quick response.

KATHY IRELAND REVEALS 'BIG RED FLAG' THAT EXPOSED ALLEGED $100M 'UNCONSCIONABLE' BETRAYAL

Ireland said she is thankful for those who helped her husband survive the ordeal. (Michael Tullberg/Getty Images)

"Most of all, we thank our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ for this miracle of his survival," she added.

Ireland also shared a note she wrote to her husband following the incident, saying her "heart is both heavy and full" because she knows how much "love, sweat and life you poured into this vessel."

Ireland shared a message for her husband in her Instagram post. (Rebecca Sapp/Getty Images for Santa Barbara International Film Festival)

"This vessel brought so much joy and so many blessings to our family and countless others," she continued.

"My heart is heavy with yours. This is more than a boat, there are many implications. My heart is mostly full. Full because of the outpouring of love and support. Multitudes were praying for you! I’m so thankful to all who rushed to pray and come to your rescue."

Ireland credited God with Olsen's survival. (Arturo Holmes/Getty Images)

"I’m so thankful God gifted you with a brilliant mind to navigate this disaster so seamlessly," she added. "I’m eternally thankful to Him for loving and rescuing you. Though the vessel is no more, the 4th Watch is forever. You named that boat so profoundly. He has so much ahead for you! I’m so proud of you."

WATCH: KATHY IRELAND SHARES THE LESSONS SHE'S LEARNED FROM WORKING AS A COMMERCIAL FISHERMAN

Fans in the comments section shared well-wishes for Ireland and Olsen, with some recounting their own experiences with losing their belongings due to a fire.

Fans in the comments section sent Ireland and her husband their well-wishes. (Rebecca Sapp/Getty Images for SBIFF)

"Unbelievable!!! I’m SO grateful your husband is ok," one fan wrote. "🙏 And having parents who lost their home in a fire I completely understand your sadness about the loss of the boat. "

"Oh my! I am so glad he is safe," another added. "The boat and gear is replaceable, but the emotions are real. So sorry!!!!" A third follower wrote, "So sorry to hear this, BUT, Thankful to God that he saved your Precious One!"

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

The TowBoatUS Ventura Instagram account also shared video of the fire and its aftermath, saying the company received a call about the fire around 3 p.m. on Wednesday afternoon, noting the vessel was "20 nautical miles west of Santa Barbara Harbor."

In its post, TowBoatUS Ventura credited Olsen for his quick thinking, noting that he "was prepared and did everything right." They wrote that he initially "attempted to extinguish the fire before ultimately activating his EPIRB and abandoning ship into a kayak."

The TowBoatUS Ventura Instagram account also shared photos of the fire on their page. (Alberto E. Rodriguez/Getty Images)

"This was about as good an outcome as one could hope for in an otherwise serious emergency," the message read. "A well-prepared mariner, good samaritans nearby, and commercial vessels equipped and ready to respond made all the difference. It is a great reminder of the importance of preparedness, cooperation, and the maritime community looking out for one another."

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

Olsen and Ireland tied the knot in August 1988 in San Diego, California, and share three children: Erik, 32, Lily, 27, and Chloe, 23.

Ireland and Olsen tied the knot in August 1988. (John G. Zimmerman /Sports Illustrated via Getty Images)

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

They celebrated their 38th wedding anniversary this year, with Ireland paying tribute to him on Instagram.

"Life with you is an awesome adventure! Our secret to our lasting love is no secret at all. It’s God’s design. He is at the center of our marriage and it is He who equips us to see each other through His eyes. My respect and love for you is bigger than life! It’s a privilege to experience God working through you in such powerful ways! Your character, courage and conviction are beautiful! I love you always, Your forever and only First Mate❤️."

Lori A. Bashian is an entertainment news writer at Fox News Digital.

articles.title: David Jones’ future looks grim. Is Myer next?
articles.excerpt:
With Myer’s profitability battered and share price languishing near all-time lows, DJs’ slide into administration raises an uncomfortable question

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news ...
articles.body_text:
With Myer’s profitability battered and share price languishing near all-time lows, DJs’ slide into administration raises an uncomfortable question

Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

When the retailer’s doors slide open, shoppers are greeted by rows of slashed price tags, frantic discounting, and all the other hallmarks of a department store closing down.

Except, this isn’t David Jones, the embattled upmarket retailer that is shutting half its 38 stores.

This is its longtime rival, Myer, where entire floors are seemingly permanently on sale.

With Myer’s profitability battered and share price languishing near all-time lows, DJs’ slide into administration raises an uncomfortable question: is Myer next?

At first glance, Myer’s headline numbers seem to defy the retail gloom, with double-digit sales growth to $4.1bn last financial year.

That lift, however, was not driven by surging demand, but by adding sales from the newly acquired apparel chains, Just Jeans, Jay Jays, Portmans, Dotti and Jacqui E, bought from billionaire businessman Solomon Lew’s Premier Investments.

Meanwhile, to keep registers ringing, Myer employed “higher than planned promotional activity to stimulate demand”, according to its annual report, which reduced its profitability.

The department store has also slashed the value of its brands, down more than $200m in one year alone, in an admission that its labels are worth far less than they once were.

Department stores have faced a “sustained erosion of relevance over the past five years”, according to IBISWorld market researchers, as online platforms win over bargain-hunters and specialists like beauty retailer Mecca prove more nimble in capturing shifting tastes.

DJs and Myer, on the other hand, have been weighed down by long-running physical property leases tied to underperforming stores in their sprawling networks.

The era of Australian families being fiercely loyal to either David Jones or Myer is long gone, replaced by a grim battle for both chains to stay relevant.

The stress on big department store profitability has been exacerbated by a period of cost of living pressures that have “entrenched deal-hunting behaviour, reshaping how and when consumers engage with department stores”, according to IBISWorld.

Myer, however, has a critical advantage over David Jones: time.

While DJs fell into administration under mounting debts, Myer finished last financial year with a $100m net cash buffer, buying management breathing space to fix the business.

It has been reducing store numbers and with it lease liabilities – down to 56 stores from 60 before the pandemic – which is something David Jones is only doing now that it has collapsed into administration.

For the moment, Myer is leaning into the discounts demanded by shoppers, in the hope that more profitable trading conditions will emerge.

Richard Hemming, the editor at Under The Radar Report, says in retail “volume is everything”.

“If you get the volumes through, that customer base will eventually be in a position to pay more, and when volumes and margins both improve, you get that double effect,” Hemming says.

While analysts have mixed views on whether permanent discounting is a smart survival tactic or a slow-motion way to go bankrupt, department stores do need to move huge volumes of stock to keep cash flowing and clear seasonal goods.

They can use those discounts to get more people signed up to their loyalty programs – such as the successful Myer One program – in the hope they will become long term customers.

Hemming sees the upside in Myer’s current pain, noting the retailer is “cleaning house earlier than rivals” precisely because investors have long priced it “like it’s going to go broke”.

Myer is revamping the business to aggressively pursue online sales.

Myer shares have been heavily sold down over the years, and now hover around the 24c mark, representing a fraction of its $4.10 float price from 2009.

It did, however, receive a price bump on the day DJs fell into administration.

With roughly two in five Myer stores sharing a shopping centre with a David Jones outlet, investors are betting the coming closure of 19 DJs sites will hand Myer an easy market-share boost, even as its own long-term turnaround demands further store cuts.

In the short term, the pain is likely to intensify for Myer as the David Jones stores marked for closure are under orders to clear stock with widespread promotions, luring customers.

Broader retail sentiment is also souring, as a string of interest rate rises and escalating cost-of-living pressures force cash-strapped shoppers to pare their discretionary spend.

The Retail Doctor Group’s chief executive, Brian Walker, says the main long-term advantage Myer has over its old rival is financial flexibility.

“Whereas David Jones was incredibly encumbered, Myer doesn’t have that issue right now,” Walker says.

“As we sit here today, Myer is financially stronger, but strategically still pretty vulnerable.”

articles.title: Kai Trump opens up about relationship with Tiger Woods, her mother's boyfriend: 'I love him so much'
articles.excerpt: Kai Trump, Donald Trump's granddaughter, shares her journey on 'Fox & Friends,' detailing her success in golf, her burgeoning social media presence and her impending enrollment at the University of Mi...
articles.body_text:
Kai Trump, Donald Trump's granddaughter, shares her journey on 'Fox & Friends,' detailing her success in golf, her burgeoning social media presence and her impending enrollment at the University of Miami to play golf. She candidly discusses balancing her personal life, studies and athletic commitments, while reflecting on her mother's ongoing breast cancer recovery. Trump highlights her competitive spirit, attributing it to her grandfather.

Kai Trump is getting some pretty good golf advice.

The 19-year-old's freshman season at the University of Miami was halted last month after she was forced to undergo another wrist surgery. But surely, her source of information has dealt with his fair share of injuries.

That, of course, is Tiger Woods, who is dating Trump's mother, Vanessa. Vanessa is the ex-wife of Donald Trump Jr.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE

Kai Trump (L) and Tiger Woods arrive to the course during the final round of The Genesis Invitational 2025 at Torrey Pines Golf Course on February 16, 2025 in La Jolla, California. (Michael Owens/Getty Images)

Trump and the 15-time major champion hard-launched their relationship in March of last year.

"He's the best. I love him so much, and he's a great guy, and he helps me whenever I want," the president's granddaughter said to Golfweek.

Shortly after Woods was arrested on charges of DUI, Vanessa Trump showed support for her boyfriend.

"Love you," Vanessa Trump wrote over a picture of herself hugging Woods as the two appeared to relax on a hammock. The photo, posted to her Instagram Stories early Friday morning, was the same photo Woods shared on X when he first announced his relationship with her.

Tiger's son, Charlie, and Kai Trump played at a tournament together at the 2025 Junior Invitational.

Kai Trump and her mother, Vanessa Trump, girlfriend of Tiger Woods, of Jupiter Links GC, look on after a match between Jupiter Links and Boston Common Golf Club at the SoFi Center in Palm Beach Gardens, Florida, on March 17, 2026. (James Gilbert/TGL/TGL Golf via Getty Images)

KAI TRUMP RECALLS ‘A LOT OF CRYING’ WITH MOM VANESSA BEFORE COLLEGE AMID BREAST CANCER BATTLE

After his highly publicized divorce from Elin Nordegren, Woods was linked to Olympic skier Lindsey Vonn in the 2010s. He was dating Erica Herman at the time he won the Masters in 2019, but they, too, had a very public breakup that included sexual harassment allegations and an NDA lawsuit filed by Herman.

Woods and Nordegren have appeared to be amicable in recent years, as they co-parent Charlie and Sam Woods. The two were recently together at Charlie's high school where he officially signed to play college golf at Florida State.

Woods has played in just 18 events since the start of the new decade, and his best finish in a major during that span is a tie for 38th at the 2020 Masters.

Tiger's return to the golf course remains to be determined — he has not played since the 2024 Open Championship. When he was arrested in March, he said he was "hoping to" play in April's Masters, but he ultimately missed the entire 2026 season.

Vanessa Trump, girlfriend of Tiger Woods of Jupiter Links GC and her daughter Kai Trump talk with Woods before a match against The Bay Golf Club at SoFi Center on March 3, 2026, in Palm Beach Gardens, Florida. (Cliff Hawkins/TGL/TGL Golf via Getty Images)

As for Kai Trump, it's not yet known when she'll return to the golf course, either.

articles.title: Explosion near Syria’s capital kills father and child
articles.excerpt:
Deadly car bomb blast kills two near Syria's capital

A blast from a suspected explosive device planted inside a car in a suburb of the Syrian capital, Damascus, has killed at least two people, includ...
articles.body_text:
Deadly car bomb blast kills two near Syria's capital

A blast from a suspected explosive device planted inside a car in a suburb of the Syrian capital, Damascus, has killed at least two people, including a child, and wounded one.

The explosion in Jaramana, on the southeastern edge of Damascus, on Saturday killed a man and his daughter, while a third person, said to be the wife of the man, was seriously injured.

Syria’s Internal Security Forces said they sealed off the area and opened an investigation into the circumstances surrounding the blast.

Jaramana is home to a large community of the Druze religious minority and has seen tensions between some Druze members and the Sunni majority backing President Ahmed al-Sharaa’s government.

Witnesses described the vehicle as a Kia Rio parked between two apartment buildings in Jaramana, which is largely considered a quiet residential area, said Al Jazeera’s Heidi Pett, reporting from the blast scene.

Pett said the security situation in the capital remains complex, despite improvements since the regime of former President Bashar al-Assad fell two years ago.

“In the last couple of months, there were two very high-profile incidents,” she said, including a double-tap attack in July during French President Emmanuel Macron’s visit, which Syrian authorities attributed to a cell affiliated with ISIL (ISIS).

“There was also a deadly attack on what’s known as the Lawyer’s Cafe, near the Palace of Justice, which has been the scene of these high-profile trials of former members of the Assad regime,” Pett said.

She added that most of the bombings and security incidents have not necessarily targeted civilians but members and locations of security forces, which authorities have also blamed on ISIL.

Last year, Damascus joined the US-led international coalition against ISIL. The coalition was formed in 2014 and has carried out operations against the group in Syria and Iraq.

On September 27, the security forces said they had arrested four members of an ISIL cell involved in planning and carrying out several attacks in different parts of the country.

Last month, Syria’s security forces said they foiled a plot to target a police patrol in the Damascus countryside, saying an ISIL cell was preparing to carry out the attack, Syrian state television reported.

They said the group was responsible for explosions and assassinations in Raqqa, Aleppo, Idlib and Homs.

articles.title: SpaceX’s Starship returns to launch pad from orbit in victory for company
articles.excerpt:
Although booster exploded, company caught upper stage for first time in campaign to make megarocket reusable

SpaceX’s megarocket Starship returned to its Texas launch tower on Saturday, a milestone i...
articles.body_text:
Although booster exploded, company caught upper stage for first time in campaign to make megarocket reusable

SpaceX’s megarocket Starship returned to its Texas launch tower on Saturday, a milestone in the company’s efforts to make the craft suitable for human spaceflight.

The 171ft (52-meter) bullet-shaped upper stage descended into the clutch of the tower’s mechanical arms, ending a 22hr mission where the craft orbited Earth 14 times.

Starship’s 15th test flight was envisioned as a historic double-catch mission, where all parts of the rocket would be returned intact to the launch site, rather than recovered from the sea as with some previous test flights.

The hulking spacecraft is composed of two parts: a lower booster stage called Super Heavy, whose Raptor engines powered the orbital ascent, and an upper stage also called Starship.

Those double-catch ambitions were dashed on Friday, when the booster diverted a few minutes after takeoff and exploded in the Gulf of Mexico.

The guidance, navigation and control (GNC) system triggered the no-go.

“It was doing what it was supposed to do. Basically, it detected that the booster was not in the place it was supposed to be to proceed with a catch,” SpaceX spokesperson Dan Huot said early on Saturday.

This week’s test flight was still a victory for SpaceX, marking the first time that the company caught its upper stage.

The feat comes as the 2028 date nears for Nasa’s plan to return humans to the lunar surface. The agency has contracted SpaceX and Jeff Bezos’s Blue Origin for the mission.

SpaceX has plans to ramp up its Starship test flights to a weekly, then twice-weekly cadence, chief executive Elon Musk said on a recent earnings call. He has sought to make Starship rapidly reusable so that it can land and take off much like standard airplanes.

Beyond another Moon landing, Musk has also pushed a plan of carrying humans to Mars.

articles.title: Fetterman warns there is no longer 'common ground' with far-left Democrats over Israel
articles.excerpt: Senator John Fetterman joins 'Saturday in America' for his first interview since the midterms. Fetterman discusses the rise of far-left candidates in the Democratic Party, potential investigations and...
articles.body_text:
Senator John Fetterman joins 'Saturday in America' for his first interview since the midterms. Fetterman discusses the rise of far-left candidates in the Democratic Party, potential investigations and facing primary challenges.

Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., told Fox News on Saturday that he no longer sees "any more common ground" with the far-left wing of his party over its stance on Israel.

During an appearance on "Saturday in America," Fetterman criticized efforts to replace Senate Democratic Leader Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., with Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., and called his new 2028 Democratic primary challenger "pro-Hamas."

"I have a strong, strong difference of opinion on Israel and the Jewish community overall now. I don't think there's going to be any more common ground," Fetterman told Fox News host Kayleigh McEnany.

FETTERMAN REVEALS WHAT IT WOULD TAKE FOR HIM TO LEAVE DEMOCRATIC PARTY

Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., speaks to reporters as he arrives at the U.S. Capitol for a vote on July 16, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

"Now I think if someone can't identify [that] Iran is an enemy, and that it's committed to destroying Israel and our nation as well, too — once again, this is the kind of individual that the Democratic Party elected," he added.

Following midterm elections that saw Democrats regain control of both the House and Senate, Schumer is facing a challenge to his leadership. Van Hollen announced his bid to replace Schumer on Thursday, with support from progressive lawmakers, including Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, D-Mich.

DEMOCRATS TURN ON SCHUMER AFTER HISTORIC ELECTION WINS AS POTENTIAL CHALLENGER EMERGES

Fetterman said a Van Hollen victory would be troubling.

"It would be troubling if my caucus elects someone like Van Hollen, that has really made his name being very... hostile to Israel," Fetterman said when asked if a Van Hollen win would cross a "red line."

Sen. John Fetterman, D-Pa., departs the U.S. Capitol following the passage of a reconciliation package on June 5, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Nathan Posner/Anadolu via Getty Images)

SCHUMER'S FORMER ALLY MOUNTS LEADERSHIP CHALLENGE AS DEMOCRATS FACE RARE INTERNAL POWER STRUGGLE

Fetterman said Van Hollen has made his name on strong "anti-Israel" views and also received attention after his high-profile trip to El Salvador to meet with Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Salvadoran migrant deported by the Trump administration.

"Other than that, I can’t really think of what Van Hollen's known for, but he became like a progressive darling, but I don't see that he has a path to be leader, but overall it's possible because just last weekend I had a lot of people protesting, demanding that we vote against Schumer," Fetterman said.

BITTER FETTERMAN-EL-SAYED FEUD THREATENS TO COMPLICATE SCHUMER'S SENATE UNITY PUSH

"We have to find a way forward. After our massive wins, we immediately go back to fighting amongst ourselves. Can't we just, you know, take the win?" he added.

Fetterman also called for bipartisan cooperation on the national debt, artificial intelligence, Iran and Social Security, expressing hope that Democrats could work with the White House.

Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., speaks during the What's Next conference on Nov. 13, 2026, in Denver, Colo. The event brought together Democrats to discuss the party's priorities and direction ahead of the 2028 elections. (Chet Strange/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"My hope [is] that our party doesn't revert to our worst impulses. I am going to extend and just hope for bipartisan solutions and work with the White House if that's possible. That's where my votes will be," Fetterman said.

Fetterman also criticized Gaza-born Palestinian-American writer and activist Ahmed Moor, who announced a 2028 Democratic primary challenge against him earlier in the week.

FETTERMAN RECEIVES NO SUPPORT FOR RE-ELECTION FROM PENNSYLVANIA HOUSE DEMOCRATS: REPORT

"This is someone that is very proud, very proud, pro-Hamas, and there are parts of my Democratic base [that] find my views more troubling or offensive, my strong support of Israel versus his views," Fetterman said.

"I'm always going to support Israel. Iran knows that the Democratic Party, it's very unlikely they're [going to] hold the Iranian regime accountable. I think we deserve to have that conversation," he added.

FETTERMAN WINS PRAISE FOR 'GUTS' AFTER GOING TOE-TO-TOE WITH JON STEWART OVER ISRAEL SUPPORT

In a statement to Fox News Digital, Moor's campaign pushed back on Fetterman's remarks, saying the candidate "condemns violence against civilians by anyone" and accusing the Pennsylvania senator of failing to represent his constituents.

"Ahmed Moor is running on a platform of dignity, justice, and the rule of law. This includes ensuring that American tax dollars are spent in ways that benefit Americans, not on killing innocent people abroad. These views are in line with the majority of Pennsylvanians, who Fetterman has failed to accurately represent in Congress," the campaign said.

The campaign added that Moor supports "an arms embargo and targeted sanctions until Palestinians have equal rights," saying he would "fight antisemitism and anti-Palestinian racism with the same conviction."

Fox News Digital reached out to Van Hollen for comment.

Madison Colombo is a writer for Fox News Digital’s Flash, Media, and Culture team, covering daily breaking news and trending topics with an award-winning background in broadcast and digital journalism.
